10620-the-works-of-francis-beaumont-and-:
Francis Beaumont, born in 1584, and John Fletcher, born in 1579, were leading English playwrights of the age of Shakespeare. Arnold Glover edited this first volume of their collected works. It gathers five plays: The Maid's Tragedy, Philaster, A King and No King, The Scornful Lady, and The Custom of the Country. The edition also notes their first collected printing in 1647.

The plays mix tragedy, comedy, and romance, with plots built on love, honor, kingship, and betrayal. Beaumont died in 1616 and Fletcher in 1625, but their joint plays stayed popular on stage for generations. This volume lets a reader meet two major Jacobean voices side by side, in texts shaped by careful editing.
11086-a-surgeon-in-belgium:
H. S. Souttar, assistant surgeon at West London Hospital and surgeon-in-chief of a Belgian field hospital, wrote this memoir of the First World War's opening weeks. Souttar sailed for Ostend one Saturday in September, thrilled to see war for himself and to care for the wounded. He lived through the siege of Antwerp, worked close to the firing line, and saw a cruiser sunk by a submarine.

Souttar insists that battles frame, but do not fill, the picture: fugitives' weary faces and a child's cry outlast shells and sinkings. Chapters follow the hospital, Termonde, Malines, the bombardment by night and day, a night journey, Furnes, and Ypres. The book gives a surgeon's humane view of war's first months, attentive to suffering civilians as well as soldiers.
12388-the-courage-of-captain-plum:
James Oliver Curwood published The Courage of Captain Plum in 1912, illustrated by Frank E. Schoonover. Curwood, a Michigan adventure writer, sets the novel on Lake Michigan in the early summer of 1856.

Captain Nathaniel Plum, master and owner of the sloop Typhoon, smokes an enormous pipe as the story opens. He then becomes entangled with the Mormon kingdom on Beaver Island and a woman in danger. Chapters follow two oaths, a whipping post, and a ship that may or may not bombard St. James. A mid-book scene has Plum learn his ship is not bombarding at all, a dash of cold water to his heroics. The novel mixes history with romance and lake adventure.
14268-historia-calamitatum:
Peter Abélard's Historia Calamitatum, translated by Henry Adams Bellows, tells the story of his misfortunes in his own voice. The medieval scholar, famed for logic and teaching, recounts persecutions by rivals, condemnations of his thought, and enemies among monks and churchmen. Philosophical reflection frames the narrative, as Abélard weighs faith, reason, and the monastic life against worldly pleasure.

St. Gildas in Brittany supplies the darkest chapter. Called as abbot after a shepherd's death, Abélard finds monks more savage than heathens and worse in life, plotting against him while he seeks refuge among enemies of Christ. Earlier passages praise Nazarites, philosophers, and saints set apart by continence and abstinence from worldly joys. Love, pride, and learning collide throughout, and the autobiography remains a firsthand window onto twelfth-century intellect and its perils.
14732-the-adventures-of-unc-billy-possum:
Thornton W. Burgess tells bedtime stories of Unc' Billy Possum and the animal folk of the Green Forest and Green Meadows. The book opens with Unc' Billy caught, Reddy Fox thinking he sees a ghost, and Unc' Billy sending for his family.

Bobby Coon enters the wrong house, Sammy Jay learns Peter Rabbit's secret, four little scamps plan mischief, and a runaway cabbage causes chaos. Prickly Porky, Mr. Toad and Old Mrs. Possum join the fun, while hunger and foolishness keep Unc' Billy from going home. Illustrated by Harrison Cady, the tales teach woodland habits gently, with humour and a nightly sense of adventure.
15726-the-camp-fire-girls-on-the-farm-or:
The second Camp Fire Girls book, by Jane L. Stewart, issued by Saalfield in 1914. Bessie King and her chum Zara visit the home of Eleanor Mercer, Guardian of the Manasquan Camp Fire. Stewart writes for girls who joined the Camp Fire movement, with its badges, laws, and outdoor work. The farm setting gives room for chores, friendship, and small adventures.

Bessie meets a new chum on the farm and faces Farmer Weeks, whose evil eyes greet her in the frontispiece. City comforts give way to farm work, camp craft, and honest talk. The girls learn to help, to endure, and to keep the Camp Fire spirit. The book charms as a period girls' tale: wholesome, busy, and warm about friendship.
1600-symposium:
Plato's Symposium, translated by Benjamin Jowett, is the most perfect in form of all Plato's works, and may contain more than any commentator has dreamed, or than the author himself knew. At a drinking party in Athens, guests take turns praising love, from Phaedrus to Socrates, who reports the priestess Diotima's ladder of love.

Through wine, wit, and Alcibiades' drunken entrance, the dialogue rises from bodies to beauty itself. Its speeches are among the finest in Greek prose. The Symposium is essential Plato, and one of the great books on love in any language.
18230-how-to-write-a-play-letters-from-a:
How to Write a Play gathers letters from French masters of the stage, printed for the Dramatic Museum of Columbia University in 1916. The set opens with Émile Augier, writing to Dreyfus on the recipe for comedies.

Augier jokes that making a play is like making a cannon: take a hole and pour bronze round it, or take bronze and make a hole through the center. Banville adds Dennery's dictum that success is easy, but success with a fine play is hard. The letters are short, witty, and wise. They give a charming, practical glimpse of the playwright's craft.
18398-diary-written-in-the-provincial-lu:
Mary Huestis Pengilly published this diary in 1885, written in the Provincial Lunatic Asylum. Pengilly, in the sixty-second year of her age, dedicates the little book to New Brunswick and Massachusetts. Driven from her home by the St. John fire of 1877, she found refuge in Massachusetts, and she writes to show the inner workings of hospitals and asylums, hoping readers will seek better methods for superintendent and patient alike.

Her entries record small, telling details. She begs for milk and is told there is not enough for all the old women. She insists she knows what nourishing food she needs to build herself up again. The diary opens with the line, the prison doors are open, I am free. Readers get a rare first-person record of asylum life, written to move the public toward kinder care.
1843-vera-the-medium:
A newspaper, the Despatch, throws the name and portrait of Stephen Hallowell across three columns with the words 'At Point of Death. ', and Vera, the medium of the title, claims a woman stands close beside him, holding out her arms and trying hard to speak. She tells a girl of the message, and doubt over whether her gift is real hangs over everything that follows.

The novel follows Vera through séances, society, and the question of whether her gift is real or a performance. Davis writes the spiritualist world of his day with a reporter's curiosity. The book's tension lies in Vera's own doubt: a woman who may be deceiving others, herself, or no one at all.
18959-a-journal-from-our-legation-in-bel:
Hugh Gibson, secretary of the American Legation in Brussels, published this journal in 1917, illustrated from photographs. It records his work in Belgium at the outbreak of the First World War. German forces had invaded a neutral country, and the American legation became a center of relief, protest, and negotiation. A portrait of King Albert of the Belgians fronts the volume.

Gibson reproduces documents of the crisis, including the German ultimatum to Belgium and passes issued by Belgian military authorities. Day by day entries show diplomats coping with invasion, refugees, and broken communications. Readers get a firsthand account of August 1914 from inside a small neutral capital, vivid on both high diplomacy and daily strain.
19498-banzai-by-parabellum:
Parabellum wrote this war novel of a future clash between Japan and America, published in Leipzig and New York in the late nineteen hundreds. The action opens in Manila and on the high seas. Then it moves to New York, the Golden Gate, and a sea fight off the coast, where the Japanese ship Satsuma takes fire.

Chapters on fathers and sons, admirals' fates, and forty-eight hours of balance give the tale a human frame for its fleet action. As a work of invasion fiction, it shows pre-war fears in raw form, and it reads today as a warning about how easily rivalry turns to war talk.
19692-peeps-at-many-lands-belgium:
George W. T. Omond wrote this children's book on Belgium for the Peeps at Many Lands series, published in London in the early nineteen hundreds with pictures by Amedee Forestier. It travels from sands facing England across the Flemish plain to towns, the Ardennes, and country pageants.

Chapters cover Belgian children, first communion, Christmas, New Year, carnival, archery games, language, and a short history, ending with the army and the Congo. A cup carried in triumph after a regimental football win shows Belgian love of procession. Folk customs include burning candles all night against evil spirits and striking unfruitful trees with an axe.
1972-history-of-the-britons-historia-bri:
Nennius's History of the Britons, translated by J. A. Giles, is a ninth-century work that gathers British legend and history into one book. Nennius, the lowly minister and servant of the servants of God, disciple of St. Elbotus, sends health to all followers of truth, and then sets out the origins of the Britons.

The history runs from Brutus the Trojan through the Roman years to the Saxon invasions. Walls were built between Britons, Picts, and Scots, and Arthur appears among the kings. The book is unreliable as history and priceless as legend, since it preserves stories, of Merlin, of Arthur, of the first Britons, that later writers would retell for a thousand years.
22206-an-old-meerschaum-from-coals-of-fi:
An Old Meerschaum is one of the tales in David Christie Murray's Coals of Fire and Other Stories. The story opens on a pretty young lady in the street. Two minutes later comes a young gentleman who seems her refined copy, save in one point. Where she is demure, impudence and mischief shine from him like light from a lantern.

That brother-and-sister contrast sets the tale moving. A meerschaum pipe, smoked and coloured by years, links the characters to an older generation's story. Murray was a practised hand at the magazine short story. His Coals of Fire tales mix sentiment, coincidence, and shrewd character in the approved Victorian mixture.
22256-sparkling-gems-of-race-knowledge-w:
Sparkling Gems of Race Knowledge Worth Reading compresses a library of Black achievement into one small compendium. Its editors launch the book with a plain hope: to instruct and encourage the coloured people. They claim to have packed a vast amount of valuable race information into a small compass. The style is good and the moral tone excellent, they promise, and every family should own it.

Inside stand sketches of Black leaders, poets, soldiers, businessmen, and inventors. Facts, speeches, and poems answer the slanders of the Jim Crow age with evidence. Such race books were sold door to door across the South. This one shows the self-help literature Black readers built for themselves.
22478-the-priest-s-tale-pe-re-etienne-fr:
Robert Keable wrote The Priest's Tale, Pere Etienne, for the New Decameron. Its narrator disclaims clairvoyance at the start of his story. He dislikes that jargon, he says firmly and plainly.

Yet he knew, he insists, whenever Pere Etienne passed his door. Even through the smoke-room door, the priest's presence registered on him. He sensed it while about to play a doubled four in no trumps. That bridge-table detail grounds the uncanny feeling in club life. Keable mixes war, faith, and quiet mystery in the tale. Readers meet a priest whose presence seems to reach through walls. The story leaves its wonder unexplained and understated.
23640-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-th:
Elbert Hubbard's Little Journeys series sent readers visiting the homes of famous men and women, and this 1916 memorial volume gathers his journeys to twelve philosophers. Socrates, Seneca, Aristotle, and Marcus Aurelius open the book, followed by Kant, Swedenborg, Spinoza, Comte, Voltaire, Spencer, Schopenhauer, and Thoreau.

Each sketch mixes life story with ideas. Socrates, who wrote no book yet left words sharp and vivid through Plato and Xenophon, was the stonecutter's son. He carried his father's dinner and listened to workmen debate the plans of Pericles. Hubbard writes warmly and plainly, aiming to make great thinkers feel like neighbors worth knowing.
24779-millennium:
Everett B. Cole wrote Millennium for Astounding Science Fiction in May 1955. On a backward planet, two salvage men from a high-level culture recover wrecked gear left by an earlier age. One find is a broken communicator kept as a holy relic in an abbey. The other is a golden mind-amplifier circlet. The tools are far beyond the skill of the folk who now own them.

When one of the men meets a local girl with strange powers, the team learns that rare beings called transvisors may still live on the eastern coast. Cole turns the tale on a sharp point: fine tools in untrained hands can do great harm. The story is a compact warning about tech, power, and cultures at very different stages.
25485-dikes-and-ditches-or-young-america:
Oliver Optic sends his Young America travellers to Holland and Belgium in this 1874 volume. The schoolboy party crosses the German Ocean in a squall, then tours dikes, ditches, and low-country towns. Their learned professor, Mr. Hamblin, believes his fame as a savant has crossed the ocean before him, since the king's chief minister courts his acquaintance.

The comedy turns on a letter: Duncan, a polite student invited into Hamblin's state-room, writes a translation that matches Mr. Stoute's, and Hamblin takes the agreement as deserved homage. Lee and Shepard published the book at Boston, from a copyright of 1868 in William T. Adams' name. It belongs to Young America Abroad, a library of travel and adventure in foreign lands.
25548-rollo-s-museum:
Rollo, aged between seven and eight one summer, stars in this 1839 children's book by the author of the Rollo learning and play tales. Rollo's Museum follows the boy as he gathers curiosities and learns how the world around him works.

Chapters take in a canal, a false alarm, a hemlock seed, a little law, confusion, and organisation, before the curiosities themselves, the seashore, the cliffs, and three northmen. Each small adventure teaches care, order, and honest talk, in the gentle didactic style of early American children's books. The Rollo sequence also covers talk, reading, work, play, school, and vacation.
25660-games-for-the-playground-home-scho:
Jessie H. Bancroft, assistant director of physical training in New York City public schools, writes this games book for playground, home, school, and gymnasium, published by Macmillan in 1922 with a 1909 copyright. Ring a Roses, from a painting by Fred Morgan, fronts the book.

Contents cover an introduction, advice to the teacher of games, counting out and choosing sides, and who is it. Miscellaneous active games, quiet games, feats and forfeits, and singing games follow. Balls and bean bags close the early sections, with specifications for balls and bean bags to aid teachers and parents.
25927-the-christmas-story-from-david-har:
Edward Noyes Westcott draws a Christmas story from his novel David Harum, in an edition illustrated from Charles Frohman's stage production with Wm. H. Crane. Printed by Appleton in 1900, the tale opens on December 23, just after closing, when Peleg has left and John has locked the vault. David Harum climbs onto a high office stool, heels on the spindle, and asks John if he knows the widow Cullom.

John knows her by sight, a tall thin woman with a stoop and a limp whose looks caught his eye. Later talk turns to childhood days, when a boy with no money for circuses refused to crawl under the canvas, saying he would enter like other folk or stay out. Mrs. Cullom sighs at the memory of that look, laughing and not laughing at once. The story is a warm Yankee Christmas tale.
26761-cerebrum:
Albert Teichner wrote this science-fiction story, illustrated by Birmingham. Its tagline says that for thousands of years the big brain had served as master switchboard for humanity's thoughts and emotions. Then the central mind showed signs of decay, and men went mad. Its hero, Connor, lives by telepathic thought-lines run through Central Switching.

Trouble begins trivially when Connor, wishing to speak to his wife Rhoda, reaches Dallas Shipping instead and is told he merely focussed wrong. A refused call on the monorail brings a synthesized sentence: for unfounded slander of Central Switching, he is suspended indefinitely from the telepathic net. Paranormal privileges withdrawn, he can communicate only in person or by writing. Fellow pariahs read books on the monorail, while passengers inside the system smile with minds tuned to music channels.
27480-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This file holds the third slice of volume three of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, running from Banks to Bassoon, part one of two of the volume. Volume and page numbers are worked into each article, and musical pitches follow Acoustical Society notation, with C4 as middle C.

The slice opens with George Linnaeus Banks, born at Birmingham on 2 March 1821, a miscellaneous writer and playwright. He edited papers including the Birmingham Mercury and the Dublin Daily Express, and died in London on 3 May 1881. Sir Joseph Banks, the naturalist, follows at once. The slice gives the eleventh edition's articles in alphabetical order, dense and authoritative.
28228-the-battle-with-the-slum:
Jacob A. Riis wrote The Battle with the Slum in 1902 as a sequel to How the Other Half Lives, reporting New York's fight against tenement misery. Riis, who knew the Five Points and Gotham Court at first hand, tracks reformers, landlords, and gangs through chapters on double-decker tenements, Cat Alley, and the Mills House. Theodore Roosevelt fronts the volume.

Riis argues that light, air, parks, and decent rooms do more than scolding, and he praises neighbours, settlements, and humane touch over force. His pictures and stories name real streets and real evils. The book remains a classic of American reform writing, urgent and practical at once.
29149-cogito-ergo-sum:
John Foster West wrote this science fiction story around a question: are spirit and flesh one thing, or separate? The magazine's introduction asks whether some great cosmic law holds the secret, and names the one dependable element as the lucky accident. West takes that riddle as his plot.

A warped instant in space separates two egos from their bodies and leaves them lost in a lonely abyss. The narrator wakes to pure reason alone. His first thought echoes Descartes: I think, therefore I am. From nothing but that certainty, he must reason out what he is, why he is, and where he is. Readers get a philosophical space tale, spare and strange, about a mind without a body.
29259-the-child-and-the-curriculum:
John Dewey published this short book in 1902 with the University of Chicago Press. Dewey, the American philosopher of education, takes up a genuine problem: the conflict between the child and the curriculum. Deep differences in theory, he argues, are never invented; they grow from clashing elements of a real problem.

Dewey refuses to choose one side. The child's interests and experience must meet the organized knowledge of the curriculum, not replace it or bow to it. The book's argument shaped progressive education. Readers get a brief, dense classic of educational thought, still quoted whenever schools debate whether to start from the child or from the subject.
30427-the-lost-kafoozalum:
Pauline Ashwell tells The Lost Kafoozalum in Analog, October 1960, with pictures by Schoenherr. One of the things about a delusion, the tagline says, is that no matter how mad someone gets at it, he cannot do it any harm. So a delusion can be a fine thing for prodding belligerents. The narrator remembers bad times back home on Excenus 23, the worst when Dad fell under the reaping machine.

Other times include getting lost twenty miles from home with a radio at twelve. Uncle Charlie caught a practice of emergency turns in a helicar round the weather-maker, and a cyber-crane chased the narrator on Figuerra. Dad deciding to send the narrator to Earth for an education counts. This time is bad in a way, with no edges but a kind of desolation. Five days have passed since the Russett College examination ended, with results still two weeks away.
30432-a-modern-symposium:
G. Lowes Dickinson stages a debate among members of a London club called the Seekers, a group that meets every two weeks in town or at a member's country house. The host chairs the evening, calls on speakers in turn, and records what follows at his home on the North Downs.

Speakers range across the political spectrum. They include a Tory lord and a Liberal prime minister, a Conservative, a Socialist, an anarchist, a professor, a man of science, a journalist, a poet, and a Quaker. Their talk tests rival views of public life, faith, and duty, with sharp disagreement held inside polite club manners. First published in 1905, the book reads as a set of linked speeches rather than a plotted novel.
31208-collectivum:
Mike Lewis's science fiction story, printed in Space Science Fiction in July 1953, is set among the Oren, a collective alien people whose strength lies in their oneness. Their sting turns victims into more of themselves. At sundown on a rickety bridge, Morgan sees a fat man whipping a girl with a board and, leaping to a conclusion, clubs him into the lagoon, where sharks begin to circle.

The girl, a gold-bronze beauty with black hair, explains that the man was her husband and that he meant to kill her. She adds that he had been stung the week before, so he was lost in any case. Tense and pulp-swift, the tale turns a rescue gone wrong into a story of survival among parasites.
31332-a-journal-of-impressions-in-belgiu:
May Sinclair's 1915 journal, published by Macmillan in September 1915, records impressions of Belgium in the first year of the Great War. Dedicated in verse to a field ambulance in Flanders, the book follows the wounded and those who gather them among ruined and immortal cities. They are Termonde and Antwerp, Dixmude and Ypres and Furnes, named like jewels on a chain.

Sinclair writes of thundering guns, shrapnel rain, curved lightning of shells, broken towers, and houses cracking like crates filled with fire. Meanwhile the ambulance goes out under grey night and returns under black. The journal is a writer's witness to war's opening months, personal, impressionistic, and unsparing.
32266-sugar-plum:
R. Bretnor's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in November 1952, is a domestic comedy set in the year 2189. Its sidenote jokes that if not for two items, this would be a funny story: the Atomic Age brought back the 1925 vogue, and inhibition is not shatter-proof. On a spring evening, Charles Edward Button comes home late for supper. He tosses his hat to the robot butler who comes out from behind the DoItAll, and announces that he has just bought a planet.

His wife Betty sits small and resigned on a plastic copy of a Victorian love-seat, while her cousin Aurelia, a large, handsome woman, stands by. Readers get a future satire of marriage, manners, and money. A man buys a planet as casually as a hat, and a robot butler catches it. The humour lies in the gap between futuristic furniture and old-fashioned domestic tension.
32928-haviland-s-chum:
Bertram Mitford opens at an English school, where a new boy faces a jeering crowd. Mpukuza, a fifteen-year-old African boy, straight-limbed and well built, with rich copper-brown skin, answers questions with a click that might mean contempt, disgust, or defiance. A thick-set bully knocks off his hat and jerks him by his short, crisp curls, while the others laugh at what they call wholesome nigger baiting.

Haviland ends it with a hearty swinging cuff to the bully's head, and asks if he wants more. The friendship that follows carries both boys through school politics, gatings, and a prefect's grudge. Mpukuza was placed at Saint Kirwin's by a missionary, under headmaster Bowen, a Tartar whom Haviland hated until his father's death showed Bowen decent at bottom. Years later Haviland learns that Bowen is Oakley's uncle, and the small world of school closes its circle.
33065-the-indian-drum:
William MacHarg and Edwin Balmer's Indian Drum, copyrighted in 1917, opens near the northern end of Lake Michigan. There, ore-carriers and wheat-laden freighters from Lake Superior push out from the Straits of Mackinac. Its chapters follow a man haunted by storm, a question over who Alan Conrad is, a discussion of a shadow, and Constance Sherrill. They then turn to a deed in trust, Mr. Corvet's partner, violence, and a walk beside the lake. Later chapters bring the land of the drum and a ghost ship.

The mystery deepens as a watch, a ferry, and a sounding drum point toward a fate on the water, and the line he killed your father sharpens the plot. MacHarg and Balmer build a Great Lakes thriller from shipping, family secrets, and a haunting sound. The novel moves briskly, and its lake setting gives it a fresh, cold atmosphere .
36616-project-gutenberg-4-july-1971-4-ju:
Marie Lebert compiled this album to celebrate the fortieth anniversary of Project Gutenberg, covering the years from July 1971 to July 2011. It is dedicated to Project Gutenberg and Distributed Proofreaders volunteers worldwide. It is also released to the public domain. The first ebook, it recalls, appeared on the Fourth of July 1971.

That first text was the United States Declaration of Independence, keyed in by Michael Hart on a mainframe. He typed in capitals, because there was no lower case yet: a file of five kilobytes, announced to the hundred users of a pre internet network. The album traces the project's boosts: the web in 1990 and Distributed Proofreaders in 2000. It is a scrapbook of the free library movement, made by one of its own chroniclers.
37064-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
A slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs from Frost to Fyzabad. Transcriber notes explain the handling of subscripts, superscripts, and side notes in plain text. Corrections are listed for the articles on fruit, fuel, Fulham, and Thomas Fuller. One fix changes a chemistry line in the fuel article. The slice is part of a dictionary of arts, sciences, and general information.

Entries here move from frost and fruit through fuel to towns and biographies. The eleventh edition's signed articles made it a scholarly standard. Gutenberg volunteers split the huge volumes into alphabetical slices for transcription. Readers can trace a single stretch of the alphabet in this file.
37188-plish-and-plum:
Plish and Plum is a verse tale for children by Wilhelm Busch, author of Max and Maurice. Charles Brooks turned the German into English rhyme. Roberts Brothers published the book at Boston in 1895, from rights dated 1882. The story is told in short rhymed chapters with the author's well known comic snap.

Old Caspar Sly sets out to drown two young dogs he counts as useless mouths. He bends over the pond with a pipe in his lips and a cold heart. The pups go in with a plish and a plum. Two boys, Paul and Peter, happen to be hiding nearby for a swim. Each dives and drags a puppy safe to land. Paul names his dog Plish and Peter names his Plum. The tale follows the rescued dogs into the boys' home.
3769-rejected-addresses-or-the-new-theat:
James Smith and Horace Smith wrote these comic verses for a real contest, when the rebuilt Drury Lane Theatre asked poets to supply an opening address in 1812. The brothers, rejected like the rest, printed their imitations instead, and the book became a hit. Byron praised it to his publisher, and the critic Francis Jeffrey called the imitations the best ever made, far above mere parody.

The verses take off the famous voices of the day, from Wordsworth and Scott to Byron himself, with a fireman poet waving his hose through smoke and flame as one jolly example. Each piece catches its target's habits of phrase and thought. Readers who like literary jokes will find a book that still amuses, even where the originals have faded from memory.
37767-the-phil-may-album:
Phil May Album gathers the comic drawings of Phil May in one volume. Augustus Moore collected the plates, and Methuen of London issued it in nineteen hundred. Edmund Evans printed the album at the Racquet Court in Fleet Street. Contents run page by page from Blowing a Cloud to short comic scenes.

An introduction of some pages sets out May life and art first. Recurring heads called On the Brain take up noted public figures in fun. The Queen, the Duke of Cambridge, and the German Emperor all appear. Three Men in a Boot, a Friend in Need, and Cheek show the range. Readers get May famed line work on the manners of his day.
38433-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-97:
An issue of Notes and Queries dated Saturday, September 6, 1851. The London weekly called itself a medium of inter-communication. Literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists formed its public. The price was threepence, or fourpence stamped. Captain Cuttle's motto heads the page: when found, make a note of. This is number ninety-seven of volume four.

The contents show the journal's working method. Notes treat Gabriel Harvey and the antiquity of kilts. Queries ask after John Knox and Cornish arms. Readers answer earlier questions on many small points. Replies discuss pendulum proof of the earth's rotation. The whale of Jonah also gets a hearing. Notes and Queries still runs today. Issues like this built its crowdsourced scholarship.
38622-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
One volume of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica fills this text, running from the entry on crocoite toward Cuba. Crocoite is a mineral, and Cuba the island republic; the slice between them holds chemistry, towns, churchmen, and wars. The transcriber's notes explain how subscripts and Greek letters in the chemical articles were handled.

The notes also list corrections made in famous articles. The article on Crowland now records that the dissolution of its monastery in 1539 was fatal to the town, which had prospered under the monks. A line on the dramatist John Crowne is set right. The article on the Crusades, one of the edition's great set pieces, begins in this volume. Alphabetical order makes strange neighbours, and this volume's run from a lead mineral to a Caribbean island shows the reach of the eleventh edition's scheme.
38701-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-10:
One weekly number of Notes and Queries, volume four, number 101, dated Saturday, October 4, 1851, sold for threepence, or fourpence stamped. The journal calls itself a medium of inter communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto is Captain Cuttle's advice: when found, make a note of. Contents list notes before queries and replies.

Dr Thurnam writes on the battle of Brunanburgh. Bolton Corney contributes on the Caxton coffer. Accuracy of printing gets a note of its own. Folk lore discoveries follow. The journal let Victorian scholars crowdsource answers to small questions of history, books, and custom. A single number shows its range at a glance.
38773-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-10:
Notes and Queries, number 102 of volume four, is the weekly issue dated Saturday, the eleventh of October 1851. The journal calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries and genealogists. Its motto, borrowed from Captain Cuttle, is: when found, make a note of. The price was threepence.

The contents show the journal at work. Notes treat the effigies of English sovereigns still in France, Arabic inscriptions, additions to Cunningham's Handbook of London, and Richard Rolle of Hampole. A funeral in Hamburgh is described, and folk lore items cover the baker's daughter, the King's evil, and bees. Bolton Corney writes on the Caxton coffer. Queries and replies follow, on names, places and books. The issue is a snapshot of Victorian scholarship conducted by post, query by query.
38799-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica fills this slice, running from Dagupan to David. Signed articles by scholars of the day treat each headword in the famous 1911 set. Transcriber's notes here explain signs for subscripts, roots and Greek letters used through the text.

Corrections to articles on Dahlmann and Dahomey are listed among those notes at the front. Dahlmann, the historian blamed by the Danes over Schleswig-Holstein, gets a long treatment in the slice. Dahlmann's part in the chain toward 1864 is weighed in the article, and entries on Dahomey and David follow amid thousands more.
38864-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-10:
Notes and Queries, volume four, number 103, is the weekly issue for Saturday, October 18, 1851, priced threepence. The journal calls itself a medium of intercommunication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of. The catalog title is the journal's own heading.

Readers wrote in with questions on inscriptions, ballads, family names, and odd customs, and other readers answered them. Dickens's world of print ran on such exchanges. A single issue holds dozens of small puzzles and their keys. Genealogists still mine the old volumes for names and dates. The issue is a window into Victorian curiosity at work, threepence worth of shared knowledge.
38926-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-10:
Notes and Queries was a weekly London journal that let readers swap facts and ask each other hard questions. This is number 104 of volume four, dated Saturday, October 25, 1851, priced at sixpence. Its motto, borrowed from Captain Cuttle, was simple: when found, make a note of it.

Inside, short notes take up old books, odd words, graves, and points of local lore. A set of minor queries asks about things like a frontispiece in Hobbes's Leviathan and the tale of a deep well near Banstead Downs. Readers of old journals will enjoy how much small, curious learning one cheap weekly issue could pack in.
39076-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-10:
Notes and Queries, volume four, number 105, is a weekly journal dated Saturday, November 1, 1851. It calls itself a means of talk for men of books, artists, and hunters of past facts and family lines. The motto, from Captain Cuttle, urges readers to make a note of what they find. No one author owns the page, since readers send in most of what is printed. Each number runs to short items sent from far and wide.

Inside are notes on Daniel Defoe and the Caxton coffer. Queries ask about Milton, kin of John of Gaunt, and bishops in Sweden. Replies take up church marriage, anagrams, locusts in the New Testament, and carved stones in Scotland. The number shows how shared notes built one wide, slow web of facts in print.
39091-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-10:
Notes and Queries, a medium of intercommunication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, issued number one hundred six on Saturday, November 8, 1851. It cost threepence, or fourpence stamped. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, bids a man make a note of what he finds. William Sidney Gibson leads with notes on Arundel House in the Strand.

Other notes tell of the dispersion of the Arundelian sculptures, of Panslavic literature at the British Museum, and of Archbishop Ussher. Queries ask the use of misereres and the tale of Joceline's legacy. Replies sort anachronisms of painters and the meaning of Agla. The number shows a learned swap shop of Victorian scholarship in full flow.
39338-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-11:
Notes and Queries, volume four, number 110, dated Saturday, 6 December 1851, is a weekly number of the journal that called itself a medium of inter-communication. Its readers were literary men, artists, antiquaries, and family historians. The price was sixpence, or sevenpence stamped. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, bids readers make a note of what they find.

The contents list notes on the aborigines of St. Domingo, a forger spared the gallows, and a passage in Jeremy Taylor. Folk lore brings a death omen by bees and the Caxton coffer. Queries ask about General Wolfe, the first coming of Christianity to Orkney, and the Roman index of 1607. Small queries crowd the rest of the page.
40127-joe-miller-s-jests-or-the-wits-vad:
Joe Miller's Jests, or the Wits Vade-Mecum, was printed and sold by T Read in Whitefriars, London, in 1739. The book bills itself as a gathering of the most brilliant jests, politest repartees, elegant bons mots, and pleasant short stories in English. Many, it claims, were taken down from the mouth of Joe Miller himself. His friend Elijah Jenkins is named as publisher, in jesting style.

The jests are numbered and short. In the first, a duke behind the scenes of The Beggar's Opera trades quips with Cibber on how the piece will read in print. In the second, the actor Wilks catches an orange thrown at him on stage and bows: this is no civil orange. Theatre folk, lords, and orange girls fill the pages. The book set the pattern for jest books for a century.
40582-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-115:
Notes and Queries was a weekly sheet for men of books, art, old things, and family lines. The copy here is book five, Number 115, dated Saturday, January 10, 1852. A lone copy cost four pence, or five pence in its stamped form. A line from a Dickens tale serves as its creed: when found, make a note of it.

Notes deal with the lives of the poets by Cibber, with the book of Job, and with a tale from New Zealand. Small notes touch on Pope, on the fall of Clarendon, and on the death of Charles the First. One note deals with birth in ear shot of Bow Bell in London. Queries ask if the lists of the kings and queens of England are full and true.
40642-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-116:
Volume five, number one hundred sixteen of Notes and Queries came out on Saturday, January seventeenth, eighteen hundred fifty two. The weekly served writers, artists, and students of old books and family lines. With its index the issue cost ten pence. A stamped copy cost eleven pence.

Notes here take up how books are bound and a fund for Caxton. One note treats a play about Pope Joan. Folk notes mark Valentine’s Day and fairy faith in Devonshire. Readers ask what the word groom first meant. Replies sort out place names and lines from old poems. The mix shows scholars pooling small facts week by week. Each short item adds one brick to a shared wall of learning.
40678-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-117:
Notes and Queries, number 117 of volume five, is the weekly number dated Saturday, January 24, 1852. The journal calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. It sold for fourpence, fivepence stamped, under Captain Cuttle's motto: when found, make a note of.

The number opens with notes on the Pantheon at Paris, Churchill the poet, and readings in Shakespeare. Folk lore follows: salting a new-born infant, Lent crocking, and Devonshire beliefs about still-born children. Queries ask after Count Konigsmark, Sir Walter Raleigh's snuff-box, sun-dials, and John of Padua. Replies settle the collars of SS, the first paper-mill in England, Yankee Doodle, and the expurgatory index of Rome. The whole number is scholars talking to scholars in print.
40713-the-spell-of-belgium:
Spell of Belgium is a travel book by Isabel Anderson, author of The Spell of Japan. The Boston edition was copyrighted in nineteen fifteen and reprinted many times. A colour picture of the market square and belfry of Furnes serves as frontispiece. The book is dedicated to the author's godchild, with a wish that he be as brave as the Belgians.

Contents move from the author's new post and diplomatic life to Brussels before the war. Older chapters treat knights and villains and the battling for a kingdom. Belgian kings, politics, workshops, and tapestries follow. Painters and letters take their own chapters, then motoring in Flanders. A synopsis of the war, letters from the front, and American relief work close the book. Anderson spent a winter in Belgium, the text says.
40716-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-118:
Notes and Queries, volume five, number 118, for Saturday 31 January 1852, is an issue of the weekly medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, priced at fourpence. Its motto, borrowed from Captain Cuttle, is the injunction to make a note of things when found.

The contents open with the calamities of authors, then notes on portraits of Wolfe, on Homer, on French revolutions foretold, and on Johnson's contributions to Baretti's introduction. Minor notes touch a bishop, foreign guide-books, wearing gloves before royalty, and the errors of poets. The queries ask after the poet Collins, portraits of Henry Purcell, the controversy about fluxions, the meaning of madrigal, Holbein, an ivory medallion of Byron, and the garrote. Replies and minor queries answered fill the remaining pages.
40742-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-119:
Notes and Queries, volume five, number one hundred nineteen, for Saturday, February seventh, eighteen fifty two, calls itself a medium of inter communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. The price was fourpence, or fivepence for the stamped form. Captain Cuttle motto, When found, make a note of, heads the page. Short notes, queries, and replies fill the number in set order.

Notes treat stone pillar worship still found in Ireland and the invasion of Britain. A note on David Mallet weighs his character and life. Queries ask for the root of the word Garsecg and chase pedigrees, old books, and valentines. Replies treat the three estates of the realm and the legend of Saint Kenelm. Readers get a lively swap shop of lore, where small facts were traded week by week.
40743-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-120:
Number 120 of Notes and Queries, dated Saturday, February 14, 1852, is one weekly issue of the London journal for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and family historians. The price was fourpence. The journal's whole method sits in its motto, taken from Captain Cuttle: when found, make a note of it. Readers sent in short notes and short questions, and other readers sent the answers.

The notes in this issue take up the old Countess of Desmond, the imperial eagle of France, and folk lore for Valentine's Day. Bee superstitions, horn blowing at Nottingham, and the blessing of apple trees share a page. Queries ask whether the walrus lives in the Baltic and what a string of old phrases mean. Replies settle points on Coverdale's Bible, sundial mottoes, and whether bishops may give up their sees.
40773-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-121:
Number 121 of Notes and Queries, volume five, appeared on Saturday, February 21, 1852, priced at fourpence. The weekly called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Readers sent in short notes, asked questions, and answered the questions of others.

This issue opens with readings in Shakespeare and notes on Homer, then turns to folklore from Cornwall. Queries ask whether Saint Paul quoted Aristotle, and chase points about fonts, portraits, and old ballads. Replies count the children of Israel and discuss serjeants' rings and men named Bacon. The number shows Victorian scholars at work in public, pooling small facts week by week. Such issues remain a rich mine for local history, word lore, and family history.
40779-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-122:
Notes and Queries called itself a medium of talk between literary men, artists, antiquaries, and family historians. Volume five, number one hundred twenty-two is dated Saturday, February twenty-eight, eighteen fifty-two. The price was fourpence. Captain Cuttle's motto heads the paper: when found, make a note of it.

The contents open with Ben Jonson's verses on a great marriage. Notes follow on Junius, on Simon of Sudbury, and on a paraphrase of the Lord's Prayer. Folk lore brings a Suffolk legend and a tale of Theodoric. Place names and local dialects get their share. The weekly swapped small facts among the curious of all Britain.
40856-little-philippe-of-belgium:
Madeline Brandeis wrote Little Philippe of Belgium, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York by pact with A Flanagan Company. The copyright is nineteen thirty. Brandeis had written Little Indian Weaver, The Wee Scotch Piper, and other child tales of far lands. Photos made in Belgium by the author fill the book. She gave the book to her daughter Marie, who loved scary tales and loved this one best.

Philippe is a small Belgian boy whose tale starts with a Brussels sprout joke. Chapters take him to Papa Pomme surprise, to new friends, and to work as a guide. He runs away, makes a hard journey, and is found in Bruges, the city of sisters. A cave of crows and a talk with Trompke add thrill. Young readers learn Belgian life, food, and towns through a boys eyes. Photos ground the tale in real streets and folk.
41090-at-the-sign-of-the-sword-a-story-o:
William Le Queux wrote a tale of love and war in Belgium that a New York house issued in 1915. The scene opens at noon on a cloudless July day in 1914. The Meuse runs broad and shallow through its deep valley of grey rock and cool wood.

Near old Dinant lies the riverside village of Anseremme, where the Lesse joins the Meuse. Artists love the place. On the terrace of a small hotel, a young man and a girl sit at lunch among the roses. They have met in secret. He came on foot with dusty boots and waited over a newspaper. She swept up in a fine grey car from the French side.
4242-belgium:
Joseph E. Morris wrote this portrait of Belgium for the Beautiful Europe series while the First World War was destroying the country he described. He calls Belgium the cockpit of the Continent, a small nation whose pledge of neutrality could not save it from invasion, ruin, and occupation.

Morris mixes travel writing with history, recalling Belgian towns, character, and customs even as he notes the harsh judgments earlier writers had passed on Belgian selfishness and soldiering. Written in wartime, the book reads as both a guide to a beautiful country and a lament for a people paying, in his view, for keeping their word.
42475-the-history-of-ancient-america-ant:
The History of Ancient America, Anterior to the Time of Columbus, by George Jones, published in 1843 in London, New York, Berlin, and Paris, is a bold work of old style speculation. Its title page states the thesis: the native peoples of America were the people of Tyre and Israel, and the Apostle Saint Thomas brought Christianity to the western world.

Jones grounds his case on the ruins of antiquity and on prophecy in Isaiah, and dedicates the book to the Archbishop of Canterbury. A royal prince, he says, advised that choice. Modern readers will not follow his proof, but the book shows how eagerly the young science of the past reached for one key.
42830-chicago-satan-s-sanctum:
Curon's attack on Chicago politics, copyrighted in 1899 and issued there by Phillips and Company, opens with a preface on the mayor's re-election. The mayor's cry, that the streets may be dirty but they still belong to the people, is granted to be catching and powerful. Curon calls it sophistical, and a debt the mayor owes for his office.

The fight behind the election was the extension of street car privileges. The legislature had repealed the law under which council corruptionists might have acted, and both of the mayor's rivals held his own views on the question. Both, Curon says, were abler and more experienced men, with records for integrity not surpassed by his. The mayor, he argues, did part of his duty bravely and hid the rest behind the danger.
43157-the-swing-of-the-pendulum:
Swing of the Pendulum is a novel by Frances Peard, in an edition dated eighteen ninety three. Chapter one is called Dislike. A gale on the North Sea has made the crossing from Hull worse than usual. The ship Eldorado nears the low land at the entrance to Stavanger in Norway.

Hardly any passengers had come to meals in the bad weather, the tale says. Now, with the worst over, they look at each other with fresh interest. A mother and daughter stand apart on deck. A gentleman strolls up and greets them with a smile. The elder lady shudders at the memory of the voyage. She says she persuaded her daughter Millie to come and now feels remorse. The pair follow a guide book that calls Stavanger the right way into Norway.
44043-the-truth-about-opium:
The Truth About Opium, by Brereton, defends the Indo China opium trade. Allen and Company issued this second edition at London in 1883 for the India Office. Brereton wrote as a man late of Hong Kong, in lecture form. A Milton line on truth and falsehood in open fight fronts the book.

His preface boasts the lectures broke the Anti Opium Society stride at last. Its secretary, Storrs Turner, fell silent after long loud attack, he claims. Letters, articles, and speeches had flown from Turner like chaff before then. Brereton cheers that his first edition was well received by press and public. Trade defence, not reform, is the lectures plain and open aim.
44099-how-to-solve-conundrums-containing:
How to Solve Conundrums is a joke book of conundrums, riddles, curious catches, and witty sayings. Frank Tousey of New York published it, and it was entered at the Library of Congress in 1900. Tousey sold cheap amusement by the ton, and this complete book of the leading conundrums of the day keeps the jokes coming one after another.

Samples show the stock. The games most played by soldiers are hazard and picket. The letter K is like a pig's tail because it is at the end of pork. A martial band needs, most of all, the drum of your ear. A blind pig is spelled in two letters, P and G, a pig without an I. Such dime joke books were the pocket fun of their day, and their puns show what made schoolyards laugh in 1900.
45988-novum-organum:
Francis Bacon, Lord Chancellor of England, published the Novum Organum in 1620, the great statement of his new method for science. Its title means the new instrument, set against Aristotle's old Organon of logic. This edition, edited by Joseph Devey, came out in New York in 1902.

Book one opens with the famous claim that man, as nature's minister and interpreter, can do and understand only as much as he has observed. Bacon's aphorisms attack the idols of the mind, the false notions that block true knowledge, and plead for knowledge built from experiment. An editor's note warns how men confound neat inference with truth. Few books have shaped the modern world more.
46179-two-years-and-four-months-in-a-lun:
Two Years and Four Months in a Lunatic Asylum, printed at Saratoga Springs in 1868, is the memoir of the Reverend H Chase. He was confined from August 1863 to December 1865. In his preface Chase explains why he waited to write: the subject sickened him after his release, and he had returned to the ministry within eighteen months. He also feared that readers would laugh at his account as a freak of insanity rather than receive it as sober truth.

Other former inmates, one of them from the Utica asylum, had already published their views of asylum life. Chase adds his own testimony, with chapters covering the whole term and a section of testimonials at the end. Such memoirs fed the century's debate over the treatment of the insane. His book is among the plainest of them: a minister's record of what confinement felt like from inside.
46248-belgium:
Belgium is a picture travel book with paintings by Amédée Forestier and text by George W T Omond, published by A and C Black of London in 1908. The book also came out in three separate parts. Bruges and West Flanders held 57 full-page illustrations in colour.

The text begins at Bruges, with its market-place and belfry. Early history follows, from Baldwin Bras-de-Fer to the murder of Charles the Good. The Béguinage and the relic of the Holy Blood get a chapter. The Bruges Matins and the Battle of the Golden Spurs come next. Damme and the sea-fight at Sluis lead to the splendour and fall of medieval Bruges. The plain of West Flanders brings Ypres and Furnes, with its procession of penitents. Nieuport and the Battle of the Dunes follow.
46281-a-monograph-of-odontoglossum:
James Bateman made a grand plate book on one prized orchid kind. The book came out in London in 1874. Bateman had wrote on the orchids of Mexico and Guatemala. He gave the book, by leave, to Alexandra, Princess of Wales. Work on it started the eve of her come to her new land.

Cool care for orchids was new when he began in 1864. That trick oped a fresh orchid world to plant men, he says. Kind by kind, each bloom is drawn and told in full. Home land, scent, hues, and growth marks fill each tale. Plant lovers get a crown work of the orchid age. Fine plates give it worth past its facts.
4756-the-love-sonnets-of-a-hoodlum:
Wallace Irwin wrote The Love Sonnets of a Hoodlum, with an introduction by Gelett Burgess. It shows how vanity stays on deck, while humble virtue gets it in the neck. Burgess opens with Phineas Fletcher complaining in 1633 that muses had left little for later ages to play upon. Three centuries, he says, brought lyric passion no higher form than the sonnet cycle, a crystal goblet holding one inspired thought so perfectly.

The sonnet was cast in the early Italian Renaissance by Dante, Petrarch, and Camoens. It was chased in the Elizabethan age by Shakespeare, and filled with stimulating draughts of song and love in the Victorian era by Rossetti, Browning, and Meredith. Irwin now turns that high form to low life, with a hoodlum lover sighing in sonnets. Readers get a comic, affectionate parody, where street slang and formal verse collide to funny, surprisingly tender effect.
48094-sumerian-hymns-from-cuneiform-text:
Frederick Augustus Vanderburgh wrote this monograph on Sumerian hymns from cuneiform texts in the British Museum. John Dyneley Prince of Columbia University supplied a note, dated October 1907. The hymns come from volume fifteen of the museum's cuneiform texts series. Many tablets are worn and hard to read.

A live dispute frames the study. Scholars argued whether Sumerian was a true language or a priestly code for Semitic speech. Prince holds it was a real, non-Semitic tongue, later crusted with Semitic loans. Vanderburgh follows that view in his readings. The hymns, sung in one language alone, test the question. They also add to knowledge of Babylonian religion, its gods, and its temple song.
49224-the-journals-of-major-gen-c-g-gord:
Major General C G Gordon kept a daily journal at Khartoum, printed here from his own hand in 1885. A Egmont Hake wrote the long notes and the first part of the book. The book has a portrait, two maps, and thirty drawings after sketches by Gordon.

Six journal books run from September to December 1884. They record life and war work in the besieged town day by day. Front essays set out Gordon's place, the relief bid, and the state of the steamers. Long notes at the back print letters to and from Gordon. Readers get a close first hand record of the siege.
50881-possum:
Mary Grant Bruce wrote Possum, published in London, Melbourne, and Toronto by Ward, Lock. Bruce was an Australian writer known for her Billabong books, and she dedicated this one to her mother. The story opens in a trim suburban garden, blazing with flowers, with a curtain of white blossom over the porch.

Chapters move from breaking bad news to a farm, a home-coming, and a day in the country. A heroine called Possum takes hold, becomes a pupil, and joins in sailing, a boating holiday, and a regatta. Bruce writes warm tales of Australian family life, and this one follows a girl growing into her place among kin, horses, and the bush.
52825-petroleum:
Pitman's series of Common Commodities and Industries produced this handbook on petroleum, amid pages of trade advertisements. Oil firms crowd the front matter: tanker builders, drilling-tool makers, refiners, and tank erectors. Its frontispiece shows England's first oil well, drilled in Derbyshire under government orders and brought in during June 1919.

The book tells how oil is found, raised, refined, and sold. Mexican fuel oil, motor spirit, kerosene, and lubricants pass in review, with the great companies named. It belongs to the moment when oil became the world's master fuel. Readers get a trade-eye view of the young petroleum industry.
52988-the-white-wampum:
Pauline Johnson, whose Mohawk name was Tekahionwake, wrote The White Wampum, a book of poems published at London, Toronto, and Boston in 1895. The catalog spells her middle name oddly, as the title page itself prints it. Verses at the front speak of the copper tinted face and smouldering fire left her by her sire.

Johnson offers the book as a belt of verse wampum. As wampums to the Redman, she writes, so to the poet are his songs: chiselled from his purest possessions and woven with meaning. The belt carries a message of peace, tradition, and fellowship with all men. She credits her mother as her mainstay in the work. Johnson, half Mohawk and half English, became Canada's best loved poet of her day.
53531-fire-making-apparatus-in-the-u-s-n:
Fire-Making Apparatus in the United States National Museum is a museum study by Walter Hough, the Smithsonian anthropologist. It catalogues and explains the tools by which peoples of the world kindled fire. A long epigraph from Bacon's Wisdom of the Ancients calls fire the help of helps, through Prometheus.

Hough begins by correcting a popular error. Making fire by rubbing two pieces of wood, he says, is not very difficult. He has repeatedly done it in thirty seconds with twirling sticks. With another apparatus he claims five seconds. The paper describes drills, saws, and ploughs of wood used across cultures. Such museum monographs recorded world technology before it vanished. Hough writes as a working experimenter, not a mere cataloguer, and his timings still serve anyone testing friction fire methods.
53692-the-flying-girl-and-her-chum:
The Flying Girl and Her Chum, by Edith Van Dyne, was published at Chicago in 1912. Reilly and Britton issued the tale, with pictures by Nuyttens. It stands in the Flying Girl series. Van Dyne had written the earlier Flying Girl and the Aunt Jane's Nieces books. Twenty nine chapters make the story. Chapter one is called The Girl with the Yacht. The second brings the girl with the aeroplane. Orissa, the flying girl, sits up in the front picture with a cry of surprise.

An aluminum chest and the last drop of gasoline set the plot moving. The girls are cast away on an island, two girls alone. A quest for the Salvador and a game of checkers follow. A siege, a captured aeroplane, and Orissa's decision close the tale.
53730-the-red-cross-girls-in-belgium:
The Red Cross Girls in Belgium is a girls' war novel by Margaret Vandercook. The John Winston Company published it at Philadelphia in 1916. It belongs to the Red Cross Girls series, which also took its heroines to the British trenches and the French firing line. Vandercook also wrote the Ranch Girls and Camp Fire Girls series.

The series follows American girls serving as nurses in the First World War. A frontispiece caption calls out a lieutenant's name at a dramatic moment. Later volumes carried the girls to the Russian and Italian armies. These books brought the war home to American girl readers as a field for courage and service.
54652-history-of-gujara-t-gazetteer-of-t:
The Government Central Press at Bombay printed a history of Gujarát in 1896, as volume one, part one, of the Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency. A note from Bombay Castle, dated 14th February 1902, praises the long work of James Campbell and his helpers. Campbell led the task for more than ten years.

The whole set of district accounts runs to twenty-seven volumes of about 500 pages each, the note says. Work on the plan began in 1843, when the government first called for such accounts. Praise from the Governor in Council hails the set as a record of fact on the land and its folk as full as any state has made.
54921-the-romance-of-war-or-the-highland:
The Romance of War, or The Highlanders in France and Belgium is a military novel by James Grant, published in London by Henry Colburn in 1847. It runs to three volumes, of which this is the first. Grant, late of the 62nd Regiment, wrote it as a sequel to his Highlanders in Spain.

An epigraph from General Erskine brings the Highlanders from the heath covered mountains of Scotia. The contents open at Toulouse and pass through adventures in Spain. The Lady of Elizondo, Cifuentes, and the Torre de Los Frayles mark the Peninsular road. Then the story moves to Flanders and Cameron of Fassifern. The 17th and 18th of June 1815 close the volume's list, which is to say Waterloo. Grant filled his novels with regimental lore and old soldiers' talk, and Victorian readers marched willingly.
56661-hacking-through-belgium:
Edmund Dane wrote Hacking Through Belgium in 1914, in the first months of the First World War. Hodder and Stoughton printed the book in London as part of the Daily Telegraph war books. Dane's aim, stated up front, is to show the great part played by a small people.

Ten chapters track the German drive through Belgium. Dane covers Liège, the work of the Belgian army, and the fall of Brussels. He then turns to Louvain, which he calls a crime, and to the siege of Antwerp. A short time line of chief events ends the book. The tone is warm praise for Belgium and sharp blame for Germany, as British readers expected in 1914.
56921-pierrot-dog-of-belgium:
Pierrot, Dog of Belgium, is a tale by Walter Dyer, printed at Garden City, New York, in 1915. Gordon Grant drew the pictures. Dyer dedicates the little tale to the Commission for Relief in Belgium, waging a bloodless battle against famine and war's ravages. The book opens with a lament for Belgium.

Across her meadows the hosts of war have marched, and her ancient cities smoke. Amid the cries of ruined homes come the weeping of a little girl named Lisa and the whining of a faithful dog. A Belgian carbineer leads Pierrot away one morning. The children called him Pierrot from the first, since Mère Marie had come from Dinant and loved all things French.
58655-tales-from-the-gesta-romanorum:
Swan turned tales from the Gesta Romanorum into English. The book came out with Putnam in New York and London. The Gesta is a Latin store of tales from the Middle Ages. Monks used such tales to teach right and wrong. Swan's book mixes the tales with talk about their roots.

Chapters trace how tales moved from East to West. They link old tales to King Lear and The Merchant of Venice. Witch lore, fairs, and crusade tales fill later parts. Each tale ends with a moral drawn from the plot. Readers get both the tales and a guide to their past.
59125-aquarium:
Aquarium is a book of poems by Harold Acton, first published in 1923. Duckworth of London issued the volume. Edith Sitwell's Bucolic Comedies is named as its companion. The contents fall into two parts. Part one, Curves, holds the title poem and its mates. Part two, Urbanities, turns to town scenes and types.

The title poem invites the reader to buy a ticket. Fish with spotted gills drift through its lines. Flower-fish and pale fish with morbid eyes follow. Later poems treat a cathedral, a young sailor, and a fox-trot. Town pieces name a typing office and a trapeze artist. Thanks are given to editors who first printed some pieces. Acton wrote as a young aesthete of the twenties. The book shows that era's bright, brittle taste.
60370-boy-scouts-with-joffre-or-in-the-t:
Boy Scouts with Joffre, or In the Trenches in Belgium, by Captain Sherman, is a war tale for boys. Donohue published it at Chicago, with copyright dated 1912. Sherman had written The War Zone and a Balkan scouting book before it.

Twenty-five chapters of peril crowd the contents. A mysterious hot box, secret service duty, and a gang stopped by Jimmie open the run. Jimmie finds a spy, and bullets greet the boys. The Gray Eagle is damaged, a battle is fought in the air, and a journey with Joffre follows. Coffee with the Kaiser, a castle's underworld, and a musketeer's mistake close the list. The tale opens quietly on Long Island, three motorcyclists speeding for New York. Two of the riders wear the badges of the Black Bear Patrol.
62643-with-trumpet-and-drum:
Eugene Field gathered verse for children in a book first printed in 1892 and reissued at New York in 1897. Field made the volume from his Little Book of Western Verse, his Second Book of Verse, and the files of the Chicago Daily News, the Youth's Companion, and the Ladies' Home Journal. With big tin trumpet and little red drum, marching like soldiers, the children come, the title song cries.

It is this way and that way they circle and file, and the heart of the book has welcome and room for all. Come on, little people, from cot and from hall, the poet calls. Songs and warm love fill the pages. Parents of the age read Field aloud at bedtime, and his child verse set a mark few have matched since.
64575-sir-henry-irving-a-record-of-over-:
Percy Fitzgerald, who wrote lives of Garrick and the Kembles, chronicles the reign of Henry Irving at the Lyceum Theatre. Chatto and Windus issued this new edition at London in 1895. It adds a fresh chapter to the first printing.

Fitzgerald opens on the risks of the actor's road. Even now, he says, all is a lottery: theatres, pieces, actors. A house wins fame with one or two hits. Then the newest play falls, and another, and another. Against that ground he sets Irving's twenty years of rule. Touring companies roll past in Pullman cars, with pets and card games aboard. The record mixes backstage detail with the public triumphs. Irving was the first actor knighted in Britain, and this book caught his fame at its height.
64702-ultimatum:
Ultimatum is a science fiction tale by Roger Dee, taken from Planet Stories for spring 1950. Its scene is a dingy little Indiana hotel room's neighborhood, and its stakes are three worlds. Winant follows a sheriff down a jail corridor of empty cells. The last cell still holds his Uncle Ivor.

The sheriff can name no real charge against the old man. Ivor burst into a restaurant naked, carrying a little black box. He called himself a visitor from Mars and demanded the president. Winant sighs that Ivor has escaped before. Last time he thought he was Mahatma Ghandi and tried to buy a bus ticket to New Delhi. Dee lets the reader guess whether the old man is mad.
64967-clara-barton-a-centenary-tribute-t:
Clara Barton: A Centenary Tribute is a biography of the founder of the American Red Cross, by Charles Sumner Young, published in Boston by Richard G. Badger in 1922. Its subtitle calls Barton the world's greatest humanitarian. The title page also credits her as author of the American amendment to the Geneva Red Cross convention and founder of the National First Aid Association of America.

Young knew Barton personally and calls the book a set of pen pictures of a friend. The foreword admits he was barred from using data Barton herself left behind. The dedication addresses the boys and girls of the world. Written a century after Barton's birth, the tribute mixes firsthand affection with public record. It stands as an early monument to a woman whose relief work reshaped American disaster response.
65372-the-allen-county-war-memorial-coli:
The Allen County War Memorial Coliseum tells how Fort Wayne built its great arena as a war memorial. Otto Adams gave the address to the Quest Club in November 1953. The public library staff prepared the pamphlet in 1954. The book belongs to a history series from the library boards.

Both parties backed the bond issue, Adams records. Their chairmen signed a joint call to vote yes. The average cost to a taxpayer came to fifty five cents a year, the pitch ran. A basketball team played a benefit game and gave seventeen hundred dollars to the cause. The civic theatre staged a show for the fund as well. Speakers stressed that the shrine must serve the living, not the dead alone. The coliseum rose as a hall for sport, shows, and memory.
65482-the-green-millennium:
The Green Millennium is a science fiction novel by Fritz Leiber, published as an Ace Book in 1953. John Schoenherr drew the cover. The story follows Phil Gish, a timid man in a world he does not enjoy.

Phil is disillusioned and hopeless, and he fears a robot will take his job. The syndicated playground called All Amusements offers fun to those with the taste for it, but mild Phil finds no kicks there. One day a cat perches on his window, and it is no ordinary cat. The cat is green. Phil names it Lucky, feels happy for the first time in years, and loses it within minutes into the amusement park. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
65792-worlds-of-the-imperium:
Worlds of the Imperium is a science fiction novel by Keith Laumer, published by Ace Books in New York in 1962. Its cover line promises double trouble for a duplicate dictator. Brion Bayard finds an alternate Earth where history took a different turn. Kidnapped there, he meets identical doubles of famous persons, including a hated dictator named Brion Bayard.

His assignment looks simple: dressed as his double, he must enter the enemy stronghold, kill the dictator, and take his place. Once he sees his mirror-image brother, though, he loses all wish to murder him. Others, meanwhile, have little wish to let him live. Laumer builds a brisk tale of parallel worlds and switched rulers.
65859-the-architecture-of-the-north-loui:
The Architecture of the North Louisiana River Parishes, Volume One, covers Ouachita Parish. It comes out of the School of Art and Architecture at Louisiana Tech University. Students in the architecture program did the fieldwork, and Lestar Martin edited the volume. The book is dedicated to the memory of William King Stubbs. Stubbs practiced architecture in Ouachita Parish for over fifty years, and federal funds from the National Park Service helped pay for the work.

Parish surveys of this kind record the built stock house by house and street by street. They cover plantation houses, town houses, churches, and commercial blocks along the Ouachita River. Each entry fixes a building's form, fabric, and history before weather or demolition can erase it. The volume is both a work of scholarship and a tool for preservation in Monroe and its neighboring towns.
66390-imre-a-memorandum:
Imre, a Memorandum was edited by Xavier Mayne and printed at Naples in 1906 in a private, limited edition, with all rights reserved. The copy named in the front matter is number ten. In a prefatory letter the writer tells Mayne that the pages give a chapter out of his own life. The episode at first seemed too hard to write even to a friend.

The book falls into three parts named Masks, Masks and a Face, and Faces, Hearts, Souls. Its theme, set on the title page, is the friendship which is love and the love which is friendship. The writer calls the tale a true and deeply personal one, laid open with care. Few books of its time spoke so openly on such a bond.
67662-our-changing-morality-a-symposium:
Freda Kirchwey edited Our Changing Morality, a symposium issued by Albert and Charles Boni of New York in 1924. The volume gathers essays on the new sexual ethics of the day. Kirchwey's own opening piece sets the theme. Old rules, she writes, no longer hold men and women.

Her essay pictures a road with hawks of obscenity at one end. Dogmatic piety shouts warnings from the other end, and chaos fills the middle. Preachers like Straton and Sunday point a pleasant way toward hell. Sensation-hunting papers make headlines of new manners, she says. Novelists stumble their characters through inner conflict to darkness. Against all this, a few quiet workers sort the elements of chaos. They hold fragments of conduct up to sun and air. The book asks what new code can replace the old absolutes.
68387-washington-album:
Washington Album is a book of plates of the chief town of the United States. Jarvis of that town put it out in eighteen ninety one. The front plates show the great house of law. They show its round hall and its two house rooms. A wide view of the town names six teen chief marks.

The coin house and the state print house stand in that roll. Two rail roads and the great shaft stand there too. Then come views of the house of the chief. Its blue room has a plate of its own. The east room, red room, and green room have plates as well. The great shaft is shown with its cap stone in the set. The shaft stands five hundred and fifty five feet high. The book is a tour of the town in plates.
68825-the-curlytops-touring-around-or-th:
The Curlytops Touring Around, by Howard R Garis, is a children's adventure in the long Curlytops series, published in New York in 1925. Julia Greene drew the pictures.

The stories follow Ted and Janet Martin and their small brother William, whose jolly nickname is Trouble. The family takes to the road on a tour, carrying the Cardwell photograph albums. Midway through the trip the albums vanish, and the children turn detective on the trail. Chapters bring a fall down a well, a farm stay, funny fish, two bears, and a night at a lumber camp. Ted falls from a horse, Jan lands in a trap, and a lost box comes back. The trip ends aboard a motor boat on the lake.
69482-the-cats-arabian-nights-or-king-gr:
Abby Morton Diaz wrote The Cats' Arabian Nights, or King Grimalkum, printed at Boston under copyright in 1881 by Lothrop. The book is profusely illustrated by Francis, Boz, Palmer Cox, and others. A front picture shows a cat jumping upon the shoulder of a girl as she sews, which sets the playful tone.

King Grimalkum, a cat of parts, tells tales in the manner of the Arabian Nights, with cats in all the roles. Diaz was a reformer and a writer for children, and her cats carry gentle morals about kindness and vanity. Young readers get story within story, jokes, and fine pictures. Cat lovers of any age will find the court of Grimalkum hard to leave.
70206-the-carriages-at-shelburne-museum:
Lilian Baker Carlisle wrote this pamphlet on the carriages at Shelburne Museum in Vermont, copyrighted in 1956 as the first of the museum's pamphlet series. The museum keeps sleighs and carriages, light and heavy, many once owned by Dr and Mrs W Seward Webb.

Carlisle opens with a census fact: in 1900 the country had more than four thousand vehicle-making concerns, employing 126,000 men. Fifty years later the carriage trade had vanished. She urges owners of old carriages, catalogues, and shop books to give them to museums before they are lost. The pamphlet then describes the Shelburne set, a saved sample of the age of horse-drawn travel.
73111-lives-of-the-queens-of-england-of-:
Doran, an English man of letters known for Table Traits, wrote these lives of the queens of the House of Hanover. Bentley of London published this fourth edition, much enlarged, in eighteen seventy-five. This file holds the first of two volumes. The book is given to Henry Hill, a zealous antiquary and kind host.

Volume one treats Sophia Dorothea of Zell, wife of George the First. Chapters trace her kin at dice for a wife, her rise in rank, and the lovers and favorites of the Brunswick court. Court tales, births, deaths, and plots fill the pages in a chatty, learned style. Doran loves a good story and tells it well, with a scholar's store of names and dates at his back.
73112-lives-of-the-queens-of-england-of-:
Lives of the Queens of England of the House of Hanover, volume two, is by Doctor Doran. Bentley published the fourth edition, revised and much enlarged, at London in 1875. Doran also wrote Table Traits and Habits and Men, the title page notes. Contents of this volume continue the life of Charlotte Sophia from chapter four.

Births, deaths, and marriages heads that chapter in the contents list. Death of the Duke of Cumberland and his military career fill its summary. The soubriquet of the Butcher given him gets note in that summary line. Marriage of Caroline Matilda and her unhappy married life follow in the contents. Doctor Struensee and royal misalliances fill out the Hanover court picture here. Anecdote rich royal biography in the Doran manner fills the volume.
73341-the-artillerist-s-manual-and-briti:
The Artillerist's Manual and British Soldier's Compendium, by Major Griffiths of the Royal Artillery, is a handbook for gunners and soldiers. The seventh edition, published by authority, came out at London in 1856. Its Latin motto bids the reader who knows better to share his knowledge, and the rest to use this book in the meantime. Wide tables fill its pages, best read in fixed width type.

Griffiths notes the chief additions made since the sixth edition for officers who own it. The manual covers guns, ammunition, drill, and the daily work of the artilleryman. It also serves the common soldier with rules and facts of service. Such compendiums were the pocket libraries of the Victorian army. This one shows the science of gunnery as the Crimean War era practised it, in tables of fire. It is a working book, made to be used, not merely read.
74395-a-short-history-of-belgium:
Leon Van der Essen wrote A Short History of Belgium, in a second revised and enlarged edition issued at Chicago by the University of Chicago Press. Van der Essen was professor of history at the University of Louvain. A special chapter on Belgium during the Great War was added to this edition. The book is given to Albert the First, King of the Belgians.

Albert is called the knight without fear and without reproach. Chapter One treats the period of formation. Feudalism and the rise of the communes follow. Politics and struggles in the time of the communes fill Chapter Four. The union of the Belgian lands under the Dukes of Burgundy comes next. The first edition came in January 1916 and the second in January 1920. Sales ran through London, Tokyo, and Shanghai houses as well as Chicago.
74768-the-swing-of-the-pendulum:
The Swing of the Pendulum is a novel by Adriana Spadoni. Boni and Liveright published the book at New York in 1919. Five printings followed within two years, a sign of its welcome. The heroine is Jean Norris, met on her graduation day at a California college.

Jean comes slowly down the library steps with her gown over her arm. Dust powders her shoes as she crosses the parched campus to a creek. She drops under a scrub oak and looks back at the buildings. Four long years have ended in a day of ceremonies and fuss. Parents in stiff clothes hurry about, fearing foolish questions. Jean's tolerant smile sizes up the scene and her own past. Spadoni follows her heroine out of college into the working world.
75392-the-wonders-of-radium:
