Maynard Shipley wrote a small book on the wonders of radium for common readers. The Haldeman-Julius Company issued it at Girard, Kansas, in 1926. It stands as Little Blue Book Number 1000, edited by E Haldeman-Julius. Seven parts run from first facts to where radium is found.

Radium rays spur plant growth and serve in the treatment of cancer, Shipley writes. Spring waters famed for cures hold radium, a fresh find of the day. Bottled waters sold as radioactive hold too little to matter, a United States report warns. Readers gain a clear, era-marked primer on a marvel of the age.
76000-a-guide-to-the-egyptian-collection:
A Guide to the Egyptian Collections in the British Museum was printed in 1909 by order of the trustees. Price half-a-crown, it carries fifty-three plates and a hundred and eighty illustrations in the text. The preface sizes the collection at nearly fifty thousand objects, many sections of it unrivalled in completeness.

The antiquities run, the preface says, from about 4500 BC, as Egypt passed out of the predynastic period under a settled government. They run down to the fall of the queens Candace at Meroe in the second or third century after Christ. Christian Egypt forms a strong series of its own, Coptic carving and art from the sixth to the eleventh century. The guide offers the visitor a general sketch of the people's origin, manners, language, writing, literature, religion, and burial rites.
76157-barnum:
Werner wrote Barnum, a biography of the great American showman, with a copyright of 1923. Phineas Taylor Barnum rose from a Connecticut country store to rule the world of popular amusement. A portrait from the 1870 edition of Barnum's own life story faces the title page.

Chapters trace the Connecticut Yankee's growing pains, his American Museum in New York, and his travels with the midget Tom Thumb. The Jenny Lind tour, the Swedish Nightingale in the American woods, takes two chapters. Then come bankruptcy, his book on the art of money-getting, and the circus that made his name immortal. Werner writes briskly, with a clear eye for both the humbug and the genius.
77316-memorium:
Basil Wells wrote this science fiction story about a future where every person's thoughts are recorded on memorium tapes. The frame asks a hard question: could you bear to have all your thoughts laid bare, from cradle to grave, for historians or for your next door neighbour? The blurb warns that an old man's memories, faithfully recorded, may change the future of mankind.

Vance Norall, at one hundred and thirty, tells his great-great-grandson about Elsie, the first of the boy's great-great-grandmothers. She was tall, dark, a fine rider, swimmer, and golfer. Her tapes, brought to Norall after her death in a car crash, showed him a side of her he never suspected. Wells builds a wry, bitter tale on the danger of perfect memory.
77351-ten-years-in-a-portsmouth-slum:
Ten Years in a Portsmouth Slum is a memoir by Robert Dolling, late priest in charge of Saint Agatha's, Landport, under the Winchester College Mission. Swan Sonnenschein of London published it with eighteen full-page illustrations. Four editions appeared between May 1896 and July 1897.

Dolling dedicates the book to his sisters and to three women workers. Their ten years of endurance, he says, are the real subject, since the book is virtually an account of their work. A prefatory note shows him in America, preaching between Philadelphia and Boston and selling out his copies. The mission stood in one of England's roughest naval parishes. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
78743-harmonium:
Wallace Stevens published his first book of poems, Harmonium, in New York in 1923. Stevens gave the book to his wife. Most poems had first run in small magazines, in Poetry of Chicago above all. Earthy Anecdote opens the book, and Invective against Swans follows.

The Snow Man, Domination of Black, and Le Monocle de Mon Oncle stand among its famed pieces. The long Comedian as the Letter C anchors the mid book. Florida, sugar cane, bananas, and sea shores give color to many poems, while cold northern scenes give contrast. Stevens mixes high thought with odd, bright images. Harmonium became a landmark of modern American poetry for later readers.
78918-senator-fulbright-s-secret-memoran:
Senator Fulbright’s Secret Memorandum is a pamphlet by James Bales, printed at Searcy, Arkansas, in 1962. Bales opens with a warning from a liberal writer on the Cold War. Many on the democratic side, that writer said, hardly know what Communism is. The pamphlet takes up a memorandum by Senator Fulbright as its theme.

The stated aim is to lay facts before the administration of the day. Supporters of the memorandum had pressed it on the government. Norman Thomas is quoted in its favour in the front matter. Bales writes from the anti communist right, against that backing. The pamphlet is a piece of Cold War polemic in print. It shows how a Senate paper could stir a fight far from Washington.
78995-gordon-at-khartoum:
Gordon at Khartoum is a personal narrative by Wilfrid Scawen Blunt, printed in London in 1911. It carries on his earlier Secret History of the English Occupation of Egypt. Twelve chapters run from the Dufferin settlement to the general election of 1885. A set of appendices holds unpublished papers of General Gordon and letters to and from the author.

Then come Gordon in Palestine, his last mission, and the blunt question of one chapter title: was Gordon disobedient? Later chapters tell of the stir about Gordon in London, Blunt's own barring from Egypt, and Gordon's death, with chaos after it. Blunt writes as a partisan of the Egyptian national movement and a foe of the occupation. The appendices print Gordon papers, correspondence with Downing Street, and the views of Arabi and Mohammed Abdu.
8744-a-sportsman-s-sketches-volume-2-wor:
Ivan Turgenev's second volume of A Sportsman's Sketches, in Constance Garnett's translation, continues the hunting narrator's wanderings through rural Russia. New sketches include Tatyana Borissovna and her nephew, Death, The Singers, Piotr Petrovitch Karataev, The Tryst, and the hamlet of the Shchigri district. TcherTop-Hanov and Nedopyuskin appear in two linked pieces, and A Living Relic, The Rattling of Wheels, and an epilogue on the forest and the steppe close the book.

The narrator's invitation, give me your hand, gentle reader, and come along, sets the tone: glorious May weather, tender blue sky. Young willow leaves frame encounters with peasants, singers, and dying men. Serfdom's human cost stays in view without preaching. Readers who finished volume one will find the same humane eye here, with some of Turgenev's finest short pieces, including the celebrated singers' contest.
9373-pax-vobiscum:
Henry Drummond wrote this short religious book in 1890, second in a series begun with The Greatest Thing in the World. Its text is Christ's call: come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Drummond heard a fine sermon on rest one morning, full of beautiful thoughts, yet with no answer to how rest is gained.

His chapters ask what yokes are for, how fruits grow, and what effects require causes. The book seeks a practical path to peace, not just praise of it. It remains a beloved Victorian devotional, simple, earnest, and warm.
9667-specimens-with-memoirs-of-the-less-:
Volume one of George Gilfillan's Specimens, with Memoirs of the Less-Known British Poets, opens with an essay on English poetry's origins. Gilfillan traces verse from Roman Britain through a glimmering dawn to Chaucer, father of English poetry, and Gower. He notes Rome left Britain nearly as rude as it found it, with no British-born Latin masters. Arthur's coronation scenes open the survey.

The volume pairs early poets with memoirs and choice pieces, guiding general readers through a young art. Gilfillan writes with warmth for forgotten voices. A reader gets a learned, readable start to English verse, and a sense of poetry's slow growth from chronicle to song.
9668-specimens-with-memoirs-of-the-less-:
Volume two of George Gilfillan's Specimens, with Memoirs of the Less-Known British Poets, covers the second period from Spenser to Dryden. Poets inside include William Habington, Joseph Hall, Richard Lovelace, and Robert Herrick, with Cherry-Ripe and To Daffodils among Herrick's pieces. Sir Richard Fanshawe, Abraham Cowley, and George Wither follow, with Marvell, Davenant, and others.

Each poet gets a memoir plus choice poems, so a reader can taste a wide age in brief. Gilfillan's notes place each voice in its time. A reader gets a rich anthology of minor masters, and a fine path into seventeenth-century English verse beyond the famous names.
a-journal-from-our-legation-in-belgium: Hugh Gibson keeps a journal from the American legation in Belgium. As secretary of the legation in Brussels, he records wartime Belgium with photographs, including King Albert. Gibson's journal gives a diplomat's close view of a country at war. The book preserves firsthand evidence of Belgium in 1914 and after. The close view helps readers grasp war as diplomats saw it day by day.
a-sportsman-s-sketches-volume-2-works-of: Ivan Turgenev continues his sportsman's sketches in this second volume, translated from the Russian by Constance Garnett. The contents include Tatyana Borissovna and her nephew, Death, The Singers, Piotr Petrovitch Karataev, The Tryst, the hamlet of the Shtchigri district, and Tchertop-Hanov with Nedopyuskin. A living relic, the rattling of wheels, and an epilogue on forest and steppe close a volume that invites the reader to walk the May countryside.
a-surgeon-in-belgium: Henry Sessions Souttar, assistant surgeon at West London Hospital and late surgeon-in-chief of a Belgian field hospital, recounts a surgeon's war in Belgium. Stepping aboard a boat for Ostend one Saturday afternoon in September, his party went to see the war for themselves. They meant to become part of it. The contents run from Antwerp and the hospital through Termonde, Malines, and Lierre to siege, bombardment by night and day, a night journey, Furnes, and Ypres.
banzai-by-parabellum:
Ferdinand Heinrich Grautoff, writing as Parabellum, published this future-war novel at Leipzig in 1908; Baker and Taylor issued it in New York the next year. Parabellum imagines a Japanese attack on the United States, opening in Manila and moving to the high seas. A frontispiece spots Togo's battleship Satsuma, and chapter titles promise the red sun over the Golden Gate.

American officers carry the story: Lieutenant Meade finds his comrade Besser, nicknamed the Reverend for his theology, hammering wildly at a piano in the officers' mess on the eve of action. Later chapters give Admiral Perry's fate, Captain Winstanley's ordeal, and a forty-eight-hour balance sheet of the war. Grautoff, a German journalist, wrote invasion fiction as warning; America's Pacific defences are his sermon in novel form.
belgium:
Joseph E. Morris's Belgium, a volume in the Beautiful Europe series, opens by apologizing for its own title. It needs an effort of imagination, he writes, to think of Belgium as beautiful Europe at this hour. The cockpit of the Continent is accomplishing its frightful destiny. No treaty, no scrap of paper, can save the weakest nation of Western Europe from drinking the cup of ruin. Morris wrote as the German invasion of 1914 made his travel book an elegy.

Inside, the tour proceeds city by city through the Belgium of the guidebooks: churches, belfries, lace, and canals, now read against the news. His chapters on Bruges, Ghent, and Brussels carry a double exposure of art and war. Readers get a minor classic of unintended history: a belle-époque travel portrait overtaken, between writing and printing, by the event that made Belgium a byword.
britannica-1911-abomasum: Abomasum is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry names the fourth or rennet stomach of ruminant animals, called caillette in French. Food passes from the omasum into it at last. The cavity is larger than the second or third stomach, though less than the first, and shaped like an uneven cone. This stomach matches the single stomach of other mammals: here food turns to chyme after grinding in the three before it.
britannica-1911-acetabulum:
Acetabulum was the Latin word for a vinegar cup, a small ancient Roman vessel also used as a liquid measure of about half a gill. The 1911 Britannica entry traces how a kitchen word became a scientific one. Anatomists and zoologists borrowed it by analogy for cup-shaped parts of the body.

Examples show the range. The suckers of a mollusc, such as an octopus, are acetabula, and so is the socket of the thigh-bone, the cup in the hip into which the ball of the femur fits. Botany borrowed the word too, for the receptacle of fungi, the part that bears their fruiting structures. One small cup gave its name to cups everywhere in nature.
britannica-1911-acroterium: An acroterium, in architecture, is a statue or ornament of any kind placed on the apex, the highest point, of a pediment. That triangular gable crowning a classical temple front carried such ornaments at its peak. This entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica adds a caution about usage: the term is often restricted to the plinth itself, the small podium or block that merely supports the ornament. Readers of architectural writing should therefore check whether a writer means the crowning figure or only its base.
britannica-1911-actium:
Actium was a promontory in northern Acarnania, Greece. It stands at the mouth of the Gulf of Arta. An ancient temple of Apollo Actius crowned it. Augustus enlarged that temple after his victory. He also renewed the games called Actia there. A small town shared the promontory's name. The place is famous for one day, though. Octavian defeated Mark Antony off Actium. The battle fell on the second of September, 31 B.C.

Fleets over two hundred strong met outside the gulf. Antony's heavy ships tried to close and crush. Octavian's light craft skirmished skilfully instead. Cleopatra suddenly withdrew her squadron mid-battle. Antony slipped away behind her, unnoticed. His leaderless fleet was burned and annihilated. Augustus built Nicopolis across the strait in memory.
britannica-1911-album:
Album, a word with a long history, is traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. From the Latin albus, white, an album in ancient Rome was a board chalked or painted white. Public business was written on it in black. The yearly records of the chief priest, the praetor's annual edicts, and the lists of senators and jurors were all displayed in that manner.

Later ages turned the word to new uses. In medieval and modern times an album is a book of blank pages where verses, autographs, sketches, and photographs are collected. Universities use the word for the official list of matriculated students, students formally enrolled. A bishop's roll of his clergy also bears the name. In law, album is the equivalent of mailles blanches, rent paid in silver, or white, money.
britannica-1911-alburnum: Alburnum, or sapwood, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as the outermost and youngest part of a tree's wood. Sap rises through this layer as the tree grows, which gives it the sapwood name. The entry sets it against the tree's harder inner and older wood, called the duramen or heart-wood. Together the two terms mark the basic division inside a trunk between the living, sap-carrying outer wood and the dense, mature wood at the core that gives the tree its strength.
britannica-1911-algum:
Algum, also spelled almug, names a prized timber named in First Kings and Second Chronicles, where the Hebrew forms are algummim and almuggim. One spelling, almug, is a mistaken form. Ships serving Hiram brought the wood from Ophir, likely part of India, together with gold and gems, for Solomon at Jerusalem.

In the temple and the royal house the timber served as pillars and stair inlay, and craftsmen made it into harps and psalteries. The tree was most likely India's red sanders, whose wood is red, dense, heavy, and tight in grain. That sets it apart from the pale, sweet-smelling sandalwood of a separate tree and family.
britannica-1911-antonini-itinerarium:
Antonini Itinerarium is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a Roman road list. The work is a register of stops and gaps along the roads of the empire. It still exists, and the entry calls it a work of real worth. It seems based on state papers from a survey begun under Julius Caesar.

No one knows for sure who made it, or just when. The first form may date to the start of the third century. The form we have is placed in the time of Diocletian. If an emperor drove the work, it was most likely Caracalla. Old printings of the work are named at the end, from 1735 on.
britannica-1911-aquarium:
Aquarium names a tank or building that holds sea plants and sea animals, and a long entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica shows how its role had grown. Once little more than home toys or popular show-places, aquaria had gained deep value for science. They let scholars study the bodies and lives of sea creatures at close hand.

The entry adds a trade value too, since knowing how food fish live is the base for better sea fisheries. It points to the zoological stations spread across Europe, the United States, and Japan. The oldest and chief of these, at Naples, is then described in detail through a staff account of its gear and aims.
britannica-1911-arboretum:
Arboretum is the name for the part of a garden or park set aside for trees. The word in this strict sense seems first used in 1838. J. C. Loudon used it in his book on tree collections. Bayley Balfour of Edinburgh gave a clear account of what such a place is. It is a living set of tree and shrub kinds, set out by some clear plan. Likeness in nature is the usual plan.

Such a collection is in essence a teaching one. Some writers stress beauty of scene more than strict order. All agree that science needs order in the planting. A woodland of this kind also does plain good. It gives shelter, softens the local air, and mends poor soils. It adds worth to the land in art and in cash.
britannica-1911-asylum:
Asylum is a word for a place of refuge. Its Greek roots mean a place safe from seizure. In ancient Greece, an asylum was a refuge that none might breach for men in flight. In a broad sense, all Greek temples and altars were safe in this way. It was a crime before the gods to drag a man by force from a god's care.

In fact, the right was held with common consent by a small count of temples alone. The shrines of Zeus Lycaeus in Arcadia, of Poseidon in Calauria, and of Apollo at Delos were of that kind. Such shrines gave full safety to the man who pled at them, inside their bounds. The right was at first held by all temples. Ill use of it led to its being cut back to a few.
britannica-1911-atrium:
Atrium is a term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains the main hall or court at the heart of a Roman house. The hall gave light and entry to the rooms placed around it. Its roof had an open space in the centre, and rain fell into a stone tank below.

The entry traces how the hall was used in early and later Roman life. At first it served for guests, meals, and daily work, with the hearth and family shrine inside. Rich homes later built rooms for each use and kept the hall for guests. The same word was also used for halls by temples and for courts in front of early churches.
britannica-1911-augusta-bagiennorum:
Augusta Bagiennorum is a ruins article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the chief town of a Ligurian tribe in Italy. The town most likely stood where the modern Bene Vagienna stands. That is on the upper Tanaro river, about thirty five miles south of Turin.

The article notes that the town kept its place as a tribal centre under Augustus. It took his name and was laid out on a set plan. Digs in recent years had laid bare a rich set of public works. The finds take in a forum, baths, a water channel, and a city gate with two towers. A great open air theatre for games had a long axis of 390 feet. A stage house near by ran 133 feet in length. The walls were built of poured stone faced with small stones and bands of brick.
britannica-1911-augusta-praetoria-salass:
Augusta Praetoria Salassorum, the modern Aosta, was an old town of Italy in the land of the Salassi, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out its Roman remains. Augustus founded it about 24 years before Christ, on the camp site of the man who had beaten the Salassi the year before. Three thousand guard troops were settled there.

Its spot gave it weight in war. The town stands where two rivers meet, at the foot of the Great and Little Saint Bernard passes, and Pliny called it the last town of Italy to the north west. The old walls still stand near complete, a square of stone faced concrete with twenty towers. Gates on the east and south survive, the south gate a fine double gate with three arches. The straight streets still keep the Roman plan, so a walker can read the first town in the modern one.
britannica-1911-auximum:
Auximum, modern Osimo, was an ancient town in Picenum. It sits on an isolated hill. The Adriatic is eight miles away. The Ancona to Nuceria road passes it. Romans selected it as a fortress site. It protected their settlements in northern Picenum. Strong fortification came in 174 B.C. Walls of large rectangular stone blocks survive. Great part of those walls still exists.

Auximum became a Roman colony by 157 B.C. at latest. Civil wars feature it often in history. Its strong position explains that prominence. Pompey was its patron in those wars. He intended Caesar to meet resistance there in 49. Imperial times kept it important evidently. Inscriptions and forum monuments prove that. Procopius calls it Picenum's chief town in the sixth century. Ancona served as its harbour then. Thomas Ashby signs the notice.
britannica-1911-avizandum: Avizandum is a Scots law term, from a Late Latin word meaning to consider. A judge who makes avizandum with a cause takes time to think over the case before giving judgment, rather than deciding at once from the bench. The short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry records just this usage, naming the practice by which Scottish courts pause for reflection before a decision is delivered.
britannica-1911-axum:
Axum, or Aksum, is an ancient city in the province of Tigré, Abyssinia, set over 7,200 feet high west of Adowa. A Greek travel account of about A.D. 67 already names it as seat of a kingdom and the trading place for ivory brought from the west.

Abyssinian kings were still crowned at Axum as late as 1871, and its chief church gave sanctuary, sheltering offenders and guarding goods in danger like a bank. The modern town of under a thousand houses covers only part of the old city. About fifty carved obelisks still stand, the tallest sixty feet high, with many more fallen, and most of the ruins still await digging. For the kingdom's history the entry sends readers to Ethiopia.
britannica-1911-barium:
Barium, symbol Ba and atomic weight 137.37, is a metallic element of the alkaline earth group. Its name comes from the Greek word for heavy, since it occurs in barytes, or heavy spar. That mineral was first studied in 1602 by a Bologna shoemaker, Casciorolus, who found it glowed after ignition with combustible stuff, earning it the name Bolognian phosphorus.

Scheele found the new earth in 1774 while examining pyrolusite. Barium occurs chiefly as barytes and witherite, and the pure metal proved hard to isolate: Davy's attempts by electrolysis failed, though he got an amalgam using mercury. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, goes on to the element's compounds, preparation, and uses in chemical detail.
britannica-1911-bateman-hezekiah-linthic:
Hezekiah Linthicum Bateman (1812–1875), an American actor and manager born in Baltimore, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Meant to be an engineer, he turned to the stage in 1832 and played young leads with Ellen Tree. He managed theatres in St Louis and New York, then in 1871 took the Lyceum theatre in London. There he engaged Henry Irving and first set him before London crowds in The Bells, with great success.

Family carries the second half. His wife Sidney Frances, an actress and writer of plays, ran the Lyceum after his death in 1875 and later took Sadler's Wells. She first brought a full American company to England with an American play, Joaquin Miller's The Danites. Of their eight children, the best known were the “Bateman children,” Kate and Ellen, who acted as girls. Kate later played Juliet, Lady Macbeth, and Tennyson's Queen Mary.
britannica-1911-batum:
Batum is a seaport of Russian Transcaucasia, on the south-east shore of the Black Sea, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies ninety miles by rail south-west of Kutais, and strong forts guard the town. Its bay is filling with sand washed in by small rivers, and harbour works have much improved the anchorage. The people grew from 2000 in 1875 to 28,512 in 1900, of very mixed races. 

Oil rules the port's trade. Batum is the chief outlet for naphtha and paraffin oil, much of it piped from Baku and the rest brought in tank rail cars. Wheat, manganese, wool, and timber also go out. The climate is very warm, with lemons, oranges, and palms in the open air, yet it is the wettest place in Caucasia and still unhealthy. The town passed from Turkey to Russia in 1878.
britannica-1911-bdellium: Bdellium, a Greek word used by Pliny and Dioscorides for a plant that gave off a sweet-smelling gum, names several gums and gum-resins. These look much like true myrrh and are sometimes mixed into it as adulterants, standing in for the real thing. The whole entry is this short note: the word’s old use, what the stuff is, and its place beside myrrh, to which readers are sent for more.
britannica-1911-belgaum:
Belgaum is a town and district of British India, in the southern division of Bombay. The town stands nearly 2,500 feet above the sea, 245 miles south of Poona by rail. An old fort of about a hundred acres holds two Jain temples of note, and a cantonment there houses a brigade.

The district covers 4,649 square miles, open and well farmed to the north and east, cut by forested spurs of the Sahyadri range to the south. Millet, rice, wheat, cotton and sugar-cane are its main crops, and cotton cloth is woven in quantity. The town’s old name, Venugrama, is said to come from its bamboos.
britannica-1911-beryllium:
Beryllium, also called glucinum, is a metallic element grouped with magnesium in the periodic table. Its symbol is Be, and its atomic weight is about 9.1. Vauquelin prepared its oxide from the mineral beryl in 1798. The metal itself came later, and in impure form at first. Bussy and Wöhler made it in 1828 by reducing the chloride with potassium. Debray made it in a compact state in 1855, using melted sodium.

The 1911 Britannica article describes a light and malleable metal. It melts at a heat below the melting point of silver. In a fine powder it catches fire when heated in air. The article then works through its chief compounds and salts. A long-running dispute over the exact atomic weight closes the piece. Rival analyses gave values that clustered close to nine.
britannica-1911-birbhum:
Birbhum is a district of British India in the Burdwan division of Bengal. It sits partly on the Gangetic plain and partly on hills, bounded south by the river Ajai. Its area is 1,752 square miles. The east is the usual delta alluvium, flat and low. The west is undulating laterite beds over rock, covered with scrub jungle. The Ajai, Bakheswar, and Mor rivers cross it, but they run as hill streams, navigable only in the rains.

Suri, the headquarters, is the district's only town, the 1911 Britannica entry notes. The 1901 population was 902,280, up thirteen percent in the decade. Silk spinning and weaving, chiefly from tussur silkworms, lead its industries. Lac factories also work in the district. The East Indian railway's loop line runs through it. Its history runs from a Hindu state of the 13th century to quiet British rule after 1789.
britannica-1911-brundisium:
Brundisium, modern Brindisi, was an important harbour town of Calabria in the ancient sense, on Italy's east-south-east coast. Its name is said to mean stag's head in the Messapian dialect, matching the harbour's shape. Tradition varies on its founders, but the town stood hostile to Tarentum and friendly with Thurii, and with fertile land around it became the most important city of the Messapians.

Rome developed it: the town came into Roman hands only after the conquest of the Sallentini in 266 BC, a colony was founded in 245 BC. The Via Appia was perhaps extended through Tarentum to Brundisium at that period. Pacuvius was born there about 220 BC. After the Punic Wars it became the chief embarkation point for Greece and the East. It received Roman citizenship in the Social War, was made a free port by Sulla, suffered Caesar's siege in 49 BC.
britannica-1911-cadmium:
The 1911 Britannica article on cadmium treats a metallic element, symbol Cd. The metal is closely related to zinc. It is found with zinc in nature. Cadmium was found in 1817 by Stromeyer in a zinc sample. The German maker Hermann found the same new metal at about the same time.

The article covers where the metal occurs. One rare mineral, greenockite, holds it in quantity. It also appears in zinc ores. The metal is drawn from the flue dust of zinc works. The article explains how it is purified. It then gives the metal's properties. These include a white colour with a blue tinge. They also include a fibrous break and a low melting point.
britannica-1911-caesium:
Caesium, one of the alkali metals, is described in a chemistry article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its name comes from a Latin word for sky-blue. Two bright blue lines in its spectrum gave the metal its name. It holds a place in history as the first metal found by aid of the spectroscope.

Bunsen announced that finding in 1860, though its salts had been handled before. Earlier workers had mistaken those salts for salts of potassium. The metal turns up in certain mineral springs in Germany, Italy, and Cornwall. It also occurs in several minerals, often alongside rubidium. Drawing it out of those sources is slow and hard work. Bunsen's method rests on repeated parting of its platinum salts, which dissolve far less freely than those of the sister metals.
britannica-1911-calcium:
Calcium is a metal element found all through nature in combined form, as a 1911 Britannica entry sets out. Davy named it from the Latin word for chalk, where it occurs. It never shows free in nature, yet its compounds are vast in scale. They form gypsum, chalk, marble, fluorspar, and much of common rock.

Lime, its oxide, was known from old times and long thought a simple earth. In 1808 Davy showed that lime joins a metal with oxygen gas. His bids to free the pure metal fell short of full success. Pure calcium stayed a rare lab item until the start of the new century.
britannica-1911-capernaum:
Capernaum, the lost town of Galilee, is hunted in a site entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its name most likely means the village of Nahum in old speech. No town ties more close to the home life of Jesus. There he preached, called pupils, and did many works of note. Yet its folk gave him a cold ear, the Gospels say.

His stern words on the town close that part of the tale. Where the town stood is a point of hot dispute still. One camp sets it at Khan Minyeh on the lake's west shore. Springs named Seven Springs by Josephus flow near that site in Galilee. The rival camp backs Tell Hum, a wide ruin field north. Its ruins prove a town of no small size stood there.
britannica-1911-capsicum:
Capsicum is a genus of plants whose fruits are peppers. This 1911 Britannica article treats the drug made from them. The botany is left to the article on cayenne pepper. In medicine, the ripe fruit is the part used. Its active principle is capsaicin, first isolated by Thresh in 1876. The article sets out its strong effects on the body. Laid on skin, it causes redness and then blistering.

Taken inwardly in small doses, capsicum rouses the stomach. It increases the gastric secretions and dilates the vessels. Long excess brings on inflammation of the stomach. Large single doses irritate the kidneys and cause strangury. Doctors valued it for a weak, slack stomach. It helped cases tied to chronic alcoholism in particular. It eased the flatulence of the aged as well. Plasters of capsicum served for rheumatism and lumbago. Capsicum wool, steeped in the oleoresin, was used for the same pains.
britannica-1911-carborundum:
Carborundum is a hard compound of silicon and carbon. It is formed by carbon acting on sand at high heat. This 1911 Britannica article describes its making and uses. Its great hardness makes it an important abrasive. It may also serve in the metallurgy of iron and steel. The name joins carbon to corundum, a form of alumina. That name rests on a mistaken view of its composition.

Acheson first obtained carborundum by accident in 1891. He was working in America with the electric furnace. He had hoped to produce artificial diamonds instead. The furnace process was then developed for industry. The article describes the furnace in full detail. It is a brick box about 16 feet long and 5 feet wide. Carbon poles pass through its massive end walls. The charge mixes coke, sand, sawdust and salt in set parts. Current from a dynamo heats the mass to reaction.
britannica-1911-carnuntum:
Carnuntum is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an important Roman fortress town in lower Austria, near Hainburg between Deutsch-Altenburg and Petronell. The town began as a Celtic settlement, and its name comes from a word for rock or cairn. It first belonged to Noricum and passed to Pannonia after the first century. Its wide ruins still stand, and a special society exists to explore them.

The entry traces the town's rise under Rome. In A.D. 6 Tiberius used Carnuntum as his base against Maroboduus, and it later anchored the Danube defences from Vienna to Brigetio. Hadrian raised it to a municipium, and Marcus Aurelius lived there for three years while writing part of his Meditations. Septimius Severus was proclaimed emperor there in 193. German attacks in the fourth century began a decline that Hungarian destruction in the middle ages completed.
britannica-1911-cavaedium:
Cavaedium is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the Latin name for the central hall or court of a Roman house. Vitruvius describes five species of it. The first is the Tuscan type, the commonest at Pompeii. Its roof timbers leave an open space in the centre, the compluvium. All light for the hall and the rooms round it came through that opening. Rain fell into a basin in the floor, the impluvium.

The other types vary the support and the roof. The tetrastyle type adds columns at the four angles of the impluvium. The Corinthian type adds more columns still. In the displuviate type the roofs slope outward, and Vitruvius warns that it always needs repair, since the rain pipes clog. The testudinate type covers a small hall with a floor above it. No example of it has been found at Pompeii.
britannica-1911-cerium:
Cerium is a metallic element found with the rare earths in nature. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its symbol as Ce in chemistry. Its atomic weight is set at a bit over 140 in the entry. It occurs in stones such as cerite, monazite, and parisite in the earth. Klaproth found the earth that holds it in the year 1803.

Berzelius at the same time judged it the oxide of a new metal. He gave that new metal the name cerium that it still bears. Workers draw the crude oxide from cerite with strong sulphuric acid. The mass is dissolved in ice cold water and passed with gas. It is then thrown down as oxalate and burned to oxide form.
britannica-1911-chenopodium:
Chenopodium is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a genus of herbs, called goose foot, in the natural order Chenopodiaceae. The plants stand erect or lie flat. They usually grow on the seashore, or on waste or cultivated ground. The green angular stem is often striped with white or red. Stem and leaves are often covered with mealy hairs. The leaves are entire, lobed, or toothed, and often roughly triangular.

The flowers are minute and two sexed. They are borne in dense clusters in the leaf axils or at the ends of the stems. The fruit is a thin walled, one seeded utricle, often held inside the lasting calyx. Ten species occur in Britain. One of them, Good King Henry, is grown as a pot herb in place of asparagus. It goes by the names mercury and all good.
britannica-1911-chromium:
Chromium is one of the metallic chemical elements, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives its place in nature and its finding. Its name comes from the fine colour of its compounds, from a Greek word for colour. It belongs to the sixth group of the elements, in the family that holds molybdenum, tungsten, and uranium. The metal is never found free in nature, and only in small amounts in combination.

It occurs chiefly as chrome-ironstone, and now and then as crocoisite and chrome-ochre. Vauquelin and Macquart first studied it in 1789. In 1797 Vauquelin showed that the lead in crocoisite was bound with an acid that was the oxide of a new metal. The entry then gives ways of winning the metal itself, a very hard steel-grey substance that takes a high polish.
britannica-1911-chrysanthemum:
Chrysanthemum is one of the most loved autumn flowers in gardens. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its home as China, from which it reached Europe. The first plant in England grew at Kew in 1790, it says. A first show of the flower in England came only in 1825.

Forms range from neat incurved blooms to loose Japanese sorts in trade. Pompon kinds with small blooms came from the Chusan daisy line. As a border plant it grows with ease and suits town air well. Chosen kinds can flower from August into late November outdoors. Cuttings in winter give the best path to new plants, it advises.
britannica-1911-ciborium:
Ciborium is a name in classical Latin for a drinking vessel, taken from the Greek kiborion, the cup-shaped seed vessel of the Egyptian water-lily. Its seeds were known as Egyptian beans, the entry notes. In the early Christian Church the word named a canopy over the altar, supported on columns. From that canopy hung the receptacle in which the consecrated wafer of the Eucharist was reserved for use.

Use of the word shifted early from the canopy to the vessel holding the reserved sacrament itself. In the Western Church the canopy took the name baldaquin instead, while pyx now names the vessel used for the sick and dying. Medieval pyxes and ciboria are often fine work by goldsmiths, enamellers and metal workers. Most take the shape of a covered chalice or of a round box with a cross-topped cover.
britannica-1911-clastidium:
Clastidium, now Casteggio, a village in northern Italy, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stood on a great Roman road, five miles east of Iria and thirty-one miles west of Placentia. It never held a government of its own. By the year 190 before Christ it had been made part of the colony of Placentia.

The article gives the village two moments of fame in war. In 222 before Christ the Roman leader Marcellus beat the Gauls there and won the highest spoils a general could take. In 218 Hannibal seized the place and its stores of corn by treachery. What can still be seen there is scant, the entry says. A fountain bears Hannibal's name, and a Roman bridge built of tiles, not stone, was found in 1857 but later destroyed.
britannica-1911-clusium:
Clusium, modern Chiusi, was an ancient town of Italy, one of the twelve cities of Etruria, set on an isolated hill at the south end of the Clanis valley. Roman tradition made it one of the oldest cities of Etruria and of all Italy. If its first name Camars is rightly linked with the Camertes Umbri, its founding goes back to pre-Etruscan times. It first appears in Roman history at the end of the 7th century B.C.

Under its king Lars Porsena at the end of the 6th century B.C. it headed the attempt to restore the Tarquins in Rome. By 391 B.C. it stood on friendly terms with Rome, and Roman envoys' breach of law there moved the Gauls to march on Rome. A battle near Clusium in 296 B.C. pitted Gauls and Samnites against Romans. When it came under Roman supremacy is uncertain.
britannica-1911-coenaculum:
Coenaculum was the term for the eating room of a Roman house. The supper, or coena, the last meal of the day, was taken there. The room sometimes sat in an upper storey. An outside stair led up to it in such cases. The name thus ties the room to the meal, not to its size or shape.

One use of the room gives the entry its weight. The Last Supper of the New Testament was taken in a coenaculum. The Gospels call it a large upper room. The entry cites St Mark, chapter fourteen, and St Luke, chapter twenty-two, for that phrase. Though short, the entry fixes both the Roman sense and the scriptural one. A reader learns where Romans ate and where a key Gospel scene was set.
britannica-1911-colchicum:
The 1911 Britannica article on colchicum describes a lasting meadow plant. It is the meadow saffron, or autumn crocus. It grows wild in rich moist meadows. It is found in England, Ireland, and much of Europe. It has pale purple flowers. It has three or four flat leaves. It has no stem.

The article follows the plant's odd yearly cycle. The corm flowers in autumn. It sends up leaves and seed the next spring. The article gives notes on growing the plant in gardens. It then turns to the plant's history as a drug. The Greeks knew it as a poison. It came into wide use in 1763. It was long valued as a remedy for gout.
britannica-1911-combaconum:
Combaconum, also called Kumbakonam, is a city of British India. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its temples and tanks. It lies in the delta of the Cauvery in Madras. The South Indian railway serves it on the line from Madras.

Its count in 1901 was near sixty thousand, up a tenth in ten years. Wide airy streets cross the large town in fair order. Pagodas and gateways of great show adorn its quarters. One gate pyramid rises twelve stories over a hundred feet. Stucco figures of men and beasts crowd its faces. A town tank is said to fill from the Ganges each twelve years. Pilgrims flock to that tank from far away as a result. The city was once capital of the ancient Chola line. Brass ware, silk, cotton, and sugar are made there.
britannica-1911-compluvium: Compluvium is the Latin word for the open gap in the roof of a Roman house hall. The 1911 Britannica note gives the term in two short lines. Rain fell through that gap and was caught in the hall floor. The gap let light pour in for the hall and the rooms round it. The word springs from a Latin root for flow to one place. The note sends the reader to the hall entry for more on the house plan.
britannica-1911-corfinium:
Corfinium, in ancient Italy, was the chief city of the Paeligni, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It lay north of Sulmona in the valley of the Aternus river. The site of the old town is held by a modern village. It most likely came under Rome in the fourth century before Christ.

It enters Roman history in the Social War of ninety before Christ. The allies took it as the capital of their new state, under the name Italia. Coins vouch for that name, the entry says. It also stands out as a fortress in the Civil War, though it resisted Caesar for only a week. Great roads met there in imperial times, so it must have been a town of some size. Carved records and the spread of its buildings support that view.
britannica-1911-corundum:
Corundum, a mineral made of native alumina, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is noted for its great hardness and, in its fine forms, for gem worth. Stones sent from India were set out in 1798 under this name. The name is thought to come from an Indian word for ruby.

The clear, rich hued forms are the ruby and the sapphire, the piece shows. The coarse, grainy forms are known as emery. Other forms, not clear enough for gems, were once called imperfect corundum. One brown kind with a pearly sheen bears the name adamantine spar. The stone forms crystals in the six sided system. Next to diamond, it is the hardest known mineral.
britannica-1911-crinum:
Crinum is a genus of bulbous plants in the natural order Amaryllidaceae. Its species have rather broad leaves and a solid, leafless stem. That stem bears a cluster of handsome funnel-shaped flowers, white or red and regular in form. The genus is wide in range, so growers treat its species in unlike ways. Some kinds need the hot, moist air of a stove house. Others thrive in a cooler greenhouse.

Among the stove kinds the entry names C. amabile from Sumatra and C. giganteum from west tropical Africa. Greenhouse kinds include C. capense and C. longiflorum from the Cape and C. Moorei from Natal. A few, such as C. asiaticum from the coasts of tropical Asia, also thrive in sheltered garden spots. The lists sort the genus by the heat each species asks for. A grower can read from them which house a given plant needs.
britannica-1911-criobolium:
The criobolium was the sacrifice of a ram in the cult of Attis and the Great Mother. It seems to have been a special rite, set up after the taurobolium rose to fame and modelled on it. The taurobolium honoured the Great Mother alone. The newer rite gave fuller standing to Attis, who formed a pair with the Mother. No proof places the criobolium in Asia or Italy before the taurobolium grew prominent after the year 134.

When both rites were performed together, the altar was almost always inscribed to the Mother and Attis alike. When the taurobolium stood alone, the Mother alone was named. The criobolium spread widely and grew so weighty that it sometimes took the taurobolium's place. Latin inscriptions cited in the entry attest that spread. Its details and effect were no doubt much like those of the bull rite it copied.
britannica-1911-crustumerium:
Crustumerium was an ancient town of Latium, on the edge of the Sabine country near the headwaters of the Allia, not far from the Tiber. It appears several times in the early history of Rome. Livy dates its conquest to 500 before Christ. The tribe named Crustumina, formed in 471 before Christ, took its name from the town. Pliny lists the place among the lost cities of Latium.

No remains of Crustumerium exist, and its exact site stays uncertain. Yet the name clung to the district long after the town vanished. The fertility of that district remained famous in later times. Town, conquest, tribe, and farmland are the whole matter of the entry. For the site question it sends readers to a paper by T. Ashby in the Papers of the British School at Rome.
britannica-1911-custos-rotulorum: Custos Rotulorum, the keeper of the county records of England, is explained in a brief law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. By that office he is the highest civil officer in his county. The Crown now names him to the post. It most often goes to the lord lieutenant of the county. In practice the clerk of the peace holds the records day to day.
britannica-1911-delirium: Delirium is a medical entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word is a Latin medical term for madness. It comes from a verb meaning to wander from the furrow, as a plough strays from its line. The entry defines delirium as a temporary disorder of the brain. It usually appears in connection with some bodily disease rather than standing alone. The short opening fixes the term's root and sense: a brief wandering of the mind, tied to sickness in the body.
britannica-1911-elysium:
Elysium, in Greek mythology, is the Elysian fields, the dwelling of the righteous after their removal from earth. In Homer the region is a plain at the far end of the earth, on the banks of the river Oceanus. Fair-haired Rhadamanthys rules there. Its people are troubled by neither snow nor storm, heat nor cold, for the air is always softened by the west wind from the ocean.

Homer's Elysium is no home of the dead and no part of the lower world. Singled-out heroes are carried there without dying, to live in perfect happiness. Hesiod gives the same picture for the Islands of the Blessed under Cronus. In later accounts, such as the Aeneid, Elysium became part of the underworld. There the righteous dead were judged worthy by Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Aeacus, while the wicked went down to Tartarus and endless torment.
britannica-1911-emporium:
Emporium, a Latin taking of a Greek word built from “in” and the stem of a verb meaning to travel for trade, names a trade centre. Such a centre is a commercial city to which buyers and dealers come from all parts of the world to do business. The entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica is only two sentences long. It gives the word's Greek build first, then its working sense.

The word is also often applied to a large shop, the entry adds. That second use is all the article offers beyond the trading-city sense. A reader gets a plain word-book notice: a term drawn from travel for trade, widened from the great market city to the single big store. The brevity is itself the record here, since the encyclopedia judged the word needed no more room than a few lines.
britannica-1911-ephebeum:
Ephebeum, from a Greek word for a young man, is in architecture a large hall in the ancient Palaestra, or wrestling school, furnished with seats. The whole entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica is three lines long. It cites Vitruvius, book five, chapter eleven, for the room's proportions. Its length should be a third larger than its width.

The hall served for the exercises of youths from sixteen to eighteen years of age. Nothing more is said: no plan, no named example, and no account of what the youths did there. A reader gets a bare dictionary notice of a room in a Greek training ground. Its value lies in fixing the term and its source. Any fuller picture of the palaestra and its young athletes must be sought in the entries the encyclopedia gives to those larger subjects, not in this stub of an article.
britannica-1911-epithalamium:
Epithalamium was a song of praise sung for bride and groom in Greece. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica draws the word from terms for the bridal chamber. Boys and girls sang it at the chamber door in chorus. One form lulled the pair at night, one woke them at dawn.

Blessings and glad forecasts filled the song, with Hymen cries between. Roman use gave the song to girls alone, with ruder lines in it. Poets raised the form to high art in time, the entry traces. Sappho and Pindar mastered it; Theocritus left its finest Greek case. Catullus gave it Latin dignity, and Spenser crowned the line in 1595.
britannica-1911-equilibrium:
Equilibrium, from Latin words for equal and a balance, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word means a state of equal balance between forces that pull against each other. Much of the entry deals with the sense of balance in the human body. That sense gives a feeling of safety when a person stands, walks, or moves through space.

The text explains how nerves from the soles of the feet and from the limbs guide each step. When those signals are weak or mixed, a person may stagger or fall, though the will to move stays strong. The entry cites the disease called locomotor ataxia, and tests such as blindfolding, to show the point.
britannica-1911-erbium:
Erbium is one of the metals of the rare earths, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. Its symbol is Er, and its atomic weight is given as 165 to 166. The tale starts with gadolinite, the first rare earth mineral, found in 1794 by Gadolin. From gadolinite came yttria, and from yttria came terbia in its turn.

Terbia was then split by Soret, Cleve, and others into erbia, holmia, thulia, and dysprosia. It was still in doubt whether any of those four is a single substance in truth. The rare earth metals are found in minerals such as gadolinite, samarskite, and cerite. They are drawn out by turning them into oxalates, then into oxides, then into double sulphates. Those salts are parted by repeated slow crystallisation or by careful settling with ammonia, a long and exact process.
britannica-1911-erechtheum:
The Erechtheum is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a temple at Athens. The temple stands on the acropolis of that city. Part of it was set aside for Erechtheus, who gives it its name. Its plan is unlike that of any other temple. In its fine work, it is the most refined case of the Ionic order. No clear proof shows when the work began.

Some place the start among the temples planned by Pericles. Others put it after the peace of Nicias in 421. War with Sparta broke the work off part way. A board was set up in 409 to report on the state of things. That board saw the temple finished the next year. The odd plan may stem from the rock's shape. It may also stem from the need to house old sacred marks. Those marks held the print of Poseidon's trident and a spring.
britannica-1911-erzerum:
Erzerum is the chief town of a key province of Asiatic Turkey, a post for troops and a fort of great worth in war. It shuts the roads from the Russian border lands, and routes from a Black Sea port and from all parts of Anatolia meet at it from the west.

The town sits at the east end of an open bare plain ringed by steep round hills. A river that forms the west arm of a great stream rises in hills a few miles north and cuts the plain. The town stands at a high lift above the sea, with hills near by twice that height in their peaks. The views round it are bold: bare vast hills, open plains, and long vales set with villages in turn.
britannica-1911-euphonium:
The euphonium is a modern brass wind instrument, known in bands by that name. In the orchestra it is called the tuba in the entry's usage. It is made of a brass tube with a cone shaped bore of wide size. The tube ends in a wide mouthed bell that faces the hearer. It is played by means of a cup shaped mouthpiece at its top.

Sound is made, as in the bombardon, by the tension of the player's lips. That tension yields the open notes of the harmonic series in order. Valves, most often four in number, fill the gaps of the scale between. Each valve opens a path into extra lengths of tubing, lowering the pitch. Makers build the instrument in two keys, one far more used than the other. Its tone is rich and full in quality, the entry says.
britannica-1911-euphorbium: Euphorbium is a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a drug of the old shops. It is a sharp resin of dull yellow or brown hue. It forms from the dried milky juice of cactus-like plants of the spurge kind that grow in Morocco. It melts into strong spirits and oils, but scarce at all into water. Pliny says the drug took its name from Euphorbus, the doctor of King Juba the Second. In former times it was prized as a fierce purge and emetic.
britannica-1911-europium:
Europium is a short science entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a rare metal element. The article gives its sign as Eu and its atomic weight as 152, and notes that its oxide turns up in very small amounts in rare earth minerals. The oxide was first got in 1896 by Demarcay, working from samarium prepared by Lecoq de Boisbaudran.

The entry then tells how Urbain and Lacombe got the pure salts in 1904. They did this by a slow sorting process, working a nitric acid mix with added salts of magnesium and bismuth. The salts, the article notes, have a faint pink colour and a faint band of light when tested, while the spark form gives a bright, clear pattern. It is a compact record of a new element still being pinned down.
britannica-1911-fayum:
Fayum is a province of Upper Egypt with an area of 490 square miles and a population of 441,583 in 1907. Its capital, Medinet-el-Fayum, lies 81 miles south-south-west of Cairo by rail. The Fayum proper is an oasis in the Libyan Desert, its eastern edge about 15 miles west of the Nile. The Bahr Yusuf channel joins it to the river through a gap in the hills. The whole region lies below sea-level, ringed by Libyan hills.

Unlike most oases, the Fayum draws its water not from springs but from Nile mud and flow brought by the Bahr Yusuf. Canals spread that water over more than 400 cultivated square miles, draining to the Birket el Kerun lake. Chief crops are cereals and cotton, and the province is noted for figs and grapes. The Assuan dam let 20,000 fresh acres be farmed in the years 1903 to 1905.
britannica-1911-folium:
Folium, in mathematics, is a curve invented and discussed by Rene Descartes. Its cartesian equation is x cubed plus y cubed equals 3axy. The curve is symmetrical about the line x equals y. It consists of two infinite branches, running out toward a straight-line asymptote, and a loop in the first quadrant of the graph. The entry shows how the curve may be traced from two equations using a varying value m, and notes that it is unicursal, drawn in one stroke.

The area of the loop is given, and it equals the area between the curve and its asymptote. It works out at 3a over 2. The short entry is pure geometry: one famous curve, its equation, shape and loop. The hosted file opens with the closing lines of Folio.
britannica-1911-gadolinium: Gadolinium, symbol Gd and atomic weight 157.3, is one of the rare earth metals. Marignac discovered the element in 1880 in the mineral samarskite. Urbain in 1905 separated the metal by crystallizing the double nitrate of nickel and gadolinium. Its salts show absorption bands in the ultra-violet, and its oxide is colourless. For the group of rare earths the entry refers to the article on erbium.
britannica-1911-galbanum:
Galbanum is a gum-resin drawn from Ferula galbaniflua, a plant native to Persia. It comes in hard or soft lumps, light-brown to greenish-yellow, more or less translucent, with a disagreeable bitter taste and a peculiar, somewhat musky smell. Analysis gives about 8% of terpene, 65% of a resin holding sulphur, 20% of gum and a trace of the crystal umbelliferone. It is among the oldest of drugs, named in Exodus among the sweet spices for the tabernacle perfume.

Hippocrates used galbanum in medicine, and Pliny ascribed it extraordinary healing powers, claiming that its touch with oil of spondylium could kill a serpent. Modern practice still gives it in doses of five to fifteen grains, for the actions common to resinous and oily drugs, though its use is falling obsolete.
britannica-1911-geranium:
Geranium is the name of a genus of plants, and the type of a natural order, and a botanical entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sorts its two senses. Botanists take the genus as the type of the order Geraniaceae. As a scientific name, geranium has a far narrower use than in common speech. Gardeners and the public use the word much more widely.

In former times the genus Geranium covered almost the whole order. The plant was a great favourite in gardens under that name. The name thus clung to its species even after science moved them. Most of the old genus has been shifted to the genus Pelargonium. That shift came in part from an error of nurserymen. They seem often to have drawn the wrong lesson from the change, and kept the old name in trade.
britannica-1911-gesta-romanorum:
Gesta Romanorum is a Latin collection of tales in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its title means Deeds of the Romans. It was probably compiled at the end of the thirteen hundreds. Nothing certain is known of who made the book.

The collection holds a twofold literary interest for later ages. It was one of the most popular books of its own time. It also fed the work of Chaucer, Gower, Shakespeare, and others after it. The book was plainly meant as a manual for preachers at their work. Its unifying thread is a moral purpose behind every tale. The tales themselves come from far wider sources than Rome. Greek and Latin legend stand beside matter from the East and from Europe. Among its stories are the germ of Guy of Warwick's romance. A tale of three sons matches the ground of Shakespeare's Lear in its main lines.
britannica-1911-gordium:
Gordium, an ancient city of Phrygia, is described in a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stood on the Persian Royal Road, not far from the Sangarius river. Its site lies near a modern village on the rail line to Angora. The entry warns not to mix it with a Bithynian town of a like name.

Legend says a Phrygian peasant named Gordius founded the city. An oracle had told the people to crown the first man who rode to the temple in a wagon. Gordius later gave his cart to the god. A second oracle said who untied the famed knot on that cart would rule all Asia. Alexander the Great, by the tale, cut the knot with one sword stroke. Gauls took and wrecked the city soon after 189 before Christ. Digs in 1900 found near no remains later than the sixth century.
britannica-1911-hadrumetum:
Hadrumetum was a town of ancient Africa. It stood on the east coast of modern Tunisia. The modern town of Susa partly covers its site. Greeks and Romans spelled its name many ways. Tyrians founded it as a Phoenician colony. It predates Carthage itself, Sallust reports. It later fell under Carthage without losing prosperity. Hannibal sheltered there after Zama in 202 BC.

The town helped Rome in the last Punic War. After Carthage fell in 146 BC it gained territory. Rome granted it the title civitas libera. Caesar landed there in 46 BC before Thapsus. Under Rome it became capital of Byzacena province. Trajan made it a Latin colony with a long honorific title. After Carthage it was Roman Africa's greatest town. Vandals destroyed it in 434. Justinian rebuilt it as Justinianopolis.
britannica-1911-herculaneum:
Herculaneum was an ancient city near Naples, overwhelmed in a few hours by a torrent of lava, pumice and water. The flow reached the sea and formed the shallow lagoon Pliny called Subitum Vadum. Many escaped from Pompeii, buried by falling stones and ash. Few can have got away from Herculaneum, and some who did sheltered at Neapolis.

The site was lost in the middle ages and found again by chance. In 1719 the prince of Elbeuf learned that peasants near Portici dug up marble and statues there. Digging ordered in 1738 soon struck a theatre, and the work ran over forty years. A buried library yielded 341 unrolled papyri, 195 published, with works by Epicurus and Philodemus. In 1908 Italy set Italian scholars and funds to the work, but money quarrels at Resina soon stalled it.
britannica-1911-hibernaculum: Hibernaculum, the Latin for winter quarters, is a term with three uses. In botany it names a winter bud. In botanic gardens it means the winter quarters where plants are kept. In zoology it is the winter bud of a polyzoan. The whole entry is a single sentence giving those three senses and nothing more.
britannica-1911-hilversum:
Hilversum is a town in the province of North Holland, eighteen miles by rail south-east of Amsterdam. The 1911 Britannica article gives its count as 20,238 in 1900. A steam tram links it with Amsterdam by way of Naarden and Muiden, two small walled towns on the Zuider Zee. The town sits in the Gooi, a stretch of hilly ground south of that sea. Pine woods and sandy heaths cover much of the district.

A rest home for the sick, the Trompenberg, was set up at Hilversum in 1874. The town has a town hall, schools for trade and craft skills, and houses of worship of several faiths, among them a synagogue. Its mills turn out large amounts of floor cloths and horse blankets. These goods are the chief trade named in the short entry.
britannica-1911-hippasus-of-metapontum:
Hippasus of Metapontum, a Pythagorean philosopher, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was one of the earliest disciples of Pythagoras himself. Two late writers, Diogenes and Iamblichus, mention his name. Nothing at all is known of the course of his life.

Diogenes says Hippasus left no writings behind him. Other authorities credit him with a secret discourse aimed against the Pythagoreans. Aristotle reports his doctrine on the first principle of things. Where the school held that number is the principle of all, he broke ranks. He sided with Heraclitus in holding fire to be that first principle. He seems to have thought the soul itself made of fiery matter. That view draws near the school's own doctrine of a central fire. In spite of the split, he is always counted a Pythagorean.
britannica-1911-hippeastrum:
Hippeastrum is a genus of bulb plants in the amaryllis family. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica counts about fifty species, all from warm parts of South America. In gardens they are widely known under the name Amaryllis instead. Showy funnel shaped blooms sit in clusters on a short hollow stem.

Colors run from deep crimson and blood red to pure white. Striped, spotted, and blended forms add still more range for growers. Care notes fill most of the entry in close detail. Offsets and seed both raise new plants with ease, it says. Heat, water, and rest shifts by season guide the whole routine.
britannica-1911-hoboken-belgium:
Hoboken is a small town of Belgium on the Scheldt River. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica rests its fame on one great yard. It stands on the right bank above Antwerp. Its count in 1904 was about twelve thousand eight hundred.

Shipbuilding gives the town its sole claim to note. The Cockerill firm of Seraing built its yard at Hoboken. Hulls for sea trade rise there on the river bank. Rich Antwerp merchants keep villas in the town as well. Leading rowing clubs on the Scheldt make it their home. Those clubs use the broad river at the town door. Short as the entry is, it fixes a working port suburb. Industry, not history, is the whole story told here.
britannica-1911-hospitium:
Hospitium, hospitality, among the Greeks and Romans was of two kinds, private and public. In Homeric times every stranger stood under the protection of Zeus Xenios, god of strangers and suppliants. Strangers were guests rather than enemies, it seems. On arrival the stranger was clothed and fed at once. No one asked his name or history until the duties of hospitality were done.

When guest and host parted, gifts often passed between them. Sometimes a die was broken in two, each keeping half, so that a family bond was made. The piece then served as a token of recognition. Members of each house found hosts and protectors in the other house in time of need. To break the duties of hospitality risked the wrath of the gods. The account goes on through the public forms of the bond, the proxeny of Greek states and Rome's treaties of guest-friendship.
britannica-1911-impluvium: Impluvium is the Latin term for the sunk part of the floor in the atrium of a Greek or Roman house. It was made to catch rain water that fell through the compluvium, the opening in the roof above it. The basin was most often marble, and it sat about a foot below the atrium floor around it. The entry is very short, giving the term, the feature's place and use, its usual material, and its depth in a few lines.
britannica-1911-jahrum:
Jahrum, a town and district of Persia in the province of Fars, is described in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The district has thirty three villages and is famed for its shahani dates, sent out in great quantities. It also yields much tobacco and fruit, though water is scarce and most watering is done from wells.

The town of Jahrum stands about ninety miles south east of Shiraz. A mud wall of three miles round, built in 1834, rings it. About fifteen thousand people lived there, half inside the walls and half outside. The town served as the market for the produce of the districts round it. Six caravanserais and a post office are listed among its features, a compact picture of a date trading town in a dry land.
britannica-1911-katagum:
Katagum was a sub province of the double province of Kano in the British protectorate of Northern Nigeria. It lies roughly between 11 and 13 degrees north, bounded by the French Sudan on the north, Bornu on the east, Bauchi on the south, and Kano on the west. It consists of several small but ancient Muslim emirates, Katagum, Messau, Gummel, Hadeija, and Machena among them.

The Waube flows from Kano through the province, past Hadeija and on to Lake Chad, a route for goods brought by rail to Kano. Katagum is a fertile province of hard working people, whose manufactures rival those of Kano. In old times it was the debated land between Bornu and the Hausa states. Though Muslim, it held out against the Fula invasion, and its northern emirates long owed fealty to Bornu.
britannica-1911-kum:
Kum is a small province in Persia, lying between Teheran on the north and Kashan on the south. It is split into seven districts and holds 45,000 to 50,000 people. It pays a yearly revenue of about £8000. The province grows much grain, and a fine cotton with a very long staple.

Its capital, also called Kum, stands on the Anarbar river, 3100 feet above the sea. The city owes its weight to the tomb of Fatmeh, sister of the Imam Reza, who died there in the year 816. Crowds of pilgrims visit the tomb through six or seven months of the year. The settled population is between 25,000 and 30,000. A carriage road of 92 miles, built in 1890–1893, links the city with Teheran, and it has post and telegraph offices.
britannica-1911-labarum:
The labarum was the sacred military standard of the early Christian Roman emperors, first adopted by Constantine the Great after his miraculous vision in 312. Gibbon held that he did not show it to the army until 323. The name seems older than Constantine, and the banner was a Christian form of the Roman cavalry standard. Eusebius describes the first labarum as a long gilded spear crossed near the top by a bar, from which hung a square purple cloth richly set with jewels.

At the top of the spear a golden wreath circled the sacred monogram made from the first two letters of the name of Christ. In later banners the monogram was sometimes worked into the cloth itself. A guard of fifty soldiers was set apart to protect the standard. The origin of the word is disputed; it appears to be linked with the Basque labarva, meaning a standard.
britannica-1911-lacinium-promunturium:
The Promunturium Lacinium, the modern Capo delle Colonne, lies 7 m S.E. of Crotona and is the easternmost point of Bruttii, the modern Calabria. On the cape still stands a single column of the temple of Hera Lacinia. The temple is said to have been fairly complete in the 16th century, then destroyed to build the episcopal palace at Cotrone. The survivor is a Doric column with its capital, about 27 ft. high.

Remains of marble roof-tiles have been seen on the spot, and the Archaeological Institute of America dug there in 1886–1887. Most of the sculpture found was buried again, but a few fragments and a 6th-century B.C. dedication to Hera are described. The temple's building is dated to 480–440 B.C., and no ancient writer records it.
britannica-1911-laconicum:
The laconicum was the dry sweating room of the Roman thermae, set next to the caldarium, or hot room. Its name marks it as the only form of warm bath the Spartans allowed. It was usually a circular room with niches on the diagonal axes, covered by a conical roof with a round opening at the top. Vitruvius describes a brazen shield hung by chains from that opening, raised or lowered to govern the heat.

The walls were plastered with marble stucco and polished, and the roof was painted blue with gold stars. Sometimes the laconicum was an apse at the end of the caldarium, as in the old baths at Pompeii. Usually it was a separate, hotter room with no bath in it, heated by a hypocaust and flue tiles in the walls. The largest, built by Agrippa near the Pantheon, was about 75 ft. across.
britannica-1911-lanthanum:
Lanthanum is the subject of a metal article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Lanthanum is one of the metals of the cerium group of rare earths. Its name comes from a Greek word meaning to lie hidden. It was first isolated in 1839 by Mosander from the cerium of Berzelius. It is found in several named minerals and is usually obtained from cerite.

The article describes how the metal can be won from its salts by heat or by electric current. It can be hammered readily, but it cannot be drawn into wire. Its weight and melting point are given in figures. It breaks cold water down slowly, but hot water violently. It burns in air and in chlorine and bromine, and strong acid attacks it readily. The text then treats its oxide, a white powder, and its other compounds in turn.
britannica-1911-lectisternium:
Lectisternium, a rite of ancient Rome, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its name comes from Latin words meaning to spread a couch. The rite was a meal offered to gods and goddesses to win their favour. Their images, busts or statues or small figures of wood with heads of bronze, wax, or marble, were laid upon a couch in the pose of a diner.

The article sets the couch in the open street, with a table of food before it. Livy states plainly that the rite was held at Rome for the first time in the year 399 before Christ. The keepers of the Sibylline books had been consulted in a time of plague. Three couches were made ready for three pairs of gods. One pair was Apollo and Latona, and Hercules stood in the next pair named.
britannica-1911-limburg-belgium:
Limburg is the smallest of the nine provinces of Belgium. It fills the north-east corner of the kingdom. The land is just a part of the old duchy of that name. Ground east of the Meuse went to Holland by the London settlement. A further slice, with the old capital at Dolhain, went to Liége.

Much of the ground is wild heath, the Campine. Coal in depth was found there not long before this account. Work on the field began only in 1906. At Beverloo, north-west of Hasselt, all Belgian troops train each year. Hasselt is the capital. St Trond and Looz stand among its towns. The whole holds 603,085 acres. In 1904 it held 255,359 people, some 271 to the square mile. The dukes of Looz take their title from one small town here.
britannica-1911-limina-apostolorum:
Limina Apostolorum is a church term for Rome itself. St Peter's and St Paul's church gives the name its force. A visit to those shrines could rest on a vow or on law. Vow trips were thick in the middle ages. Popes put pilgrims on that road under guard of a ban.

Law trips held more weight. A Roman synod of 743 bound bishops near Rome to come each year. Gregory VII spread the charge to all western archbishops. Sixtus V set fixed terms by bull in 1584. Italy's bishops came each three years. France, Germany, Spain, and like lands came each four. Far Europe came each five. Lands past the seas came each ten. Benedict XIV spread the call in 1740 to abbots and like heads with land rule.
britannica-1911-lugudunum:
Lugudunum is a place-name article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Lugudunum, or Lugdunum, was an old Celtic name meaning the fort of the god Lugos. The Romans used it for several towns in ancient Gaul. The greatest of them stood where the Saone meets the Rhone, at modern Lyons.

The entry explains that Roman Lyons had two distinct parts. On the hill stood a self-governing colony of Roman citizens. Apart from it stood the Temple of Roma and Augustus, kept separate by design. Each summer the sixty-four cantons of Gaul sent delegates to that temple. They held games and honoured the emperor in solemn worship. That rite was meant to bind the provinces tightly to Rome. Together the two parts formed the chief city of Roman Gaul. The article gives readers the civic shape of a capital built on loyalty.
britannica-1911-lycopodium:
Lycopodium is the principal genus of a natural order of fern allies, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a plant entry. They are flowerless herbs, with a stem that may stand erect, lie flat or creep, and branch widely. Small simple leaves thickly cover the stem and the branches. The fertile leaves are set in cones.

Those cones bear spore cases in the hollows at the leaf bases, holding spores of one kind only. The growth that springs from a spore is a mass of tissue below ground, of considerable size. It bears both the male and the female organs of the plant. There are about a hundred species, spread widely in temperate and tropical climates. Five occur in Britain, on heaths and moors and chiefly in mountain districts, where they are known as club mosses. The commonest is also called stag horn moss.
britannica-1911-lysis-of-tarentum:
Lysis of Tarentum (died about 390 before Christ) was a Greek philosopher, and a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives what little is known. His life is obscure, the entry admits at the start. It is generally accepted that he fled a persecution of the Pythagoreans. That persecution struck at Crotona and Metapontum in Italy.

Lysis escaped and went to Thebes, in Greece. There he came under the sway of Philolaus, the Pythagorean thinker. As a friend and companion of Pythagoras, he has been credited with many works. Those works are usually given to Pythagoras himself. Three books are assigned to Lysis by Diogenes Laertius. Some scholars even give him the Golden Verses. The entry judges those verses a gathering of lines by many hands.
britannica-1911-manbhum:
Manbhum, a district of British India in Bengal, is the subject of a regional entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its headquarters are at Purulia, and its area is 4,147 square miles. The entry gives it 1,301,364 people in 1901, a rise of about nine percent since 1891. The district forms the first step down from the table land of Chota Nagpur to the delta of lower Bengal.

The north and east of the district are open, rolling downs dotted with lone cone shaped hills. The west and south are more broken and far more scenic in character. Dalma, at 3,407 feet, is the chief peak named, and the old fort of the rajas of Panchet crowns another hill. Dense jungle covers the hills. The chief river is the Kasai, which bears a floating trade in sal timber. The most numerous aboriginal tribe is the Sontals, the entry says.
britannica-1911-mancunium:
Mancunium is the name often given, perhaps in error, as the Roman British name of Manchester in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Near the Medlock, in the district still called Castlefield, a Roman fort once stood. A cohort of Roman helper soldiers manned that fort. Houses, railways, and a canal now hide the site.

Traces of Roman ramparts can still be seen there, and more remains came to light in 1907 and before. Signs of Roman British life show up near the cathedral as well. Yet there was no town on the spot. The fort guarded roads that ran north through Lancashire and east into Yorkshire. Homes of families and traders would have grown up outside its walls. Old Roman writers give two name forms, and it is not clear that either one is right.
britannica-1911-mare-clausum-and-mare-li:
