Closed sea and free sea face off in a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Latin pair names a long fight in the law of nations. States once claimed whole oceans and seas as their own ground. Spain claimed vast seas, and Britain claimed her narrow waters round. Such claims drew fierce pushback from the rival powers of the age.

Grotius wrote his Free Sea in 1609 for the open claim. Selden wrote his Closed Sea in 1635 for the shut claim. Clash of claims forced states to trim their vast demands back. Rule of the sea would start from the shore of the land. Bynkershoek set that reach at the range of a shore gun. That rule grew into the three-mile belt of coast waters.
britannica-1911-marruvium: Marruvium is named in a 1911 Britannica article as chief town of the Marsi, in Italy. It stood on the east bank of the Lacus Fucinus, on the Via Valeria, south of Cerfennia. The town was no doubt of great age. Yet nothing is known of its history before the imperial period. The remains seen there, walls, buildings, and an amphitheatre, all date from that later age. They show it was a place of some weight. On the site now stands the village of St Benedetto.
britannica-1911-mausoleum: Mausoleum is a short term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, for a monument built to hold the remains of the dead. A like monument with no body inside is called a cenotaph. The word comes from the tomb Queen Artemisia raised in 353 BC for her husband, King Mausolus. What was left of it reached the British Museum in 1859. The tombs of Augustus and Hadrian at Rome rank among the largest of the kind.
britannica-1911-meerschaum:
Meerschaum, a German word for a soft white mineral, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is at times found floating on the Black Sea. Its look recalls sea foam, which gives it its French name as well. Glocker called it sepiolite, from a faint likeness to the bone of the cuttle fish.

The mineral is opaque and white, grey, or cream in colour. It breaks with a shell like or fine earthy break and can be scratched with a nail. Most meerschaum of commerce comes from Asia Minor. The plain of Eski-Shehr yields the bulk of it in lumpy masses in loose deposits. Workers dig those deposits widely to win the stone.
britannica-1911-misenum:
Misenum was an old port town in Campania in Italy, south of Baiae at the west end of a gulf. Till the end of the free state it hung on Cumae and served as a place for fine homes. Agrippa then made its fine bay the chief base of the fleet. A town grant came with that change.

A famed ruler died in his home there, and the base held its rank for ages. Saracen raids razed the town in eight ninety. The entry maps the two basins of the port and the town site. Homes, a play house, baths, and tomb rows can still be traced.
britannica-1911-nasturtium:
Nasturtium is the subject of a plant article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The nasturtium, or Indian cress, is a lasting climber native to Peru. In gardens it is grown as a hardy annual. It climbs by the long stalk of its round leaf, which grasps like a tendril. Its odd flowers have five outer parts joined at the base, one drawn into a spur.

The article gives use and growing advice in plain terms. The flowers are sometimes eaten in salads. The leaves and young green fruits are pickled in vinegar as a stand in for capers. The plant wants a warm spot and light, rich soil. Seed should be sown thin in April near a fence or wall. A dwarf form called Tom Thumb makes a fine border flower about a foot high. Kin kinds with orange and scarlet blooms are also named.
britannica-1911-nomentum:
Nomentum, now Mentana, was an old town of Italy on a road north east of Rome. Some held it a Latin town, some a Sabine one. With two sister towns it was left out of the first region when a great emperor redrew the map, and a river was made its north bound.

The 1911 Britannica entry notes the towns civic rank: it won town rights with no vote at Rome after the last Latin war. In its town rule, its chief officer kept the grand old title of dictator down to the days of the empire. Old writers praise the rich soil of its fields. The site is well guarded by gullies on all sides but one. No old work stands in place, the entry says, but carved stones and relics have been found.
britannica-1911-noricum:
Noricum, a district of the ancient world, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It was bounded north by the Danube, west by Raetia and Vindelicia, and east and south by Pannonia and Italy. It matches most of modern Styria and Carinthia, with parts of Austria, Bavaria, and Salzburg. Its first people seem to have been Illyrians. After the Gauls' great migration they fell under Celtic tribes.

The chief of those tribes were the Taurisci, probably called Norici from their capital Noreia. The country is mountainous and its soil poor, but it was rich in iron. It fed the arms factories of Pannonia, Moesia, and northern Italy. The famous Noric steel was widely used for Roman weapons. Its people were brave and warlike, paying more mind to cattle than to farming. Gold and salt were also found there in quantity.
britannica-1911-nymphaeum:
Nymphaeum, in Greek and Roman antiquities, was a monument sacred to the nymphs, above all those of springs, explains an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Such monuments began as natural grottoes said to be the homes of local nymphs. Some were fitted out to supply water.

The entry tells how built forms later took the place of grottoes, with round halls decked with statues and paintings in the Roman period. They served three ends at once: shrines, reservoirs, and meeting rooms, with a special use for weddings. Examples stood at Corinth, Antioch, and Constantinople, and about twenty remains were found at Rome.
britannica-1911-oranienbaum:
Oranienbaum, a town in European Russia, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the south coast of the Gulf of Finland, across from Kronstadt. It lies in the province of Saint Petersburg, a short rail ride west of that city. In 1897 it held a little over five thousand people.

The town is best known for its imperial palace and grounds. Folk from the capital crowd there in the warm months. In 1714 Peter the Great gave the site to Menshikov, who built a fine country seat. The crown seized it in 1727 with the rest of his wealth. In 1743 the empress Elizabeth set the place aside for Peter the Third. He raised a small fort there for his Holstein troops.
britannica-1911-pallium:
Pallium, or Pall, a vestment in the Roman Catholic Church, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name comes from the Roman pallium or palla, a woollen cloak. At first the vestment was peculiar to the pope alone. For many centuries the pope has bestowed it on metropolitans, primates, and archbishops. It stands as a sign of the jurisdiction given to them by the Holy See.

In its present form the pallium is a narrow band, three fingers broad, woven of white lamb's wool. A loop rests on the shoulders over the chasuble, with two hanging ends before and behind. Seen from front or back it looks like the letter Y in shape. Six purple crosses mark it, and three jewelled gold pins garnish it. Its origin as church dress is lost in antiquity.
britannica-1911-patavium:
Patavium, the modern Padua in Italy, was an old city of Venetia described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lay fifty five miles east of Verona by road. A central place gave it great weight in the region. Roads ran from it to Ateste and across the Po, and to Altinum and Concordia as well.

Canals linked the city to the sea, about thirty miles away. The old town stood forty feet above sea level on a peninsula ringed by the Bacchiglione. A canal guarded the one open side to the south. Four bridges that cross the canals of modern Padua go back to Roman times. Digs in the centre turned up parts of a grand public building, perhaps from the forum, and a large mosaic with patterns in shape.
britannica-1911-picenum:
Picenum was a district of ancient Italy between the Apennines and the Adriatic, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells of its people and their fate. The Senones bounded it on the north and the Vestini on the south. By tradition its people were an offshoot of the Sabines. Strabo tells how their migration was led by a woodpecker, a bird sacred to Mars.

From that bird, picus, they took their name Picentini, much as a neighbouring people took theirs from a wolf. Rome conquered the district early in the third century before Christ. In 232 its whole land was divided among Latin-speaking settlers under the Lex Flaminia. For that reason records of any older tongue spoken there are very scant.
britannica-1911-plum:
Plum is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a tree and its fruit. The plum tree belongs to the genus Prunus. That genus sits in the rose order, Rosaceae. Garden plums are thought to spring from one of two wild kinds. One is the wild plum, the other the bullace. Their shoots and fruit shapes help tell them apart. A third kind is the sloe, or blackthorn.

The sloe bears stout spines on its branches. Its flowers open before its leaves appear. Its fruit tastes very rough to the tongue. The wild plum is a native of Anatolia and the Caucasus. It is held to be the only kind naturalized in Europe. The bullace grows wild in southern Europe and Armenia. It also grows along the shores of the Caspian Sea. The entry warns that these marks do not always hold.
britannica-1911-potassium:
Potassium is a metal element of the alkali group, treated at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is never found free in the wild state. Yet in bound forms it is one of the most wide spread of metals. The seas hold huge stores of its salts, though few are drawn from them.

The great mines at Stassfurt in Germany made the metal a trade good. Their beds hold sylvine, carnallite, and kainite side by side with rock salt. The same salts show up in mines in the Carpathian hills as well. Most rock in the crust of the earth holds some potash in its stone. As that stone rots, the salts wash into the soil. Plants draw them up, and their ash yields the potash of old farm use.
britannica-1911-regium:
Regium is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a city of south Italy. It stood on the east side of the strait of Messina. Settlers from Chalcis and Messenia in Greece founded it long ago. That founding falls in the eighth century before the Christian era.

About the year 494, Anaxilas made himself master of the town. He then joined his folk in taking Zancle across the strait. Coin types of the age back the tale, the entry notes. A free rule was set up after his sons were driven out. In 433 the town made a treaty with Athens as a friend. It joined Athens against Syracuse, then sat out a later war. A long fight with Dionysius ended in its ruin in 387.
britannica-1911-regium-donum:
The Regium Donum, or Royal Gift, was a yearly grant once made from public funds to Presbyterian and other Nonconformist clergy. It covered Great Britain and Ireland. The grant dates from the reign of Charles II. After his declaration of indulgence of 1672, he had sums paid to Presbyterian clergy, but those gifts soon stopped. In 1690 William III made a grant of 1,200 pounds a year to Irish Presbyterian clergy.

That grant was a reward for their service in his fight with James II. The Irish House of Lords blocked the pay in 1711 and in some years after. George I brought it back in 1715 and raised it to 2,000 pounds a year. More was added in 1784 and in 1792. By 1868 the sum for Irish Presbyterian clergy stood at 45,000 pounds. The grant was withdrawn by the act of 1869 that broke up the Irish church.
britannica-1911-rhodium:
Rhodium is a rare white metal found with the kin metals of the plat group in raw ore. It was found in eighteen three by a man who worked on that ore. The entry gives the lab steps to draw it from the dregs left when the chief metal is drawn out. Rose red salts mark its path in the work.

The pure metal looks much like a light white metal in hue. It melts at a more high heat than its chief kin. It will not melt in sour baths, a trait that parts it from its kin. It drinks in the light gas with ease.
britannica-1911-rochefort-belgium:
Rochefort is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a small town in Belgium. The town stands on the Lomme, a stream that feeds the Lesse. It lies in the south east of the province of Namur. The Ardennes hills stand close by. A count in the text gives the town just over three thousand people. In summer that count is said to double.

The town is old, and its site made it count for trade. Two roads crossed there, one from Liege to Bouillon. Ruins of the old castle still stand above the town. Counts who held that castle could mint their own coins. The castle went through many sieges and much harm. Summer guests now come for the famed caves near by and for the clean air.
britannica-1911-rubidium:
Rubidium, a metallic element with the symbol Rb, is the subject of a science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It belongs to the group of alkali metals. It occurs in minerals such as lepidolite, petalite, mica, and carnallite, and in some mineral waters. Traces also turn up in tea, cocoa, coffee, tobacco, and beetroot ash.

Bunsen and Kirchhoff found rubidium in 1860 while they studied spring water residues with the spectroscope. Two clear red lines marked the new element out. The best source of its salts is the residue left after lithium salts are drawn from lepidolite. The entry sets out ways to part its salts from those of potassium and caesium. It also gives methods to prepare the pure metal, by heat with carbon or other agents. The metal was first got by electric means in 1910.
britannica-1911-ruthenium:
Ruthenium is a chemistry article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a metallic element. The entry gives its symbol and notes that it is found with platinum, in platinum ore and in a related mineral. The metal can be won from the residues left when osmium is split from that mineral.

The article sets out one method in careful steps. Residues are washed, burned, and fused with caustic potash and nitre. The melt is dissolved in water and acid is added until a colour linked to a ruthenium salt fades. A solid oxide then forms, is gathered, and is fused at high heat. The entry also points to other methods and to a way of making a purer metal by heating it in oxygen.
britannica-1911-saepinum: Saepinum was a Samnite town, known today as Altilia near Sepino, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stood on the ancient road from Beneventum to Corfinium and was captured by the Romans in 293 BC. The original town sat on the mountain, far above the Roman town, and remains of its walls in great block masonry still exist. The Roman town's walls were built by Tiberius before he became emperor. Inside them are remains of a theatre and temples of Jupiter and Apollo.
britannica-1911-saguntum:
Saguntum was an ancient town of eastern Spain near Valencia. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sums its fate in one flash of glory. It stood in a rich district close to the coast. At the start of the Second Punic War it was large and rich in trade.

The town was of native stock, not Greek planting. It sided with Rome against Carthage in the quarrel. That choice drew the first blow of Hannibal in 219. Its long brave stand ranks with great sieges of Spain. Livy told that stand in words as noble as the deed. Hannibal took the town in 218 and marched on to Italy. Quiet wealth then marked its Roman years for centuries. A theatre whose ruins lasted long proves that later ease.
britannica-1911-samarium:
Samarium is a rare earth metal, marked by the symbol Sm in the science of chemistry. The 1911 Britannica article gives its atomic weight as 150.4 and lists the men who worked to split it from its kin. The metal is gained by the reduction of its oxide with magnesium. It joins with hydrogen to form a hydride. Most of its salts take a yellowish colour.

Its chloride is a salt that melts away in damp air. Heated in acid gas, it gives a dry chloride, which strong heat can cut down to a lower form. That lower chloride is a brown powder that water breaks apart. The article goes on through its fluoride, its sulphate, and its carbide. The carbide forms when the oxide is heated with carbon in an electric furnace. The whole piece is a lab record in brief.
britannica-1911-selenium:
Selenium, a non metal first found in eighteen seventeen, is set out in a chemists entry in the 1911 Britannica. Berzelius found it and named it for the moon in Greek. The name nods to its close kin, tellurium, named for the earth. It shows free in the wild at rare spots. More oft it sits bound with metals in ores of more than one kind.

Dust from the flues of acid works is its chief trade source. Steps with strong acids draw it out of that dust in stages. A salt bath route by Nilson is set out as a twin path. Heat and strong water baths free it from its ore in a third route. Trade stock holds taints of sulfur and tellurium, so wash steps end the text shown.
britannica-1911-slum: A slum is a foul, dirty street or quarter in a town, home to the most poor and cast off folk. Crowding is oft a mark of such a place, the 1911 Britannica entry notes. The word is fair new and its root is not sure. It has been tied, with doubt, to a local use of slump for a marshy spot, with kin words for mud set by its side.
britannica-1911-sorghum:
Sorghum, a group of grasses, is the subject of a plant article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. One kind in the group ranks among the key grain crops of the warm parts of the world. It goes by many names: great millet, Indian millet, or Guinea corn in English. In India it is called jawari, jowari, cholum, or jonna, by tongue and district.

The article describes a strong grass that grows from four to eight feet tall, and at times to sixteen. Its leaves are broad, and its dense heads hold round, hard, glossy grains a bit larger than mustard seeds. The crop is grown across India and other parts of Asia, in the United States, and in the south of Europe. Its stems and leaves make fine feed for cattle, and the grain serves the same uses as maize or rice.
britannica-1911-speculum: Speculum is a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the Latin word for a mirror. The term is used above all for the metal mirror of a reflecting telescope. In early instruments such mirrors were made from an alloy of copper and tin. The article notes that these metal mirrors have now been displaced by the more handy silver-on-glass mirror. It closes by remarking that various forms of specula are also used in surgery, for examining organs inside the body.
britannica-1911-spy-belgium:
Spy is a commune near Namur in Belgium, famed for a find of early man. The 1911 Britannica article tells how in 1886 two men dug in the Betche aux Roches cavern there. At a depth of sixteen feet they found two near whole skeletons, a man and a woman. Tools of the Mousterian type lay with them. The bones are now held in the Lohest store at Liège. The skulls had huge brows and low foreheads.

The jaws were massive, with a weak chin and large back teeth. The bones of the fore-arm curved apart in a marked way. The shin bones were short and stout past any known race. The build of hip and leg forced the head and trunk to lean forward, as in the gait of the great apes. With the bones lay those of dead beasts: the woolly rhinoceros, the mammoth, and the cave bear.
britannica-1911-stein-heinrich-friedrich:
Heinrich Friedrich Karl, Baron vom und zum Stein, a German statesman born in seventeen fifty seven, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at the family estate near Nassau, he was the ninth child of Karl Philipp. His mother came from the von Simmern house. His father had a stern and sharp temper, which the son took from him.

With that temper the son joined gifts of mind his father lacked in full. The family held rank as free knights of the Holy Roman Empire. They owned their own lands and owed faith to the emperor alone, but had no vote in the diet. In old age Stein gave thanks for the faith and the true German knightly model of his parents. He said his view of the world came from home. The entry sets up a life of reform from deep roots.
britannica-1911-stillicidium: Stillicidium is a term of architecture for the dripping of water from the eaves, as a brief note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica records. The Latin name joins words for a drop and for falling. Vitruvius used the term for the dripping eaves of an Etruscan temple roof. Like eaves are found in most Greek Doric temples. Ionic temples handled roof water in a different way. There the water was gathered in a gutter and thrown out through the mouths of carved lions.
britannica-1911-strontium:
Strontium is a metallic element described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It belongs to the group of alkaline earths. It is found in small amounts in rocks and soils across the world, and in mineral waters. Its chief sources are three minerals, strontianite, celestine, and barytocelestine. The metal was first found in a mineral dug at Strontian in Scotland.

Cruikshank marked it in 1787, and Crawford did so in 1790, and Hope and Klaproth then proved the find. Sir Humphry Davy set the metal free in 1807 by use of an electric current on its moist compounds. The pure metal is silver-white and can be drawn out. It melts at a high heat, takes fire in air when hot, and dulls fast in the open. The article goes on to its compounds, such as its hydride.
britannica-1911-summum-bonum: Summum bonum is a Latin phrase for the highest good, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains in the field of ethics. It names the ideal of human attainment in a moral system. What the term means turns on the character of the system in which it is used. It may be viewed as a perfect moral state in itself. The text adds a sharp caveat: if we drop the view that acts are good or bad in themselves, the term loses any real significance.
britannica-1911-sunium:
Sunium, now Cape Colonna, is a cape at the south tip of Attica. The 1911 Britannica entry notes its temple of Poseidon on the height. That temple serves as a landmark for ships that near Athens from the east. The rocky point held a fort with walls and towers in old days. Athenians walled it in 413 before Christ against the Spartans.

Runaway slaves from the Laurium mines seized the fort soon after that. In the 300s it was still kept up as a strong place of arms. An inscription found in 1898 proved the temple was Poseidon's own. A temple of Athena stood a short way off to the north east. The extant temple was most likely built in the time of Pericles.
britannica-1911-surrentum:
Surrentum is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an ancient town of Italy. Its modern name is given as Sorrento. The town lay in Campania, south of Naples. It stood on the north side of a promontory. That headland forms the south east end of the Bay of Naples. Legends link Surrentum closely with the isle of Lipara. They suggest it began as a colony of Lipara. Through imperial times it stayed largely Greek in character.

Before Roman supremacy, the town answered to Nuceria. It shared that town's fortunes up to the Social War. It joined the revolt of ninety years before Christ. Like Stabiae, it was reduced to obedience the next year. A Roman colony seems to have been planted then. Its prosperity dates from the imperial period onward. Capreae was then a favoured home of emperors. Many tomb inscriptions of imperial slaves were found there.
britannica-1911-synaxarium:
Synaxarium is the name used in the Greek Church for a book much like the martyrology of the Roman Church, explains an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Greek verb meaning to bring together. Such books list the saints in the order of their feast days.

The entry sets out two kinds: plain lists of saints, and fuller books that add short lives of each saint. The lives are drawn from the great collections for the twelve months of the year. The oldest books of the fuller kind seem to date to the tenth century. Other eastern churches keep their own forms, in Arabic, Ethiopian, and Armenian among them.
britannica-1911-tantalum:
Tantalum, a metal element with symbol Ta, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It turns up in small amounts in nature, almost always with columbium. That link tangles the past of both metals. Hatchett found columbium in a mineral from Massachusetts in 1801. Ekeberg found tantalum in Swedish minerals the next year.

For years men argued whether the two were one and the same. Later work sorted out a crowd of claimed new metals. Some proved to be the same stuff, and some were mixes. Berzelius made an impure metal in 1820. Pure metal came only in 1905, when Werner von Bolton fused his product in an electric furnace with air shut out.
britannica-1911-tate-nahum:
Nahum Tate, an English poet laureate and playwright who lived from 1652 to 1715, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Dublin in 1652, the son of Faithful Teate. He studied at Trinity College in Dublin and took his degree in 1672. He printed a book of poems in London in 1677 and became a steady writer for the stage.

His own plays include Brutus of Alba and The Loyal General. He is best known for his reworkings of old plays by other men. His King Lear gave the tale a happy end, with a marriage for Cordelia and Edgar. His Richard the Second was shut down on its third night for fear of a political reading. He also shared in the New Version of the Psalms in 1696.
britannica-1911-taurobolium:
Taurobolium was the sacrifice of a bull in an old eastern rite. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes the rite and its spread. It linked most often with worship of the Great Mother of the Gods. Its first known use in Italy came at Puteoli in the year 134.

A poet of the time tells how the rite was done. The priest stood in a pit under a floor of pierced planks. A bull decked with flowers and gold was killed above him. Blood rained through the holes onto his face and tongue. He then came out washed clean and born anew, the rite claimed. Later ages used it for one soul rebirth, good for twenty years or for all time.
britannica-1911-teetotum: A teetotum is a small top used in games of chance. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica shapes its body as a many sided block. Letters or numbers mark its sides. The side left uppermost when the top falls decides the game. In its earliest form the body was square with four sides. Latin letters on those sides told each player his fate. One letter meant take from the pool, one meant pay a fine. A third meant nothing, and a fourth meant take all.
britannica-1911-tellurium:
Tellurium, a chemical element, is the subject of a science article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is found in nature in small amounts in its pure state, but chiefly joined with other metals in ores. Small amounts also turn up in iron pyrites, and so in the dust of acid works. Klaproth first marked it out as a distinct element in 1798.

The article gives several ways to draw the element out of its ores. One heats an ore with a soda ash, washes the fused mass with water, and lets the air bring the tellurium down as a grey powder. Another boils the ore in strong acid, thins the fluid, and adds a gas that drops the element out. The steps can be repeated when a purer yield is wanted. The entry is a working guide to the chemistry of a rare metal.
britannica-1911-thallium:
Thallium is a metal element, found by a new path of science in the early eighteen sixties. A British worker, in a study by light of the dust from ore ovens, saw a green line in the spectrum that matched no known stuff. He held that the ore held a new element, and named it from a Greek word for a green twig.

He first thought his find was kin to sulphur and its mates. A French worker, who beat him to the pure metal, showed it was a true metal. Most of what men know of its ways comes from the British finders work, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Its traits are odd: a famed chemist once called it the duck billed freak of the metals, so mixed is its nature. In body it is much like lead.
britannica-1911-titanium:
Titanium, a metal first known in the late part of the seventeen hundreds, is set out in a chemists entry in the 1911 Britannica. William Gregor found a new earth in a dark ore in seventeen eighty nine. He took that earth for the rust of a new metal at the time. Klaproth found the same metal in rutile stone four years later. He gave it the name titanium that still holds for the stock.

The pure rust was first made clean by Rose in eighteen twenty one. Pure metal came much later, as the text shows with care. The stock spreads wide in the rock world but in thin counts. It oft sits bound with iron in its ores at large. Heat with salt and sodium gave the first crude yields of the metal.
britannica-1911-tusculum:
Tusculum, an old city of Latium, is placed by the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on the north edge of the Alban crater ring. It stood high, at 2,198 feet, with a wide view over the Campagna to Rome, 15 miles away. Two roads linked it to Rome, the Via Latina and the Via Tusculana. Old tales said it was founded by Telegonus, son of Ulysses and Circe.

When Tarquin was cast out of Rome, the chief of Tusculum backed his cause. That chief led the Latin host at Lake Regillus in 497 BC and was killed there. Rome then rose to first place among the Latin towns. In 381 BC the folk of Tusculum bowed to Rome in full and won Roman rights. They had no vote, but the town kept the rank of a free town from then on.
britannica-1911-uriconium:
Uriconium, more correctly Viroconium, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a large Romano British town. It is now Wroxeter on the Severn, five miles east of Shrewsbury. The town was the chief place of a tribe named in the entry. It may first have been a Roman legionary fort, held against the Welsh hill tribes in the years soon after the conquest.

Its garrison soon moved on, and the place became a flourishing town, the article says. It had a stately town hall, baths, and other marks of a fully Roman city life. It was larger and likely richer than Silchester, a better known site. The lines of its walls can still be traced, enclosing one hundred seventy acres. Parts of the town hall and baths have been uncovered by digging.
britannica-1911-venafrum:
Venafrum was an ancient town of Campania in Italy, near the borders of Latium and Samnium. Its site is held by the modern Venafro, a village on a rail line. That village held four thousand seven hundred sixteen people in nineteen o one. Old writers tell little of Venafrum, save that Rome sent it a yearly prefect. In the Social War the allies took the town by treachery.

Augustus founded a colony at Venafrum and built an aqueduct for it. A long decree on that water work survives in stone inscriptions. The town seems to have been a place of some weight in its day. Its olive oil was the best in Italy, Cato and others say. Brick works and iron works are also named among its trades. Of its old remains, almost nothing is left standing today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ad-limina-apo: Ad limina apostolorum names the pilgrimage to Rome's sepulchres of St. Peter and St. Paul. The journey runs to the Prince of the Apostles' basilica and to St. Paul's basilica outside the walls. The entry gives this brief definition of the Roman pilgrimage and its two shrines, and nothing more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adytum:
Adytum, from adyton, a privative plus dyo, to enter, is a secret chamber, a place of retirement in ancient temples. Held most sacred, the innermost sanctuary or shrine, only officiating priests might enter, and oracles were given from this place.

Solomon's temple's Holy of Holies, or Sanctum Sanctorum, shared the pagan adytum's nature, since none but the high priest entered it, and he only once a year. Among Egyptians the secos was the same thing, as Strabo describes. A well-preserved adytum stands in the little temple at Pompeii, raised some steps above the temple floor and without light. In Christian architecture the word sometimes means a church's chancel, or altar end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agaunum:
Agaunum, today St. Maurice-en-Valais, in Sion's Swiss diocese, owes its fame to an event St. Eucherius, Bishop of Lyons, relates: the martyrdom of a Roman legion, the Theban Legion, early in the fourth century. For centuries this martyrdom passed as fact, but since the Reformation it has drawn long and violent controversies, recounted exactly in Franz Stolle's work.

Sources for the Theban martyrdom are few: two editions of their Acts, entries in calendars and martyrologies, and Eucherius's letter of 450. To these may be added Passiones of Theban martyrs who escaped Agaunum but later fell in Germany and Italy. Only under Theodore of Octodurum, bishop 369 to 391, long after the event, did attention turn to the massacre. Then, Eucherius says, a basilica rose for the martyrs, whose presence Theodore learned by revelation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amphilochius-:
Bishop of Iconium from early in 374, Amphilochius was a fourth-century churchman born in Cappadocia around 339 or 340. He was probably a cousin of Gregory of Nazianzus. Trained for the law, he worked briefly as a barrister at Constantinople. He then left that career for religious life near Gregory, before Basil of Caesarea drew him into church affairs.

He is best remembered for defending the divinity of the Holy Spirit against the Macedonians. Basil dedicated his own treatise on the Spirit to him for that cause. Amphilochius wrote a similar work, now lost, and attended the Synod of Constantinople in 381. He left letters and fragments, some genuine and some wrongly ascribed to him, that still help scholars trace early teaching on the Spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Borglum, in Denmark, embraced the ancient districts of Vendsyssel and Thy, the whole extreme north of Jutland beyond the Limfjord. The see began at Vestervig, formed out of Viborg on the death of Bishop Val in 1059. Magnus, first Bishop of Vestervig, drowned in the Elbe about 1060, returning home after consecration by Adalbert I of Hamburg.

Albrik, Dean of Bremen, served as second bishop from 1066 to 1085. Vestervig had sheltered Saint Thoger, a missionary from Thuringia and chaplain to Saint Olaf. He retired there after Olaf's death in 1030, built a church of thatch and wattle, and preached to the district. Thoger died on 24 June 1067 and was canonized despite the opposition of King Svend Estridsen and Bishop Albrik, becoming patron of the diocese. Bishop Sylvester moved the see in 1134 to 1136 to the Premonstratensian abbey of Borglum, whose canons formed the chapter that elected the bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anemurium: Anemurium, now called Estenmure, was a titular see of Cilicia, a church title preserving the name of an ancient diocese. In antiquity it stood on a high bluff knob marking the southernmost point of Asia Minor, facing Cyprus across the sea. Its ruins, including theatres, tombs, and walls, are still visible to visitors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antimensium:
Antimensium, also Antiminsion, Greek for instead of the altar, is a consecrated corporal used only in the Greek Rite. In Russian and Slavonic it is antimins, substantially the Roman Rite's portable altar. It is a strip of fine linen or silk, about ten by thirteen inches. It is ornamented with the Passion instruments or Our Lord in the Sepulchre. It contains saints' relics sewn in and certified by the bishop.

It must lie on the altar in Greek churches, as an altar-stone does in Latin churches; no Mass may be said without it. It is unfolded at the Offertory quite like the Latin corporal. Outside Mass it rests folded in four on the altar. Since 1842 each Russian church must register its antimensia exactly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arcanum:
Arcanum is an encyclical on Christian marriage, issued by Leo XIII on 10 February 1880. Since family life is the seed of society and marriage the basis of family life, the health of civil and religious society depends on marriage. That health rests on the inviolability, or unbreakability, of the marriage contract. Christ's mission, it argues, was to restore humanity in the supernatural order, benefiting first the individual and then society as a whole.

From that principle the letter treats Christian marriage as sanctifying the family, society's unit. The marriage contract, set up by God, had from the start two properties, unity and indissolubility. Human weakness corrupted it over time: polygamy, many spouses, destroyed unity, and divorce destroyed indissolubility. Christ restored the original idea and, to sanctify the institution more fully, raised the marriage contract to sacramental dignity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arcosolium:
An arcosolium, from arcus, arch, and solium, a word Latin writers sometimes used for sarcophagus, was one form of tomb in the Roman catacombs. An inscription published by Marchi still stands in the Palazzo Borghese courtyard. It records that Aurelius Celsus and Aurelia Hilaritas had this arcosolium with its little wall made for themselves and their friends, in peace. The tombs were cut in the soft tufa walls of the catacombs.

Builders first hollowed a space like an ordinary loculus, or wall niche, topped by an arch. Then they opened an oblong cavity downward into the rock facing the arch, and laid a marble slab horizontally over the opening. The tomb thus became a kind of sarcophagus hewn from living rock, its closing slab forming a table-like top beneath the arch. The entry gives a builder's view of how early Christians buried their dead in stone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atrium:
In early church building, an atrium was a large open court set before the church itself. Covered walks ringed it on four sides, and worshippers crossed it between porch and nave. A fountain at its center let them wash their hands before going in, a custom that lives on in the holy-water font. Penitents stood there to ask prayers from those entering, and the court also served as a burial ground.

Famous early examples include old St Peter's in Rome and Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. The form survived in places such as St Clement's in Rome and St Ambrose in Milan. The entry adds a second, secular sense from Roman houses, where the atrium was the main entrance hall. There it was lit through a roof opening called the compluvium, with rain caught in a floor basin called the impluvium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-axum:
Axum, is a titular metropolitan see of ancient Christian Ethiopia, with bishops listed from the mid-fourth century to 650. Modern Axum, capital of the Tigre province of Abyssinia, nestles in a valley beneath an Adoua peak. It stands 7,545 feet above sea level. A plain below it feeds streams that run toward the Nile. A recent traveler describes a sacred enclosure, nearly a mile round, holding the cathedral, monastery, and the bishop's house.

The city is ancient. Greeks and Romans knew it with Adule as a trade center for gold dust, ivory, leather, hides, and aromatics from Africa's interior. Its people mix Ethiopic and Arab blood, and Himyaritic inscriptions nearby show Arabia's influence, as do stone monuments bearing sun and star worship. Greek coins older than the fourth century and Ethiopic coins titled Negush Aksum have been found there, and sixth-century Gheez inscriptions aid the history of the Semitic alphabet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belgium:
Belgium takes up a long historical entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It traces the small kingdom through revolution, foreign rule, and independence. Its narrative runs from the French armies of 1794 through Dutch rule and the break of 1830, with the Church present at nearly every turn. Bishops, clergy, schools, and political parties all shape the story it tells.

Much of the entry follows the long fight over schools and the place of faith in public life, from state-run universities to laws on private and public teaching. It also covers the Catholic party in power, the growth of religious orders, and Belgian mission work abroad, including the Congo and India. Readers get a dense political and church history rather than a short gazetteer note.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblia-pauper:
Biblia Pauperum, the Bible of the Poor, was a picture book pairing scenes from Christ's life with Old Testament foreshadowings, described in this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. A series of forty or fifty pages, each divided into nine sections, puts the Gospel scene at the centre, prophets above and below, and Old Testament scenes at the sides.

Corner texts explain the links, making the book a picture concordance of the two Testaments, gathering the Church's traditional reading of types and figures as taught in liturgy and preaching. Though called the poor man's Bible, it likely served preachers and the literate too. The entry presents a medieval teaching aid in pictures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bullarium:
A Bullarium gathers bulls and similar papal documents, whether general or tied to one order, house, or place. The name came from the canonist Laertius Cherubini, whose 1586 folio of 1,404 pages held 922 papal constitutions from Gregory VII to the reigning Sixtus V. Later collections followed his model, but three cautions govern them all.

First, each editor chose by his own judgment, so no collection held official standing. The exception is Benedict XIV's first volume of his own bulls, sent to Bologna in 1746 as a source of law. Second, no collection claimed completeness, or even all constitutions of general interest. Third, editors meant at first to exclude pronouncements already inside canon law's corpus, aiming instead to rescue enactments the corpus compilers had missed or popes had issued since. Mazzutellus's 1579 volume of 723 documents shows the form before Cherubini fixed it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caeremoniale-:
The Caeremoniale Episcoporum is the book of rites and ceremonies for bishops and lesser prelates at Mass, Vespers, and other functions in metropolitan, cathedral, and collegiate churches. It also settles precedence among clergy and official layfolk. After Sixtus V set up the Congregation of Sacred Rites in 1587, Clement VIII had the book corrected and issued it in 1600.

Errors crept in, so Innocent X had it revised in 1650, Benedict XIII issued a new edition in 1727, and Benedict XIV published an amended and enlarged one in 1741 and 1752. A standard edition of 1886 now rules all others. Its first book covers the bishop's duties, dress, and ministers, and its second the Divine Office and Mass through the year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesarius-of-:
Caesarius of Prum, born of the noble Milendonk family, was abbot of the rich Benedictine house of Prum near Trier, elected in 1212. Prum then ranked among the richest monasteries in Europe, but many of its monks were noblemen living in comfort, and their example wore down discipline. After five years Caesarius gave up the abbacy to live a stricter life as a humble monk at the Cistercian house of Heisterbach.

At Abbot Kuno's request he wrote in 1222 a commentary on the Register of the Estates of Prum. Drawn up in 893, it has become a key source for thirteenth-century law and civilization. Leibniz and later editors printed the register with his commentary, and recent research also credits him with the history of the abbots of Prum, long assigned to Caesarius of Heisterbach.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capharnaum:
Capharnaum, also called Kapernaum, was a town of Palestine whose name means village of Nahum, or consolation. The Gospels make it Jesus's home after rejection at Nazareth. There he called Peter, Andrew, James, John, and Matthew as disciples. There he healed a paralytic, Peter's mother-in-law, the centurion's servant, and others. There too he spoke the discourse on the Eucharist.

Its people, urged on by the Pharisees, broke with him, and on leaving he pronounced a curse on the city. Under Constantine a converted Jew named Count Joseph built a church there. Pilgrims visited it into the sixth century. After that the town fades from Palestinian history, surviving now only as a Latin titular see whose exact origin the entry leaves unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cariati-pater:
Cariati is a diocese of Calabria in the province of Cosenza, suffragan to Santa Severina, in a healthy site near the sea. Menecrates, present at the Roman synod of 499, is the first bishop on record. Gregory the Great later commended its church to the Bishop of Reggio. A union with the diocese of Cerenza in the eleventh or twelfth century is possible but first appears in record in 1342.

Noteworthy bishops include Polychronius, founder of a monastery at Santa Severina in 1099, and the Cistercian Matteo, who first led the abbey of San Giovanni di Fiore as abbot. The soldier turned nuncio Alessandro Crivello and Fra Filippo Gesualdo, who died in the odor of sanctity, also appear. Pius VII joined Strongoli and Umbriatico to the see in 1818, leaving a diocese of 60,000 people with 28 parishes, 70 churches and chapels, and 61 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casium:
Casium was a titular see of Lower Egypt near Pelusium, by the sandhills Greek geographers called Kasion Oros, today El-Katieh or El-Kas. A temple of Zeus Kasios, the Aramean god Qasiou, stood there, and Pompey, murdered nearby, was buried at the place. Geographers and church lists name it as a bishopric under Pelusium in Augustamnica Prima, from Georgius Cyprius and Hierocles to a notice of about 840.

Only one bishop is known, Lampetius, who attended Ephesus in 431. Cyril sent him with Hermogenes of Rhinocorura to Rome, where both attended the consecration of Pope Sixtus III. Many letters of Isidore of Pelusium are addressed to Lampetius, whose name survives through that correspondence and the council record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cathedraticum:
Cathedraticum is a yearly sum paid for the bishop's support, given as a mark of honor and a sign of submission to the cathedral church. In the early Church such gifts came by custom rather than law. The earliest law on the subject seems to be a Braga canon of 572. It bound only parish churches and chapters to pay, since the sacraments were then given in parish churches alone.

As other endowed churches and chapels multiplied, Pope Honorius III extended the duty to them as well. The sum was paid at the bishop's annual visitation. The ancient amount was fixed at two solidi, a solidus being one seventy-second of a pound of gold. Later rulings, including decisions of Propaganda, kept the payment a binding law for those concerned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chrismarium: A short glossary entry on the chrismarium, a word with two church meanings. In the first sense it is the place in a church set apart for giving Confirmation, where the bishop anoints candidates. In the second sense it is a round jar, usually of silver or pewter, used to hold the holy oils for anointing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ciborium:
An entry on the ciborium, a chalice-like vessel holding the Blessed Sacrament. Some derive the word from Latin cibus, food, for the heavenly bread it holds, while others trace it to Greek kiborion, cup, for its first shape. In early Christian times the term also meant the canopy crowning the altar, but modern liturgical use restricts it to the sacred vessel for reserving the consecrated species.

Today two vessels reserve the Sacrament: the pyx, a small round box for carrying it to the sick, and the ciborium, used for distributing Communion and keeping particles in the tabernacle. Shaped like a chalice with a round bowl, conical cover, and cross, it must be gold or silver, lined with gold within. It is blessed rather than consecrated, and veiled in white silk or cloth of gold while holding the Species. Only sacred ministers may handle it when full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-circesium:
Circesium, a titular see of Osrhoene, was founded under Diocletian and restored by Justinian. Today's identification is Abu Serai, a village on the Euphrates' left bank at the meeting of the Khabur. An older city called Sirhi had stood there before it. Benjamin of Tudela wrongly identified Circesium with Kharkamis, a Hittite capital.

The city was a bishopric in Osrhoene, suffragan to Edessa, and appears only in a list of about 840. Lequien names five bishops, from Jonas at Nicaea, mutilated in an earlier persecution, to Thomas in 553. Fourteen Jacobite bishops are also recorded, from 793 to 1042.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercian-ab:
Loccum, in Hanover, a Cistercian abbey of the Minden diocese, was founded in 1163 by Count Wilbrand von Hallermund. From Volkenrode in Thuringia came its first monks, under Abbot Eccardus, placing it in the Morimond line from Citeaux. An old writer calls its site a place of horror and vast solitude haunted by robbers. After want and harsh neighbours, the monks tilled the land and taught the people the fear of God.

The abbey filled its place in Brunswick church life until Lutheranism swept Catholicism from the country. Its chief interest now lies in its buildings, almost perfectly preserved as a Protestant seminary. The cruciform church, built between 1240 and 1277, measures about 218 feet by 110, beside a fine cloister, refectory, chapter-house, sacristy, dormitory, and lay-brothers wing. The head of the house still bears the title of abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-citharizum:
Citharizum, a titular see of Armenia, lay in Asthianene or Balabitene, north of Commagene and Mesopotamia, between Masius and Anti-Taurus. Justinian built a castle there with a garrison under a duke and placed the city in Armenia Quarta, the province he had just formed. In 613 it fell to Ashot, general of the Persian king Chosroes the Second.

Only one bishop is known: Marianus of Kitharizon, named in the records of the Trullan Council of 692. The city appears about 840 in Parthey's first Notitia as part of Armenia Quarta under Melitene's metropolis, it is identified with the modern village of Keterig.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-collectarium:
Augustin Joseph Schulte's entry defines the collectarium, also called collectarius or orationale. It is the book that holds the Collects. In the Roman Missal, the word Statio often stands before the Introit of a Mass. It marks the church where clergy and people once gathered to celebrate the mysteries on a saint's day or feast.

Before walking in procession to that church, they met nearby to receive the pontiff. He recited a prayer called the Collect. The name may come from the assembled people, or from the prayer summing up all favors asked, or from its brief form of the feast's spirit. In time the name spread to prayers before the Epistle, to Secrets and Post-Communions, and to prayers of the Divine Office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coracesium:
Sophrone Pétridès's entry covers Coracesium, a titular see of Asia Minor. Ptolemy places it not in Cilicia Tracheia but in Roman Pamphylia. It had belonged to Isauria, and from A.D. 74 probably fell within Lycia-Pamphylia. Its port was the Cilician pirates' chief centre. There Antiochus VII killed Diodorus Tryphon, and Pompey destroyed the pirates, levelling their fortress.

Coracesium became suffragan of Side, metropolis of Pamphylia Prima. Lequien mentions only four bishops, the first at Constantinople's Council in 381, the last in 681. The see still appears in the Notitiæ episcopatuum as late as the twelfth or thirteenth century. Today Coracesium is a little town of about 2,000 inhabitants, 500 Greeks, chief centre of a caza in Konia. Its Turkish name is Alaya. Armenians have disappeared, though the town ranked important in the Rupens' time. Curious ruins, walls, and ancient tombs survive, with many romantic stories attached.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cotiaeum:
Cotiaeum, an ancient city of Phrygia Salutaris, claims Aesop as a native son and a long career as a Christian centre. Heresy took root there from the second century, and Socrates records its Novatian bishop. At first a suffragan of Synnada, it rose to an autocephalous archbishopric, then a metropolis with as many as thirteen suffragans.

Ten bishops appear in Lequien's list, the last in the fourteenth century, beginning with Cyrus, sent by Theodosius II after townsfolk slew four bishops. Ruins, a Byzantine castle, and a church survive from antiquity, and Timur sacked the town in 1402. Modern Kutaya, famed for earthenware, counts about 22,000 inhabitants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crisium:
A diocesan entry describes Crisium, a Graeco-Slavonic rite diocese in Croatia centred on the little town of Krizevac, north-east of Zagreb. About 1600 many Serbs emigrated from Serbia and Bosnia into Croatia, where they joined earlier settlers called Wallachians. Through Bishop Dimitrovich of Agram, their leader Simeon Vratania gained a monastery and became bishop of the Catholic Serbs in 1611.

His successors stayed loyal to Rome despite schismatic propaganda and conflicts with Agram. In 1671 Bishop Paul Zorcic became vicar-general of Agram for Slavonic-rite Catholics. Only in 1777 did Pius VI re-establish the Uniat diocese as Crisium. Its bishops have resided at Krizevac ever since, serving a flock counted alongside 225,000 schismatics in the territory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-curium:
A short entry describes Curium, a Cypriot titular see suppressed by the papal legate Pelagius in 1222. Legend says Koureus, son of Kinyras, founded Kourion on the south-west coast and settled Argives there in 1595 BC. The city became capital of one of the island's kingdoms.

On the ruined site stands the modern village of Episkopi, near the sea, where Cesnola found the antiquities now in New York's Metropolitan Museum. In the Middle Ages Episkopi passed first to the Ibelin family, then to the Venetian Cornaro, owners of rich sugar plantations. Curium's recorded bishops number only two: Zeno at Ephesus in 431, and Michael in 1051. The tomb of Saint Hermogenes is kept in its church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diaconicum:
An entry on the diaconicum, a word with two linked senses in the Greek Church. As a book it lays out the deacon's functions, and as prayers it names the orations for peace he says before the people. First of all, though, it meant an annex to the basilica where altar supplies were kept and preparations made for the sacrifice.

Prothesis, the small room for receiving the people's offerings, stands distinct from it, and the two commonly flank the apse. A great church's diaconicum majus held several rooms: a reception hall for the bishop, a treasury for vessels and books, and the diaconicum proper. Syrian examples rise two stories on a rectangular plan, and the form recurs in Byzantine churches, African basilicas, and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-didascalia-ap:
The Didascalia Apostolorum claims to be the teaching of the apostles at the Council of Jerusalem. In truth it is a church manual put together in the third century. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry untangles its tangled afterlife, from its first printing in Syriac in 1854. In 1900 scholars found an old Latin version, more than half of which has perished.

The first eight books of the later Apostolic Constitutions simply rework the Didascalia. Scholars can thus rebuild much of the lost Greek original by setting the two texts side by side. The entry leans on the 1906 edition by Funk, and it shows how a manual for early Christian conduct survived in fragments across three tongues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-docimium:
Docimium was a titular see in Phrygia, a region of Asia Minor. Its coins call its people Macedonians, so it must have been founded by Antigonos Dokimos. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives its shifting names, from Dokimeion to Dokimion, and notes its fame for marble quarries. The site is now the village of Istcha Kara Hissar, northeast of Afion Kara Hissar.

Many Christian inscriptions later than Constantine have been found there. Synnada in Phrygia Salutaris held authority over Docimium, whose known bishops number six or seven between 344 and 879, plus one more from an inscription. The entry is a compact study in coins, quarries, and bishop lists fixing a lost city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominus-vobis:
Dominus Vobiscum, Latin for the Lord be with you, is an ancient greeting taken into the liturgy as a prelude to formal prayer. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces it to Scripture, to Ruth and Chronicles, and to Christ's promise in Matthew that he is with his people. Church use dates likely from apostolic times, and the Council of Braga named it in 563. It also stands in the Gelasian Sacramentary of the sixth or seventh century.

The phrase bears a deep weight, since the Lord's presence pledges divine protection and earnest of every good gift. The entry follows its place in Mass and office, showing how a few words open the Church's solemn prayers. For readers of the liturgy, it unpacks a greeting heard at every altar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dorylaeum:
Dorylaeum, a titular see in Phrygia Salutaris, Asia Minor, was already an ancient city under Phrygia's kings. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets it at Karadja Hissar, six miles southwest of modern Eski Shehir. Near the end of the fourth century before Christ it moved to Shehir Euyuk, where it stayed through the Byzantine age. Known bishops number seven, spanning the fourth through the ninth century.

The most famous, Eusebius, denounced in turn the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches. As late as the twelfth century it still appears among Synnada's suffragans, before fading from record. Seljuk Turks took and destroyed the town about 1070, yet crusaders won a battle there on 1 July 1097, a date the entry preserves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durham-dunelm:
Durham is an ancient English diocese holding a unique place among bishoprics. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that its border position against Scotland led its bishops to take on political and constitutional roles beside their spiritual office. Their rights were peculiar and wide, and even today the Anglican bishop of Durham ranks above all English prelates save Canterbury, York, and London.

Its line runs back to the Anglo-Saxon see of Lindisfarne, which Saint Aidan founded in 635. Aidan came from Iona at the call of King Oswald of Northumbria to preach to the newly conquered heathen kingdom. He built his monastery on Holy Island, and the entry follows the see from Lindisfarne to Durham through its prince-bishops and their coins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
The ecclesiastical forum is the Church's judicial and coercive power, expressed in the Latin word for a place holding a tribunal of justice. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry argues that this power is plain from the constitution given by the divine founder. As a perfect society, the Church holds within herself all powers needed to guide her members to their appointed end, with a matching right to be obeyed.

That right is called jurisdiction, the source of all church action not drawn from the power of holy orders. It grounds church law, binding both outwardly and inwardly, and from apostolic times rulers have put it into practice. The entry notes that civil encroachment has in our day shrunk the forum in practice, though unwarrantably, to spiritual causes alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-of-d:
Eusebius of Dorylaeum was the layman turned bishop who led the orthodox fight first against Nestorius and then against Eutyches in the fifth century. Trained as an advocate at Constantinople, he publicly challenged a sermon by the chaplain of Nestorius in 423. Later he broke into a sermon by Nestorius himself to protest that the eternal Word had taken a second birth, of a woman, in the flesh. 

As bishop he then turned on his former friend Eutyches, charging him with false teaching before Flavian's synod at Constantinople in 448. Eutyches was condemned, but the council of Ephesus in 449, run by Dioscurus, deposed and banished both Flavian and Eusebius amid cries against him. Eusebius fled to Rome, appealed to Pope Leo, and at Chalcedon in 451 stood as accuser of Dioscurus. He also helped frame the definition of faith that cleared his own name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flabellum:
The flabellum is a liturgical fan of leather, silk, parchment, or feathers. Deacons waved it at the altar to keep insects from the Sacred Species and the priest. The Apostolic Constitutions of the fourth century already order two deacons to hold such fans. Latin use faded about the fourteenth century; Greek use continues to the present day.

Greek deacons receive the sacred fan at ordination and wave it from Offertory to Communion. Rich examples survive, like the thirteenth-century Kremsmünster fan shaped as a Greek cross. Fans also served as marks of honour: two are borne beside the pope on the sedia gestatoria. In 1902 Leo XIII gave the old Vatican fans to Mrs. Joseph Drexel of Philadelphia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gesta-romanor:
The Gesta Romanorum was a medieval Latin collection of anecdotes, each paired with a moral reflection. It was most likely assembled by a priest late in the thirteenth century or early in the fourteenth. Older guesses that named Berchorius or Helinandus as its author no longer stand. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces how the book grew, spread, and reached print.

Each tale opened under a heading naming a virtue or a vice. It then told its story and closed with a moral reading, giving preachers ready examples for sermons. Copies multiplied across Western Europe with local additions, and split into three manuscript families. The first printed editions appeared between 1472 and 1475, and an enlarged Vulgate held 181 stories. Poets from Chaucer and Boccaccio to Shakespeare and Schiller later mined the same tales. Many of them survive today inside famous works of European literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hadrumetum:
North Africa's Hadrumetum, a Phoenician colony older than Carthage, served Hannibal as a base against Scipio at the end of the Second Punic War. It grew rich under Rome, when Trajan raised it to a colonia. By the third century's end it was capital of the new province of Byzacena. Justinian restored it after the Vandals as Justinianopolis.

Arabs afflicted it again, the Aghlabids rebuilt it in the eleventh century as Susa, Normans held it briefly in the twelfth, and France took it in 1881. Modern Susa counts 25,000 people with a museum, garrison, harbour, and oil wells nearby. The entry closes with nine known bishops between 255 and 551, the last being Primasius, whose works survive in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-birn:
Cologne Carthusian Heinrich Birnbaum, born in 1403, entered the order at thirty-two and became a reformer of houses by sheer example. Esteemed for scriptural and theological learning, he was made prior of Mont Saint André at Tournai only three years after entering, in 1438, and held that post eleven years.

Successive priorships at Wesel, Rettel, Trier, Diest, and Liège followed, each house's few abuses yielding to his restoration of St. Bruno's austere discipline, until ill health sent him back to Cologne in 1463. His last decade went to ascetic writings, including a defence of the Immaculate Conception. The entry warns against confusing him with his jurist uncle of the same name, dead in 1439.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-busem:
Hermann Busembaum was a German Jesuit moral theologian, born at Notteln in Westphalia in 1600 and dead at Münster in 1668. He joined the Society of Jesus at nineteen, taught classics, philosophy, and moral and dogmatic theology, and served as rector of the colleges at Hildesheim and Münster. He also became confessor and trusted adviser to Christoph Bernard von Galen, the prince-bishop of Münster.

His lasting fame rests on one short book, the Medulla theologiae moralis, first issued in the mid-1600s. It packs a wide range of moral teaching into a small volume, set out in a clear and orderly way for priests facing hard cases of conscience. Later writers kept adding notes to it, which shows how widely priests used it. Readers meet here a teacher prized for sound judgment, plain method, and practical help.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-homiliarium:
A homiliarium is a collection of homilies, familiar explanations of the Gospels, read with the recitation of the Divine Office. From very early times the Fathers' homilies stood in high esteem for this purpose. Gregory the Great refers to the custom, and Benedict mentions it in his rule, proving it as old as the sixth century.

Homilies of Leo I, terse and suited to liturgy, were prized above others. As new feasts entered the Office, demand for homilies grew, and by the eighth century, the age of liturgical codification, collections began to appear. Many homiliaria survive, and medieval references name many more, including a very old Gallican collection, one by the Roman priest Agimundus, and one compiled in England by Bede.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-iconium:
Iconium was a titular see of Lycaonia, which Xenophon calls the easternmost town of Phrygia, while Cicero, Ammianus, and others place it in Lycaonia or Galatia, since provincial boundaries often changed. Anthony gave it to Polemon, dynast of Olbe, who reigned from 39 to 26 BC, and it later joined the Roman province of Galatia, becoming a colony under Claudius.

Paul preached there on his first mission and converted many Jews and pagans, returning soon after to organize the church he had founded, and he elsewhere recalls persecutions endured there. Thecla was one of his converts. Christianized early, Iconium hosted a council in 235 decreeing heretical baptism invalid. Le Quien names thirty-six bishops down to 1721, best known being Amphilochius, friend of Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-in-partibus-i:
An entry on a Latin phrase that once followed the title of a bishop who held a see he could not live in. The phrase means “in the lands of the unbelievers,” and it was added to the names of old Christian sees that had fallen under non-Christian rule. Such bishops were called titular bishops, and the entry sets out how the practice grew.

Early bishops driven out by invaders kept their titles. Other churches gave them shelter. Some even ran empty sees for a time. Later the Church kept the names of lost sees alive by giving them to helper bishops and to bishops in mission lands. The entry traces that shift and dates regular titular appointments to the time of the Twelfth Lateran Council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-invitatorium:
An invitation to the faithful to join the Divine Office opens this liturgy entry, which takes its name from that call to prayer. Psalm 95, the Venite, has served as the invitation from the earliest times. The life of Porphyrius of Gaza pictures him having it sung so the people could join in, answering Alleluia after each verse. Benedictine practice made it a daily fixture.

In the Benedictine night office the Venite opens the nocturns and is never left out. The antiphons sung with it shift with feasts and weekdays, repeated twice before the psalm and once after the Gloria Patri. Benedict's Rule calls the psalm the Invitatorium, while an older Frankish rule calls it the exhortation response. Readers get a small chant's long history in one place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-itinerarium:
A prayer for setting out on a journey, printed at the Breviary's end for easy finding, is the itinerarium treated here. Monks and clerics used it before travel, and the custom likely grew from monastic rule. Desert fathers Anthony and Pachomius, and Basil too, legislated in detail how monks should behave abroad, with set duties and restraints for the road.

Benedict's rule shaped Western church custom more than any other. In chapter 67 it ordered that brethren sent on a journey first commend themselves to the abbot's and community's prayers. The community remembered them daily while away. Short absences brought their own customs, the entry notes. Readers get a small prayer set inside a whole discipline of traveling as a monk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-nepomu:
Johann Nepomuk von Nussbaum was a Munich surgeon who helped bring antiseptic surgery into Germany. Born in 1829, he studied at Munich. He traveled to study under leading surgeons in Paris, Berlin, and Wurzburg. In 1860 he became professor of surgery at Munich, a chair he kept for close to thirty years. His lectures were prized for their practical cast.

After studying under Spencer Wells in England he advanced pelvic surgery, and after learning antisepsis from Lister he spread it through German surgical clinics. His guide to antiseptic wound treatment ran through five editions and was translated into several languages. Among nearly a hundred publications, the best known dealt with ovariotomy, bone transplantation, hernia operations, and cancer treatment. He also served as consultant surgeon-general to Bavarian troops in the war of 1871.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julian-of-ecl:
Julian of Eclanum was the most learned leader of the Pelagian movement. Born about 386, son of Memorius, a bishop in Apulia, he rose through lector and deacon to Bishop of Eclanum about 417. When Pope Zosimus condemned Pelagius in 418, Julian stood among eighteen Italian bishops who refused to sign, and Emperor Honorius exiled them.

Driven from Italy in 421, Julian systematized the teachings of Pelagius and Coelestius and became the party's intellectual chief. For years the struggle was largely a duel between Julian and Augustine, whose works quote Julian's lost books at length. Julian sought reopening of the case under each new pope and met fresh condemnations until his death in Sicily in 454.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liber-diurnus:
The Liber Diurnus Romanorum Pontificum is a collection of church formularies used in the papal chancery through the eleventh century. It holds models of the chief papers the chancery prepared. They cover a pope's death, election, and consecration, bishops' installation, professions of faith, pallium grants, privileges, dispensations, monastery foundings, property confirmations, chapels, and decrees.

It opens with superscriptions and closings for writing to emperor, empress, Patricius, Exarch, kings, consuls, patriarchs, and clerics. It matters for legal and church history, above all Rome's. Its models come from earlier papal papers, especially Gelasius I (492-496) and Gregory I (590-604). Compiled in the Roman chancery, it began small, grew over time, and has no systematic order. In final form, in two manuscripts at the Vatican and Milan's Ambrosian Library, it dates to the eighth century. Scholars dispute the date: Garnier gives 715, Zaccaria the ninth century, Roziere 685 to 751.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyrs-of-sc:
Martyrs of Scillium were six Christians condemned to death by the sword at Scillium in 180, by Vigellius Saturninus, proconsul of Africa. Their Acts rank as the most ancient we possess for Roman Africa, and their trial stands out because the accused faced no torture. The proconsul, free of prejudice against Christians, urged them to obey the law and suggested time to think.

The Christians quietly said their minds were made up. Saturninus sentenced the six: having affirmed living as Christians and, offered a remand to Roman life, persisted in contumacy, they must perish by the sword. The dialogue's calm and legal form mark early African martyrdom, showing a magistrate who sought compliance before punishment. Their Acts remain a key source for second-century African Christianity and its clash with Roman authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-menologium:
Menologium, also written Menology or Menologe, is in strictness a service book of the Greek Church, though writers have stretched the word to other uses, and this entry chiefly untangles that confusion. From men, a month, the term means month-set: a book ordered by months. Like lectionary, it has borne several quite distinct senses among authorities.

First, Menologium often stands for Menaion. The Menaia, usually twelve volumes, one per month, form an office book matching, very roughly, the breviary's Proprium Sanctorum. They hold the movable parts of saint-day services, above all the canons sung at Orthros, the office matching Lauds. Synaxaries, historical notes on the day's saints, sit between the canon's sixth and seventh odes. Those notes are read much as the day's Martyrology is slipped into Prime in Western offices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-milevum:
Milevum, a titular see of Numidia, appears in Ptolemy's Geography under the name Mileum or Mireon. In the Roman era it was called Colonia Sarnensis Milevitana, after the Sarnus River in Campania, whence its colonists had emigrated, a name often found in the city's inscriptions. With Cirta, Collo, and Rusicade it formed the confederation known as the Four Colonies.

Under Justinian in the sixth century, Milevum gained a strong wall, which survives as a bulwark of the Arab town of Milah. Two councils were held at Milevum, the more famous in 416 against Pelagianism, attended by Augustine and sixty bishops. Its bishops included Optatus, the great opponent of the Donatists, and Severus, Augustine's friend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-myriophytum:
Myriophytum was a titular see of Thracia Prima, suffragan to Heraclea, whose early history is unknown. It first appears in connection with an earthquake that destroyed it in 1063, and John Cantacuzene visited it about 1350. Under the joint title of Peristasis and Myriophytum it enters an episcopal list near the fifteenth century's end, Peristasis alone dating to 1170.

In the sixteenth century Myriophytum displaced Peristasis in the diocese's name, and in 1908 the Greeks raised it to an autocephalous metropolitan see. Today it is a busy port on the Sea of Marmora counting 5,000 Greeks and 400 Turks. Its schismatic archdiocese holds only ten parishes with about 22,000 souls, Peristasis alone accounting for some 6,000.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nahum:
Nahum, seventh in the traditional list of the twelve Minor Prophets, bears a Hebrew name probably meaning full of consolation or comfort, hence consoler or comforter. The name was not rare: Luke's genealogy names a Nahum, the Mishna cites Nahum the Mede, a famous second-century rabbi, and inscriptions show it among Phoenicians.

All we know of the prophet must be gathered from his book, since no other canonical Scripture names him, and extracanonical Jewish writers are hardly less silent. His short prophecy denounces Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, in vivid images of siege and sack, promising Judah's deliverance. The entry weighs its date, its poetry, its place among the prophets, and the city whose fall it celebrates with fierce satisfaction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neum:
A neum, from Latin neuma or pneuma and Greek pneuma, a nod, is a term in medieval music theory, seemingly unused before the eleventh century. From then it bore two senses: a kind of melody, and a notational sign. Guido of Arezzo takes it in a third sense, comparing music's tones, syllables, neums and phrases to metrics' letters, syllables, feet and verses.

As a melody, a neum is a series of tones sung without words, generally on a text's last vowel. Its older name is jubilus, which Saint Jerome defines as praise beyond words, syllables, letters or speech. Saint Augustine calls it a song of joy without words, fitting above all for the ineffable God. The entry traces neums as notation, from early signs above texts to the staff systems that grew from them, and their role in chant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notitia-digni:
The Notitia Dignitatum, or Register of Offices, is the handbook of civil and military posts in the later Roman Empire. Its surviving Latin form dates to the early fifth century, with eastern additions reaching 397 and western notices running into the reign of Valentinian III.

Eastern and western halves each list central officials first, then provincial and diocesan officers, civil beside military, with drawings of their insignia. The chief of the chancery used it to draft appointment notices, and the entry weighs its date, gaps, and value for Roman administration. Its eastern additions reach 397, while western notices run into Valentinian III’s reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notitiae-epis:
Notitiae Episcopatuum are the official lists that rank metropolitan and suffragan sees in the Eastern churches. Unlike Rome, where rank followed date of consecration, or Africa, where age ruled, the East ranked each bishop by his see: Caesarea first in Constantinople's patriarchate, Ephesus second, and so on.

Each list runs from patriarch through greater metropolitans, autocephalous metropolitans, archbishops, exempt bishops, and suffragans. The entry explains how ranks held unless a later list changed them, and why these lists matter for Eastern church geography. In Constantinople’s patriarchate Caesarea ranked first and Ephesus second among metropolitans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-octavarium-ro:
The Octavarium Romanum, a liturgical book akin to an appendix of the Roman Breviary, supplies lessons for the days within octaves. Sixtus V first ordered such a book for greater variety in lessons, but his plan died with his pontificate from 1585 to 1590.

Under Clement VIII, consultors including Baronius favored the project, and Gavanti carried it out, publishing at Antwerp in 1628 with Urban VIII's brief of approval. Its body gives second and third nocturn lessons for octaves, especially of local patrons and titular feasts. Its title describes lessons for the second and third nocturns within octaves of feasts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ostensorium:
An ostensorium, from the Latin for to show, is a vessel made to display an object of devotion in plain view. The word and its kin, monstrance, once covered every goldsmith's vessel fitted with glass or crystal to reveal its contents, whether the Sacred Host or a saint's relic. Modern English use narrows both terms to vessels for exposition of the Blessed Sacrament, and the entry keeps to that sense.

Such vessels could only follow the practice of exposing the Sacrament or carrying it in procession, which dates no earlier than the thirteenth century. Lanfranc's rules for Canterbury monks around 1070 already had priests carry a shrine holding the Lord's Body on Palm Sunday, but with no hint that the Host was shown. Later pages trace the shapes of ostensoria, from tower and sunburst forms to modern types, and the rules for their use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pallium:
The pallium is a circular band about two inches wide, worn round neck, breast, and shoulders. Two pendants hang front and back, each two inches wide and twelve long, weighted with lead wrapped in black silk. White wool forms the rest, part of it from two lambs given yearly by the Lateran Canons Regular and blessed on Saint Agnes's feast at Saint John Lateran.

Six small black crosses mark it, one each on breast, back, shoulders, and pendants, with gold pins set with stones on three. The pope and archbishops alone wear it, and archbishops only after leave from the Holy See, and only in their own dioceses on set days.
