Bishops may receive it as a favour, but it adds no power or rank. Later pages trace its history, symbolism, and rules of use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paraetonium:
Paraetonium was a titular see of Libya Secunda, or Marmarica, suffragan of Darnis, famed for its port. Some say the city should be called Ammonia. From its harbour Alexander visited the oracle of Amun, and Mark Antony halted there before Actium. Justinian walled it to shield Egypt on the west. It has since vanished, its port partly sand-covered, and its site, long called Baretoun by Arabs, is now Mirsa Berek near Benghazi.

Three bishops are named: Titus at Nicaea in 325, Siras, an Arian, and his successor Gaius at Alexandria in 362.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parium:
Parium was a titular see, suffragan of Cyzicus in the Hellespont, where a Christian community stood before 180, as the Acts of martyr Onesiphorus prove. Other saints of note are Menignus, martyred under Decius and honoured on 22 November. Theogenes, bishop and martyr, is kept on 3 January. Basil, bishop and martyr of the ninth century, is kept on 12 April.

Le Quien names fourteen bishops, the last living in the mid-fourteenth century, plus an anonymous Latin bishop noted by Innocent III in 1209 and a titular bishop in 1410. Autocephalous as early as 640, Parium stayed so till the late thirteenth century, when Andronicus II raised it to a metropolis as Pegae and Parium. In 1354 both sees were suppressed, the metropolitan taking Sozopolis in Thrace instead. Its ruins lie at Kamares on Cape Tersana-Bournou.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pelusium:
Pelusium was an Egyptian frontier city guarding the eastern edge of the Nile Delta. Its name, from a word for mire, matched the marshes around it, and its harbour joined the sea to the Pelusiac branch of the Nile. Pharaohs fortified it, and armies fought over it for a thousand years: Nebuchadnezzar, Cambyses, Xerxes, and Artaxerxes all moved against it before Alexander took it in 333 BC.

Later conquerors kept coming, from Antony and Augustus to the Persian shah Chosroes, the Arab general Amru, and Baldwin I of Jerusalem, who burned it in 1117. When the Nile branch silted up and the sea flooded the land, the city sank into a desert of mud. A ruin-covered hill called Tell Farameh now marks the site. The entry also lists its early bishops and honours St. Isidore, who died there in 450.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philomelium:
Philomelium was a titular see in Pisidia, suffragan to Antioch, on the road from Synnada to Iconium. Ancient writers place it in south-west Phrygia near Lycaonia's border, inside Synnada's judicial district, and its coins show alliance with neighbouring Mandropolis. In the sixth century it belonged to Pisidia, its people pronouncing the name Philomede or Philomene.

Medieval Byzantine historians mention it often in wars against the Seljuk sultans of Iconium. In the twelfth century it ranked among the sultanate's chief cities under the Turkish name Ak-Sheher, White City. Today it is the chief town of its district with 4,000 inhabitants, nearly all Muslims, on the Eski-Shehr to Konieh railway. Seven bishops are known, from Theosebius at Constantinople in 381 to Euthymius in 879, and Smyrna's church wrote to Philomelium of Polycarp's martyrdom in 196.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plenarium:
A plenarium is any book that gathers in one volume material otherwise scattered across several books. The mortuary office as a whole, Vespers, Matins, Lauds, and Mass, was called a plenarium, as was a complete copy of the four Gospels, an evangeliarium plenarium. Examples include the Book of Gospels at Lichfield and the book Athelstan gave to Christ Church, Canterbury.

When priests were scattered singly and private Masses grew common, the complete missal, the missale plenarium, came into use. It held all prayers for Mass that had once been split among sacramentary, lectionary, evangelistary, antiphonary, and gradual. In Germany the name also meant a popular book giving German Epistles and Gospels for Sundays and feasts with short expositions, last printed under that title at Basle in 1522.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polemonium:
Polemonium was a town on the Pontus coast that gave its name to the province of Pontus Polemoniacus. It stood at the mouth of the Sidenus in the region called Sidene, on the site of an older town called Side. It is believed to have taken its new name in honour of Polemon, made king of Pontus by Mark Antony about 36 B.C.

Its harbour gave it some weight, and it is now the village of Pouleman in the Trebizond region, with ruins of an octagonal church and ramparts across the river. Six of its bishops are known, from Aretius at Neocaesarea in 320 to John at Constantinople in 869 and 879, and the see is listed until the thirteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polystylum:
Polystylum, a titular see in Macedonia Secunda, sat under Philippi. Once Philippi rose to metropolitan rank, Polystylum stood among its subject sees. Leo the Wise's lists near 901, the Nova Tactica near 940, and thirteenth-century records all name it so. Innocent III counted it among Philippi's Latin subject sees in 1212.

Its Greek bishop Peter rose to lead Christopolis in 1363, and Maronia took the see over. Around then Emperor Cantacuzenus rebuilt and walled the town, styling it old Abdera. The entry doubts that styling: Polystylum is present-day Bouloustra, set inland from genuine Abdera's ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pretorium:
Pretorium comes from the Latin praetorium, in later Greek to praitorion. At first it meant the general's or praetor's tent in Roman camps. Then it meant the military council judging there, and later the governor's official house, a palace or castle. In the Gospel it marks the house Pilate held at Christ's Passion. Two such castles stood, both built by Herod.

The first rose where the tower of Birah stood, called Baris by Josephus. That tower stood on a rock near the Temple enclosure, cut sheer on the south and parted from Mount Bezetha by a broad ditch on the north. On this rock, now held by Turkish barracks, Herod built a new fort, with two broad courts ringed by porticoes between rock and Temple enclosure.  Herod later built a second palace on Mount Sion's north brow, at the town's west edge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-proprium:
The Proprium names the worship texts that change with the day. This encyclopedia entry explains its two blocks: the Proprium de tempore, for the seasons of the church year, and the Proprium Sanctorum, for saints' feasts. Both sit inside the Breviary, the book of prayer, and the Missal, the book of the Mass, supplying introits, prayers, lessons, responses and antiphons fitted to each occasion.

From Advent through Pentecost, the de tempore block maps the church year: Christmas, Septuagesima, Lent, fifty Easter days and the Sundays after Pentecost. Saints' days join the round from Saint Andrew's feast on 30 November. Early Christians knew almost no fixed yearly cycle beyond Easter, Christmas and Sundays, singing psalms and hearing Scripture readings instead. Rome in the fourth century, under Pope Damasus, began fitting prayers to seasons and feasts, and the shared Common of Saints grew from single feasts like those of Peter and Paul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prum:
Prüm, a former Benedictine abbey in Lorraine now in the Diocese of Trier, was founded on 23 June 720. Its founders were the Frankish widow Bertrada and her son Charibert, with Angloardus as its first head. This encyclopedia entry follows a house that became a Carolingian favourite. Bertrada's granddaughter Bertha married King Pepin. Pepin rebuilt the monastery and showered it with estates in 762. Monks from Meaux under Abbot Assuerus filled its cloister.

The abbey church, dedicated to the Saviour, was finished only under Charlemagne. Pope Leo the Third consecrated it on 26 July 799. Charlemagne and his successors patronized Prüm generously. Several Carolingians took the habit there, among them Lothair the First. He became a monk in 855, and his grave was found again in 1860. Sources from Trier histories to a 1907 chronicle study round out an entry on a monastery woven into Frankish royal history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prusias-ad-hy:
Prusias ad Hypium was a titular see, a bishopric in name, under Claudiopolis in the Roman province of Honoriad. This encyclopedia entry opens with its tangled naming. Prusias the First of Bithynia reigned from 237 to 192 BC. He seized the town of Kieros from the Heracleans, joined it to his kingdom and renamed it for himself. Later copyists confused it with another Prusias, the town of Kios. The entry untangles the two.

Pliny and Ptolemy merely note the place. One sets it below Mount Hypius, the other near the River Hypius. Its known bishops run from George in 325 through Olympus, Dometius, Theophilus, Constantine and Leo. The list ends with Saint Paul, martyred by the iconoclasts in the ninth century. When the see vanished is unknown. French and German travellers and archaeologists, from De Hell to Perrot, supply the entry's sources on this vanished Bithynian town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psalterium:
The Psalterium, the Book of Psalms as copied and used in worship, is the subject here. As a private prayer book it is treated elsewhere; this entry deals with its liturgical life. In church use it held the bulk of the Divine Office. Companion volumes stood beside it: the Lectionary, the Antiphonary with its Responsoriale, and the Hymnary. For centuries the Western Church sang from two Latin versions, both owed to Saint Jerome.

Jerome revised the older Latin text in 383 at the request of Pope Damasus, following the Septuagint closely, and Rome kept that corrected text for many centuries. In 392 he undertook a fresh version, and the entry follows the fortunes of both texts through medieval manuscripts. Studies of famous copies, from the Bosworth Psalter to the Utrecht Psalter, close a piece for readers curious about the book Christians prayed from day by day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ratio-studior:
Ratio Studiorum, short for Ratio atque Institutio Studiorum Societatis Jesu, names the educational system of the Jesuits. This long encyclopedia entry renders the title as the Method and System of the Society of Jesus's Studies. The Society's Constitutions counted teaching among its chief aims. They list catechism for children and the ignorant, schooling for youth in schools and colleges, and lectures on philosophy and theology in universities. Education stood so high that the Society could rightly be called a teaching order.

Even in Saint Ignatius's lifetime colleges opened at Messina, Palermo, Naples, Gandia and Salamanca, with Ingolstadt foremost among the later foundations. The entry then faces objections to the system. Father Martin, the general of the Society, said in 1892 that the Ratio's marks are not to be sought in its subject matter, nor in the order of its studies, but elsewhere. The entry weighs that claim at length.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regino-of-pru:
Regino of Prüm, Benedictine abbot and writer, died at Trier in 915; his birth date is unknown. Later accounts make him a nobleman's son, born at Altrip's stronghold on the Rhine near Speyer. His life is a blank until his election as abbot of Prüm in 892. His election and his writings show a diligent student who had joined the Benedictine Order, probably at Prüm itself.

Prüm had suffered badly from Norman raids, seized and ravaged in 882 and again in 892. After the second devastation Abbot Farabert resigned, and Regino took his place, labouring to restore the house while rival parties fought over Lorraine. In 899 he was driven from office, and his remaining years connect him with Saint Maximin near Trier. The entry rests on his writings and on later histories of the Trier archdiocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rerum-novarum:
Rerum Novarum, the opening words and title of Leo the Thirteenth's encyclical of 15 May 1891, treats the condition of labour. It follows traditional teaching on property rights and duties and on employer and employee, but applies the old doctrines to modern conditions. Opening with the grievances of the working classes, it refutes Socialist theories, defends private ownership, and seeks the remedy in the joint action of Church, State, employer, and employed.

The Church claims its place because the question bears religious and moral aspects. The State holds the right and duty to intervene for justice and social well-being, while employers and workers should form associations in their own interest. On wages the encyclical admits how hard it is to state justice's full demands, yet growing numbers regard its statement as the most fruitful principle of industrial justice ever uttered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-responsorium:
The responsory, or respond, is a series of verses and responses, drawn from Holy Scripture and varying with feast or season. Two kinds exist, those of the Proper of the Mass and those of the Divine Office, differing in history and form. The Mass responsory grows from the psalmodic solo, the oldest Christian chant, apparently derived from the Synagogue: one chanter recited the psalm, and the people answered with a refrain.

That refrain might be the psalm's alternate verses, one verse repeated again and again, or a sentence from elsewhere. Psalm Confitemini Domino, with Quoniam in aeternum misericordia ejus answering every verse, is the typical example, though sometimes the refrain was an Alleluia. In the Office the precentor at last began the respond again, singing to the verse, and the choir closed with a repetition. The first responsory of the year, Aspiciens a longe, carried several verses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rex-gloriose-:
Rex Gloriose Martyrum is the hymn at Lauds in the Common of Martyrs in the Roman Breviary. It holds three strophes of four verses in classical iambic dimeter, rhymed in couplets, with a fourth concluding strophe, a doxology in unrhymed verses varying with the season. Its opening stanza addresses the glorious King of martyrs and crown of confessors, who leads earth-spurners to heaven, and shows the scheme at work.

The hymn's date is uncertain and its author unknown: Mone assigns it to the sixth century, Daniel to the ninth or tenth. The Breviary text revises an older form for classical prosody, changing, for instance, terrena to terrea in the line about spurning earthly things. Manuscript references and readings fill Blume's Analecta Hymnica, and English renderings appear in Donahoe's Early Christian Hymns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rex-sempitern:
Rex Sempiterne Caelitum is the Roman Breviary hymn for Matins on Sundays and weekdays in Paschal Time, from Low Sunday to Ascension Thursday. Cardinal Thomasius prints its primitive form in eight strophes, and Vezzosi's conjecture identifies it with the hymn Caesarius and Aurelianus of Arles name as Rex aeterne domine in their Rules for Virgins. Pimont agrees, and modern hymnologists confirm the identification without hesitation.

The hymn draws special interest from Bede. In De arte metrica he picks it from many Ambrosian pieces to show the difference between classical iambic metre and the accentual rhythms that imitate it. Bede, usually brief in comment, nevertheless refers to it. English readers meet it in Bagshawe's Breviary Hymns and Missal Sequences and Donahoe's Early Christian Hymns, and Moultrie's translation stands in Bute's Roman Breviary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robber-counci:
The Robber Council of Ephesus, or Latrocinium, was the synod of 449 whose acts survive because they were read aloud at Chalcedon two years later. Convoked by Emperor Theodosius II with the pope's agreement, it met on 8 August 449 under Dioscorus, Patriarch of Alexandria. Western bishops had no time to attend, save Julius of an unknown see, a priest, and the deacon Hilarus, who spoke for Pope Leo.

The question was whether Flavian of Constantinople had rightly deposed the archimandrite Eutyches for refusing two natures in Christ. Flavian and his fellow judges were barred from sitting. Dioscorus refused to have Leo's dogmatic letter read, admitted the monk Barsumas by imperial order, and steered the council to vindicate Eutyches. The rest of the acts survive only in a Syriac version by a Monophysite monk, copied in 535.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schola-cantor:
A schola cantorum is a place for teaching and practising church chant, or a body of singers joined to render music in church. In the primitive Church clergy sang, but trained singers were brought in to free priests for their proper work. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces the Roman singing school from legend to firm history.

Pope Hilary, who died in 438, is sometimes credited with the first schola, but Gregory the Great, by John the Deacon's account, set the school on a firm footing and endowed it. Sergius II rebuilt its house in 844, having trained there himself, as had Sergius I, Gregory II, Stephen III, and Paul I. The school sang at most papal functions under a prior or cantor, and its chant shaped Western music.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scriptorium:
A scriptorium is commonly a large room in a monastery set aside for the community's scribes or copyists. Where no special room existed, little cells called carrels were built in the cloister, each scribe with his own window and desk. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia describes the medieval book factory.

Gloucester's cloister, now the cathedral, gives the finest surviving example of carrels. The scriptorium answered to the precentor or his helper the armarius. He supplied desks, ink, parchment, pens, penknives, pumice for smoothing parchment, awls for ruling lines, and reading frames for books to copy. Most supplies were made on site: at Westminster the precentor made ink in the tailor's shop. Rules varied by house, but artificial light was forbidden for copying, and the entry lists the craft's tools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sirmium:
Sirmium, near modern Mitrovitz in Slavonia, claims a church founded by Saint Peter. The Szerém district fell under Kalocsa's archbishop after Hungary's Christianization. In 1228 the archbishop, pleading his diocese's vast extent, asked the Holy See for a new bishopric. In 1229 Gregory IX set up the See of Szerém, covering almost wholly the country on the Sava's right bank.

The see passed under Turkish rule in 1526. From 1537 to 1578 no bishop held it, and after 1624 titular bishops held it. Re-establishment with some territorial changes came in 1709. Clement XIV joined it with Bosnia and Diakovár in 1773, and the entry's sources trace its bishops and fortunes through Farlati's Illyricum Sacrum and Hungarian church histories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-isidore-of:
Isidore of Pelusium, monk and letter writer of the fifth century, fought unworthy clergy with a voluminous pen. Born at Alexandria late in the fourth century, dying not later than 449 or 450, he left family and possessions for a mountain near Pelusium, whose name joined his own. In the Lychnos monastery he grew remarkable for exact observance and austerity, and a passage in his letters suggests he held the abbot's office. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 warns he is sometimes misnamed Isidore of Damietta.

Facundus and Suidas call him priest, though neither names his church, and he may have been only the monastery's priest. His correspondence shows him battling clerics whose elevation to priesthood and diaconate endangered and scandalized the faithful. Laymen, he complained, avoided sacraments to escape contact with such men. The entry preserves a monk whose letters policed a church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-maris-mar:
Maris, Martha, Audifax, and Abachum were martyred at Rome in 270. This entry tells of a Persian noble family who reached Rome under Claudius II, comforted persecuted Christians, and buried the bodies of the slain. That charity exposed them to the judge Muscianus, who failed to make them give up their faith.

Torture followed, then death: Maris and his sons were beheaded thirteen miles from Rome at Nymphae Catabassi and their bodies burned, while Martha was thrown into a well. A Roman lady named Felicitas rescued the half-burned remains and hid them in a catacomb. Their commemoration is kept on 19 January, leaving the twentieth for Sebastian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syntagma-cano:
The Syntagma Canonum is a canonical collection made in 1335 by Blastares, a Greek monk about whom nothing certain is known. He aimed to make canon law handier than Photius's Nomocanon and fuller than earlier epitomes by Stephen, Aristenus, and Arsenius. His matter runs in alphabetical order through twenty-four divisions, one per Greek letter, split into 303 titles.

Titles cover civil law as well as church law, some purely one or the other, with church rules quoted from older collections and civil extracts often copied without naming their source. The book soon gained general clerical use and kept authority under Turkish rule. Servian, Bulgarian, and Russian translations followed, and a Servian abridgment entered King Douchan's code of 1349.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-targum:
Targum is the distinctive name for Aramaic translations or paraphrases of the Old Testament. After the exile, Aramaic gradually replaced decaying Hebrew as everyday speech. By the last century before Christ, Hebrew survived mainly in schools and worship. Since most people no longer knew the sacred tongue, Sabbath readings in Hebrew needed an explanatory oral translation. That need created the Targum.

At first only hard passages were rendered, then in time the whole text. The Mishna lays down how the work was done. For Torah readings only one verse at a time went to the translator, for Prophets three, unless a verse stood alone. Some passages were read but not translated. Over-free or allegorical renderings drew warnings. Synagogue Targum was not to be written down, though private and study copies existed early, including one on Job from Gamaliel's day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tavium:
Tavium, or Tavia, was a titular see in Galatia Prima, suffragan of Ancyra. It was chief city of the Galatian tribe of Trocmi, and its place on trade roads made it an important trading post. Coins of Marcus Aurelius and Elagabalus survive. Its temple held a colossal bronze Jupiter, greatly venerated by Galatians. The site is now generally placed at ruins near Nefez Keui, east of the Halys, in a fertile plain.

The ruins, partly reused to build Yuzgad, keep a theatre and possibly a Jupiter temple, with mostly Byzantine inscriptions. The see appears in the episcopal lists to the thirteenth century as Ancyra's first suffragan. Five bishops are named. Dicasius attended Neocaesarea and Nice, Julian the Robber Synod and Chalcedon, Anastasius Constantinople in 553, Gregory the Council in Trullo, and Philaretus Constantinople in 869.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-te-deum:
The Te Deum is a hymn in rhythmical prose, named from its opening words Te Deum laudamus. Its earliest known title appears in the Rule of St Caesarius for monks, written before 502 when he was Abbot of Lérins. It is also called the Ambrosian Hymn, and the Roman Breviary still styles it the hymn of Ambrose and Augustine at Sunday Matins. Pius X's new Psalterium, printed in 1912, retitled it simply Hymnus Ambrosianus.

Tradition says Ambrose and Augustine composed and sang it alternately on Augustine's baptism night in 387. That tale dates only from the eighth century and is now generally rejected. No early Milan manuscript links the hymn with Milan, and Milan's own eleventh-century breviary gives it no title at all. The entry then traces the hymn's text, use, and many translations, including Luther's German rendering and the English versions based on it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-te-lucis-ante:
Te lucis ante terminum is the hymn at Compline in the Roman Breviary. Ambrose's authorship, defended by Pimont, is rejected by the Benedictine editors and by Biraghi. The hymn appears in an Irish-script hymnary of the eighth or early ninth century. Its classical prosody, with one exception, points to a much earlier origin. In that hymnary it shares Compline with Christe qui lux es et dies.

An earlier arrangement under Caesarius about 502 paired Christe qui lux with Christe precamur adnue at the twelfth hour, alternating through the year. Later the two hymns swapped places by season, with Christe qui lux used in winter and Te lucis in summer and on festivals. Many houses replaced Te lucis with Christe qui lux from Lent to Holy Thursday, as Dominicans still do. Rome assigns Te lucis daily, except from Holy Thursday to the Friday after Easter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-coliseum:
Rome's Flavian Amphitheatre, begun by Vespasian in 72 and dedicated by Titus in 80, is the monument described here. Four stories rise, each in a different order: Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and composite, built of famed travertine. A marshy hollow between Caelian, Oppian, Velian, and Palatine hills, once Nero's Golden House fishpond, gave it ground.

Elliptical in form, 790 feet around, 620 long, 525 wide, and 157 high, it held a wooden arena sanded for gladiators and wild beasts. A low wall and railing shielded crowds, guards patrolled the passage to the podium, and awnings shaded spectators. Later ages quarried it, Christians honoured it, and the entry traces building, games, and ruin with measured detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-martyrs-o:
Nineteen Catholics seized at Gorkum in the Dutch revolt are the martyrs of this entry. By 1572 Luther and Calvin had torn much of Europe from the Church, and Calvinism, after its first synod at Embden in 1571, swept the Netherlands. Sea-beggars took Briel in April 1572, then Dortrecht and Gorkum in June, capturing nine Franciscans in the town.

Two lay brothers joined them, with parish priest Leonardus Vechel of Bois-le-Duc, learned at Louvain. Taken to Briel, they were pressed to deny the Eucharist and papal primacy, refused, and were hanged. Canonization, feast, and relics follow, preserving a story of priests and brothers who died for doctrines their captors hated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-themisonium:
Phrygian titular see Themisonium, suffragan of Laodicea, carries a legend of deliverance in this entry. A city of Phrygia near Pisidia's edge, it sometimes counted as Pisidian. During a Gallic invasion, warned by a dream ascribed to Hercules, Apollo, and Hermes, inhabitants fled with wives and children to a grotto thirty stadia away. They set the three gods' statues at its mouth for protection. 

Coins show Lycabas Sozon as the city's god, and the site may match Kara Eyuk Bazar in Smyrna's vilayet. Le Quien names only one bishop, who truly belongs to Temenothyrae. Thampsiopolis, with bishops Zosimus in 451 and John in 869, proves the same see under another name in lists from the tenth to thirteenth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-of-s:
Monk Theodore of Studium, bold defender of holy images, was the East's last great voice for a free and united Church. Born in 759, he died on the Tryphon peninsula near Akrita on 11 November 826. A high-born, well-schooled man, he counted among his brothers Joseph, Archbishop of Thessalonica. Priest in 781, he took his uncle's place in 794 and pressed for strict keeping of monastic rules.

When Constantine VI put away his wife and wed again, Theodore spoke out, and the emperor sent him to Thessalonica. The emperor's fall brought him home in triumph. In 799 he left Saccudion, threatened by Arabs, and took charge of the Studium house at Constantinople. He gave it a rule that monks across the Byzantine world copied, alive yet on Athos and in Russian houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tradition-and:
Tradition and the Living Magisterium treats how revealed truth reaches the Church apart from Scripture, and who guards it. Tradition, from the Greek paradosis, means both the thing handed down, such as a doctrine, account or custom, and the organ of handing down, the church's preaching. At first only traditions claiming divine origin were in view, then oral tradition distinct from written Scripture.

The question is whether all revealed truth lies in Scripture, or whether Christ gave the apostles divine teachings, by word or inspiration, that they passed on without writing them down. It then treats the living magisterium, the official teaching authority, as the organ that preserves and hands on such truth. Five points follow: its existence and divine founding, its relation to Scripture, how truth lives in the Church's mind, its organization and limits, and the identity of faith through changing formulas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-triduum:
A span of three days chosen for prayer or other devout practice, in private or in public by congregations, parishes, religious communities, seminaries or schools. The three days usually precede a feast, and the feast sets the choice of exercises. Examples are the Holy Week triduum, the Rogation Days, and the litanies before the Ascension.

Church authority also allows tridua for the Holy Trinity, the Holy Eucharist and St. Joseph. The Trinity triduum, instituted by Pius IX on 8 August 1847, may be made at any time of year. The Eucharistic triduum, instituted by Pius X in 1907, falls on the Friday, Saturday and Sunday after Corpus Christi, with sermons and Benediction each day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-viaticum:
Viaticum is the provision for a journey, in Christian usage the sacrament given to the dying for their passage into eternity. The word comes from Latin viaticus, of or for a road. The entry traces it from Greek farewell suppers and travellers' supplies in Plautus and Pliny to its figurative sense as spiritual strength for life's last journey.

In ancient practice almost any sacrament given at death's door, baptism, confirmation, penance, or anointing, could count as viaticum, but the term settled on the Eucharist received by the dying. Later sections set out the rite in detail, the sickroom's table, crucifix, candles, holy water. Cloth, the altar preparations, and the priest's actions, showing how carefully the Church ordered this final communion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-victor-bishop:
Victor of Tunnunum was a North African bishop and zealous defender of the Three Chapters who died about 569, probably confined in a Constantinople monastery. For refusing Justinian's edict of 544 condemning the Chapters, he was imprisoned at Mandrakion monastery, exiled to the Balearic Islands and then to Egypt.

In 564 summoned with five other African bishops before emperor and patriarch and ordered to submit. All remained obstinate and were confined in separate Constantinople monasteries. Victor's fame rests on his chronicle from creation to 566, of which only the portion from 444 survives. It holds great historical value on the Eutychian heresy, the Three Chapters controversy, the Arians. The Vandal invasion, was first edited by Canisius in 1600, and was newly edited by Mommsen in 1894. A continuation to 590 came from John of Biclar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zephyrium:
Zephyrium is the Cilicia Prima titular see, suffragan of Tarsus. Nothing is known of its history, though numerous ancient authors mention the city off Cilicia's coast, between Cilicia Tracheia and Pedias. It had many coins, and here was prepared the best molybdenum, white lead, drawn from the neighbouring mines of Coreyra. Today it is Mersina, chief town of a caza in Adana vilayet, with about 14,000 inhabitants, of whom 3,000 are Greeks, 1,000 Armenians, and 650 Catholics, a population growing quite rapidly.

Le Quien names four bishops of Zephyrium: Aerius, present at Constantinople's council in 381, and Zenobius, a Nestorian, at Constantinople's council in 432 to 434. Hypatius, present at Chalcedon in 451, and Peter, at the Council in Trullo in 692, complete the list. Mersina's Latin parish is run by Capuchins, with Sisters of Saint Joseph of the Apparition, schools for boys and girls, and hospitals.
diary-written-in-the-provincial-lunatic-:
A patient's protest fills Mary Huestis Pengilly's small book, published by the author in 1885. She inscribes it to the Province of New Brunswick and the State of Massachusetts. Pengilly, in her sixty-second year, says a sad experience makes it her duty to lay the inner workings of asylums before the public.

Driven from her St John home by the great fire of 1877, she had found refuge in Massachusetts. The diary opens in December: they will not let her go home, and she writes for fear of forgetting. She tells of being stuffed with food when she had asked only for milk, of threats to lock her in her room, and of Dr Steeves on election day. The book pleads for better methods, for keepers and kept alike.
doe-osti-3001271-ab-initio-equation-of-s:
McKinley Paul, Jadon Despain, Mark Mathis and colleagues at Los Alamos compute vanadium's equation of state from first principles in LA-UR-25-30913, issued 4 November 2025. Hydrodynamic simulations, the kind that model shocks and explosions, are incomplete without an equation of state. It links pressure, volume and temperature. The team built one for the body centred cubic phase of vanadium, aimed at the OpenSesame database used across the complex.

The Helmholtz energy is assembled in three parts. The first is a cold curve, the static lattice energy at absolute zero. The second is a vibrational term, for atoms jiggling in their sites. The third is an electronic term, for electrons promoted by heat. Each comes from quantum mechanical calculation rather than fitted experiment, the meaning of ab initio here. Vibrational effects matter near melting; electronic ones grow at extreme temperatures. The report documents the build and checks.
doe-osti-3014292-baseline-cost-model-for:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/3733, by Gbadebo Oladosu and Yu Ma, dated October 2025, documents the 2025 update of the Baseline Cost Model for Hydropower. New hydropower development in the United States has been slowing, and project costs vary enormously with site conditions. A shared cost model lets analysts compare candidate projects on equal footing before detailed engineering begins.

The updated model draws on data from planned and active projects to fit parametric equations for initial capital cost and for operations and maintenance cost. The documentation presents the data sources, summarizes the project sample, and specifies each cost equation. It is the reference volume for the model that national assessments, including non-powered dam studies, use to turn capacity estimates into dollars.
doe-osti-3020149-expanding-the-boundarie:
A final technical report by Thomas Albrecht of Colorado School of Mines and Florida State University sums up a long-running DOE Heavy Element Chemistry program on the heaviest elements. Grants DE-FG02-13ER16414 and DE-SC0010677 supported work on elements past plutonium, which can only be studied in milligram amounts because they are intensely radioactive. A crystal the size of a sand grain of one berkelium compound decays over a hundred million times per second.

The program published nearly 90 research articles and described several hundred new f-element compounds whose structures were confirmed by crystallography. Highlights include the first single-crystal structure of a berkelium compound. The work also showed californium acting as a second transition point in the actinide series. The report closes with the publication record and the case for the synthesis methods developed along the way.
doe-osti-3021386-lithium-divertor-intera:
University of Missouri final report for DOE award DE-SC0020292, led by Karl D. Hammond with Jennifer Fiegel, covers a September 2019 to August 2025 project on helium and hydrogen inside lithium. Liquid lithium is a candidate coating for the plasma-facing walls of fusion reactors, where helium ash and hydrogen fuel constantly bombard it. Knowing whether those gases dissolve, move, cluster into bubbles, or escape decides whether lithium walls can work.

The project produced the first comprehensive peer-reviewed dataset on helium energetics and migration in lithium. Helium broke the rules seen in other body-centered cubic metals. It prefers interstitial positions over substitutional ones. Its migration barriers run more than ten times lower than in tungsten or iron, suggesting nearly barrier-free motion. The team also built a lithium-helium interatomic potential and began simulations of lithium-tungsten interfaces.
doe-osti-3395071-steady-state-radiolysis:
Idaho National Laboratory experimental report INL/EXP-25-85928, dated July 2025, presents steady-state radiolysis polyhalide accumulation products, in a poster-style layout. The Idaho authors are Alejandro Ramos Ballesteros, Stephanie Castro Baldivieso, Jacy Kathleen Conrad, and Gregory Peter Holmbeck. Ruchi Gakhar and Jon Stoner of Idaho State University join them. The subject is what radiation does to molten salts over long exposure.

Steady-state radiolysis simulates the prolonged irradiation that alloys and molten salts endure inside reactors. The team electron-irradiated molten lithium chloride-potassium chloride and lithium iodide-potassium iodide systems. One run used an 8 kilogray exposure. The team tracked the polyhalide species that accumulate, such as triiodide. They followed them through light absorption at wavelengths including 460 and 780 nanometers. Measurements at 400 and 600 degrees Celsius show how the product mix shifts with temperature.
govdocs-archive_org-the-complete-books-o:
Charles Fort collected facts that science would not touch: rains of frogs, objects falling from clear skies, people vanishing and reappearing. The Complete Books of Charles Fort joins his four works in one volume: The Book of the Damned, New Lands, Lo!, and Wild Talents.

Fort called his outcast facts damned data, and he presented them with wit and open contempt for smug experts. He did not prove a theory; he proved a habit of ignoring. That stance made him the father of fortean inquiry, and his books still supply the field's founding cases and its fighting tone.
historia-calamitatum:
Peter Abelard, the medieval thinker, wrote this account of his own misfortunes. The hosted copy is an English translation by Henry Adams Bellows. Abelard tells his life as a letter of comfort to a friend. A long modern essay on his age opens the volume.

Abelard recalls fame in the schools, love, and ruin. One chapter tells how a council forced him to burn his own book. Abbots and brethren then hounded him, he writes, at every turn. The work is frank, proud, and sad at once. It stands among the first true life stories of the Middle Ages.
history-of-the-britons-historia-brittonu:
Nennius, who calls himself a lowly minister and disciple of Saint Elbotus, compiled the History of the Britons in Latin, here translated by J A Giles. His prologue confesses dull intellect and rude speech, and says he gathered the work from ancestors' traditions, writings, and monuments. It is less a history than a heap of British antiquities.

The text gives the Romans, the Saxon advent under Hengist, who demands Kent as his daughter's price through an interpreter, Saint Patrick, and Vortigern. Arthur appears as a war leader winning twelve battles, the earliest Arthur in any history. Brief and credulous as it is, the Historia Brittonum shaped Geoffrey of Monmouth and every later British chronicle.
how-to-write-a-play-letters-from-augier-:
This slim volume gathers letters on playwriting from famed French dramatists. The Dramatic Museum of Columbia University issued it in 1916. William Gillette contributes a piece dated May 1916. Augier, Banville, Dumas, Labiche, Sardou, and Zola are among the letter writers.

Augier answers with a joke about cannon founding. Take a hole, he writes, and pour bronze around it. Whether comedy needs the same core, he leaves open. His one counsel: soak the fifth act in gentle tears, and salt the other four with wit. Labiche gets a warm study as France's richest comic force. Aspiring playwrights got masters' shop talk, brief and bright.
nasa-tm-19650010883-analysis-of-oxygen-i:
Glenn R Zellars compiled the minutes of a NASA round-robin meeting held at Lewis Research Center on June 4, 1964. The subject was measuring oxygen inside potassium metal. Several labs had each analyzed the same potassium samples, then compared results. Groups taking part included Dow Chemical, General Electric, Oak Ridge, and Pratt and Whitney.

Two methods were in use, mercury amalgamation and vacuum distillation. A round-robin test shows whether different labs get the same answer. If they do not, the method needs work. Minutes like these preserve that check in detail, including who took part and what was discussed at the meeting.
nasa-tm-19680001040-thermal-contact-cond:
Harry L. Atkins, of the Space Thermodynamics Branch at Marshall Space Flight Center, reports contract results on how heat crosses a touching joint in vacuum. Two surfaces bolted together pass heat only at scattered contact points. In space, no air helps, so the joint's conductance must be known.

The work plots conductance against applied pressure for four metals. Stainless steel, magnesium, aluminum, and copper samples all appear. Atkins also studies a kink in the aluminum curves when plotted on log-log paper. Squashed cones, hemispheres, and ellipses reproduce the same kink, suggesting scaled-up models of real contact points.
nasa-tm-19680020447-back-flow-from-jet-p:
Norman T. Grier of Lewis Research Center wrote this 1968 paper, TM X-52468, for a July 1968 symposium on rarefied gas dynamics in Cambridge, Massachusetts. His concern is back flow: exhaust gas from a rocket jet that spreads backward in vacuum. Such gas can coat or disturb the very spacecraft that fired the jet.

Grier estimates the back flow density at points level with the nozzle exit plane. His model treats the young plume as a smooth gas flow, then as free flying particles once the gas grows too thin for collisions. He runs the approximate calculation for helium, nitrogen, and argon jets. The result is a practical way to judge a plume's backward reach.
nasa-tm-19690028938-tensile-properties-o:
Adolph C. Spagnuolo and Phillip L. Stone of Lewis Research Center measured the pull strength of pure tantalum in this September 1969 memo. Samples of varied shapes and from varied heats were pulled at high heat. Tests ran in hard vacuum to shield the metal from air.

Peak stress values spread widely among sample shapes at the top test heat. Samples cut from the same heat, by contrast, matched each other well. Tube samples from one heat sat in a narrow strength band. The spread warns engineers to rate tantalum by heat and form, not by book values alone. Tantalum serves in hot aerospace and nuclear gear.
nasa-tm-19700017669-effect-of-adding-lit:
John L. Anderson and Wendell Mayo of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in May 1970. It studies a fast-spectrum nuclear critical assembly ringed by molybdenum. The team added four materials, one at a time, and watched the effects.

The added materials were lithium nitride, hafnium, tantalum, and tungsten. For each case the report tracks the fuel loading the assembly needed. It also tracks the resulting neutron energy spectrum, the spread of neutron speeds inside. Such tests guide the design of compact reactors, where each added material changes how the core behaves.
nasa-tm-19710019446-quenching-of-vacanci:
H H Grimes and E R Gotsky of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a September 1971 meeting in Mol, Belgium, on defects in refractory metals. It concerns vacancies, the empty spots left when atoms are missing from a crystal. The team quenched molybdenum, freezing vacancies in place for study. Such defects shape radiation damage, diffusion, and strength in hot metals.

Fast quenching into ultrapure liquid helium had worked well for tungsten. That cold bath keeps the metal clean during the plunge. Earlier teams used the method to measure the energy needed to form a vacancy. Grimes and Gotsky applied the approach to molybdenum, a body centered cubic metal. Their work extended a proven technique to a new material.
pax-vobiscum:
Henry Drummond published Pax Vobiscum in 1890, the second of a series that began with "The Greatest Thing in the World." The title takes Christ's words, "Peace be with you." The book opens on his promise of rest to all who labour and are heavy laden.

Drummond complains that popular religion uses great words like rest, joy, and peace without saying how to get them. His chapters, with titles like "Effects Require Causes" and "How Fruits Grow," try to give working answers. He writes as a scientist and a preacher at once, in short, plain chapters.
peeps-at-many-lands-belgium: What is hosted here shows only the front matter of Peeps at Many Lands: Belgium, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names George W. T. Omond as author and Amédée Forestier as illustrator, published in London by Adam and Charles Black in 1909. The contents cover the Flemish plain, Belgian towns and the Ardennes, children and their festivals, Christmas and carnival, the languages spoken, a short history, and the Belgian army and the Congo.
podcast-dannyjones-7RD8FxI0yuM:
Greg Carlwood hosts a long-running conspiracy podcast of his own. On Danny Jones's show the two hosts trade territory. Their subject is the darkest conspiracies in the world, as Carlwood's years of interviews have mapped them. The episode is a tour led by a man who has heard nearly every theory in circulation.

Carlwood ranks and connects the claims, from secret societies to hidden history, with the ease of a guide who knows which doors open and which are painted on. Jones, playing guest in spirit, asks the questions his own listeners would ask. Nothing here is verified, and both men treat the material as a landscape of belief rather than a court record. That is the point of the archive copy: a map of modern conspiracy culture drawn by one of its native guides.
podcast-tuckercarlson-r_eFGCBPuuM:
Saudi investor Prince Alwaleed bin Talal talks with Tucker Carlson about markets, media, and change. Alwaleed built wealth over four decades and once held a large stake in Fox News. He later backed the platform X.

He says he feels hopeful as a new Trump term begins. The pair discuss tariffs, debt, and border policy in broad terms. They also touch on DeepSeek and the race in smart software. The episode offers a rare long interview with a royal investor who has bet on media and tech for years. Few guests bring his mix of royal rank and market skill.
rejected-addresses-or-the-new-theatrum-p:
James Smith and Horace Smith wrote the mock addresses in this book, here in a new edition from John Murray of London in 1879. Lord Byron's letters to Murray from October 1812 are printed at the front in praise. Byron forgave the brothers for their satire and thought their imitations first-rate.

He called the book the best thing of its kind since The Rolliad, and the best imitations ever made of hard originals. The pieces were addresses meant for a theatre opening, cast in the styles of famed poets of the day. Their wit made the brothers' name, and Murray's edition keeps Byron's verdict as its warrant.
specimens-with-memoirs-of-the-less-known: Rev. George Gilfillan edits Volume II of Specimens with Memoirs of the Less-Known British Poets, in a set of three volumes, with a first essay of his own. The contents place this book in the second period, from Spenser to Dryden, continued. William Habington comes first, with a letter to the Honorable W. E. and A Description of Castara. Joseph Hall, Bishop of Norwich, gives two satires, and Richard Lovelace gives songs that name To Althea, from Prison, and A Loose Saraband.
symposium:
Plato's Symposium appears here in Benjamin Jowett's English translation, with Jowett's long introduction at its head. Jowett calls the dialogue the most perfect in form of all Plato's works, a work holding more than any commentator has dreamed of and more, perhaps, than the author himself knew.

He insists that Plato was no mystic. He was no sentimentalist either. Eastern influences never touched him, though they later spread over the Alexandrian world. The Symposium is Greek in style and subject. It has a beauty as of a statue. The dialogue itself reports a drinking party. Socrates and his friends make speeches in praise of love. The playwright Aristophanes is among them. The young Alcibiades comes late. Each speaker tops the last. At the end Socrates reports the teaching of Diotima.
tanakh-jps-1917-nahum:
Nahum is a brief prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, presented in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 English rendering. It is called the burden of Nineveh, the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.

God is shown as slow to anger yet great in power, who will not clear the guilty. His path lies in whirlwind and storm, with clouds as the dust of his feet, and seas dry up at his rebuke. The verse then turns its force on Nineveh, the vast Assyrian capital, and foretells her fall. Readers get fierce, compact poetry of doom for a cruel empire, paired with relief for Judah, long crushed under its yoke.
the-adventures-of-unc-billy-possum: With art by Harrison Cady, The Adventures of Unc' Billy Possum joins Thornton W. Burgess's Bedtime Story-Books. Little, Brown, and Company printed it at Boston in 1920. Chapters listed open with Unc' Billy caught. Reddy Fox then thinks he sees a ghost. Unc' Billy sends for his family next. Bobby Coon enters the wrong house after that. A runaway cabbage stands near the end.
the-camp-fire-girls-on-the-farm-or-bessi:
Jane L. Stewart wrote The Camp Fire Girls on the Farm, or Bessie King's New Chum, volume two of the Camp Fire Girls Series. The Saalfield Publishing Company put it out, with rights dated 1914. A plate shows a girl turning to look up into the evil eyes of Farmer Weeks. Chapter I is called In the City.

Bessie King speaks first, eyes open with admiration and wonder. She asks her chum Zara if she ever dreamed of such a lovely room. The room is in the home of Eleanor Mercer, Guardian of the Manasquan Camp Fire. Both girls are new members of the organization. Bessie has lived all her life in the country, and has known nothing of the luxuries city girls take as a matter of course. In Mercer's house she has found something new to astonish her in almost every room.
the-courage-of-captain-plum:
James Oliver Curwood's The Courage of Captain Plum, dated 1912 with pictures by Frank E. Schoonover, opens in the early summer of 1856. Captain Nathaniel Plum, master and owner of the sloop Typhoon, sits hidden on Beaver Island, smoking an enormous pipe and watching Lake Michigan at sunset.

Plum is eight or nine and twenty, lean and tanned, full of good humor, though his thoughts run on an unpleasant subject. Three miles off, his sloop rides between two islands, and no other sail is in sight. Trees and vines screen his back, so only a boat edging close around the island's end could find him. He knocks out his pipe on his boot-heel and checks a long-barreled revolver, powder and ball, with care.
the-dash-for-khartoum:
G. A. Henty's The Dash for Khartoum, a tale of the Nile Expedition dated 1892, was published in London by Blackie and Son with ten page illustrations by Joseph Nash and John Schonberg. A publisher's list at the front prices his other historical tales, from The Cat of Bubastes to With Clive in India, at five or six shillings each.

In a preface addressed My Dear Lads, Henty says the Nile Expedition is too recent to need historical introduction. His moral concerns two lads brought up as brothers: never act in haste, for repentance follows. A generous impulse can mislead as surely as an evil one, he warns, and hiding trouble from a father or best friend springs from cowardice. Lay the case frankly before your natural advisers, he urges, and bear their displeasure rather than risk lasting injury.
the-love-sonnets-of-a-hoodlum:
Wallace Irwin's The Love Sonnets of a Hoodlum opens with an introduction by Gelett Burgess on the sonnet itself. Burgess calls the sonnet cycle the highest form lyric passion has reached, likening a sonnet to a crystal goblet holding one inspired thought so perfectly that another drop would overflow. He traces the form from Dante, Petrarch, and Camoens through Shakespeare, then to Rossetti, Browning, and Meredith in the Victorian era.

Into that polished line steps slang. Burgess argues that the twentieth century's new influence is the enthusiasm of slang, which has slowly won verbs, nouns, idiom, and diction. His subtitle promises to show how vanity is still on deck and humble virtue gets it in the neck. The introduction presents street language as fresh blood for a conventional, thinning literary style.
the-works-of-francis-beaumont-and-john-f: Volume one of The Works of Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher gives their birth and death dates on its title pages. Beaumont lived from 1584 to 1616, Fletcher from 1579 to 1625. Five plays are named, including The Maid's Tragedy and Philaster. Arnold Glover edited the text. A note begins by describing the first collected edition of 1647. That folio's size and title page are recorded for collation. The plays themselves start beyond the pages shown here.
vera-the-medium:
Richard Harding Davis opens Vera, the Medium with a newspaper making the most of a scoop. The Despatch has spread the name of Stephen Hallowell, his portrait, and a picture of his house across three columns, under the words At Point of Death. Yet the news lands flat in New York. Only city editors, vexed at missing it, and railroad presidents, figuring fast on slips of paper, take much notice.

Davis explains the coolness. In the early eighties Hallowell had been a national figure, a power in western railroads and eastern markets, when a few millions still counted as colossal wealth. His start came from a patent coupling pin devised by his brother-in-law, which he pushed on the new western roads. Twenty years on, greater giants have dwarfed him. The tale turns to the medium Vera, and to what a dying man's fortune draws out of people.
